“No,” she exclaimed suddenly, “I could not have been disappointed with a

“Aha! Strong feeling,” I muttered, thinking to myself censoriously: like
this, at once, all in a moment!

“What did you say?” inquired Miss Haldin innocently.

“Oh, nothing. I beg your pardon. Strong feeling. I am not surprised.”

“And you don’t know how abruptly I behaved to him!” she cried
remorsefully.

I suppose I must have appeared surprised, for, looking at me with a
still more heightened colour, she said she was ashamed to admit that she
had not been sufficiently collected; she had failed to control her words
and actions as the situation demanded. She lost the fortitude worthy of
both the men, the dead and the living; the fortitude which should have
been the note of the meeting of Victor Haldin’s sister with Victor
Haldin’s only known friend. He was looking at her keenly, but said
nothing, and she was--she confessed--painfully affected by his want of
comprehension. All she could say was: “You are Mr. Razumov.” A slight
frown passed over his forehead. After a short, watchful pause, he made a
little bow of assent, and waited.

At the thought that she had before her the man so highly regarded by her
brother, the man who had known his value, spoken to him, understood him,
had listened to his confidences, perhaps had encouraged him--her lips
trembled, her eyes ran full of tears; she put out her hand, made a step
towards him impulsively, saying with an effort to restrain her emotion,
“Can’t you guess who I am?” He did not take the proffered hand. He
even recoiled a pace, and Miss Haldin imagined that he was unpleasantly
affected. Miss Haldin excused him, directing her displeasure at
herself. She had behaved unworthily, like an emotional French girl.
A manifestation of that kind could not be welcomed by a man of stern,
self-contained character.

He must have been stern indeed, or perhaps very timid with women, not
to respond in a more human way to the advances of a girl like Nathalie
Haldin--I thought to myself. Those lofty and solitary existences (remembered the words suddenly) make a young man shy and an old man
savage--often.

“Well,” I encouraged Miss Haldin to proceed.

She was still very dissatisfied with herself.

“I went from bad to worse,” she said, with an air of discouragement very
foreign to her. “I did everything foolish except actually bursting into
tears. I am thankful to say I did not do that. But I was unable to speak
for quite a long time.”

She had stood before him, speechless, swallowing her sobs, and when
she managed at last to utter something, it was only her brother’s
name--“Victor--Victor Haldin!” she gasped out, and again her voice
failed her.

“Of course,” she commented to me, “this distressed him. He was
quite overcome. I have told you my opinion that he is a man of deep
feeling--it is impossible to doubt it. You should have seen his face.

I said. ‘Maybe you have heard of me.’”

“And had he?” I interrupted.

“I don’t know. How could it have been otherwise? And yet.... But what
does that matter? I stood there before him, near enough to be touched

out both his hands then to me, I may say flung them out at me, with
the greatest readiness and warmth, and that I seized and pressed them,
feeling that I was finding again a little of what I thought was lost
to me for ever, with the loss of my brother--some of that hope,
inspiration, and support which I used to get from my dear dead....”

I understood quite well what she meant. We strolled on slowly. refrained from looking at her. And it was as if answering my own
thoughts that I murmured--

“No doubt it was a great friendship--as you say. And that young man
ended by welcoming your name, so to speak, with both hands. After that,
of course, you would understand each other. Yes, you would understand
each other quickly.”

It was a moment before I heard her voice.

“Mr. Razumov seems to be a man of few words. A reserved man--even when

“But you escaped all right?”

She understood me, and smiled too, at my uneasiness.

[Scenario]
A police inspector who has spent years cultivating informers among London's foreign revolutionaries is ordered by a new superior to make an arrest that will please the newspapers. The only man he can plausibly arrest is the informer who has kept him safe.
Setting: Soho and Scotland Yard, London, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
It was in the heavy, rain-washed dusk of a late November evening that I found myself descending the narrow stairs from my room in Scotland Yard, carrying within my breast the weight of an order which, though worded with the bland civility of a new superior, possessed for me the somber finality of a death sentence pronounced by some blind, indifferent fate. The gaslight in the stone corridor flickered as if uncertain of its own reality, casting long, distorted shadows that seemed to mock the very notion of justice I had, until that morning, believed myself to be serving. Assistant Commissioner Voss—a man recently transferred from the Colonial Service, possessing the immaculate boots and untroubled conscience of one who has never had to look into the eyes of a man he is about to betray—had spoken to me across the polished mahogany of his desk with that air of administrative brightness which is perhaps the most terrible form of cruelty, because it is entirely unconscious of itself. He desired an arrest. The newspapers, he observed, had been troublesome of late, suggesting that the authorities were lethargic in the matter of foreign anarchists. He wished to demonstrate energy. He did not much care, I perceived, whether the individual arrested was guilty of any particular crime, so long as the individual was plausibly connected to the circles that met in the back rooms of Soho, and would furnish the morning papers with a photograph of sufficient notoriety to satisfy the public appetite for vigilance. I had listened, I believe, with an expression of attentive composure, while within me there stirred something that was not precisely indignation—for indignation presupposes a surprise I had long ceased to feel—but rather a profound, weary recognition of the manner in which the machinery of institutions grinds forward, indifferent to the flesh it crushes between its wheels.

For three years I had cultivated my network among the exiles, the refugees, the dreamers and the desperate who congregated in the shabby rooms above the eating-houses of that quarter. It is a work of patience, of moral equivocation, of a slow insinuation into confidences that leaves one’s own sense of integrity suspended in a grey twilight where the distinction between fidelity and treachery becomes, by imperceptible degrees, impossible to discern. I had informants, of course. Several. But there was only one upon whom I could rely with that absolute certainty which is the sole luxury permitted to a man in my position, and that was Ladislas Korom. He was a man of some education, a Hungarian by birth, who had fled his native country after the suppression of what the newspapers called a disturbance, but which those who lived through it knew to have been a convulsion that tore apart the very fabric of their lives. He kept a small shop where he repaired watches and clocks—a trade at which he was remarkably skilled, his long, pale fingers possessing a delicacy of touch that seemed almost incongruous with the coarseness of his circumstances. It was through him that I had learned of the meetings, the printing presses, the caches of pamphlets whose incendiary rhetoric was, in truth, more pathetic than dangerous, but which nevertheless constituted, under the letter of the law, grounds for prosecution. He had given me names. He had given me warnings. On two occasions, the information he provided had prevented acts of violence that would have resulted in loss of life, and the knowledge of this—that I had, through him, preserved certain persons from death—had sustained me through the long periods of moral unease that are inseparable from the life of a police inspector who moves among men as a deceiver.

I found him that evening, as I had expected, in the narrow room above his shop, seated at his workbench beneath a single gas-jet that cast a yellowish, unhealthy glow over the disassembled mechanism of a clock. The room smelled of brass filings and strong tobacco. He looked up as I entered, and the expression on his face—that expression of guarded welcome which I had come to know so well, in which trust and suspicion were held in a balance so delicate that a breath might disturb it—produced in me a sensation I can only describe as a kind of nausea of the soul. He offered me a chair. He offered me tobacco. I accepted both, and for some minutes we sat in that silence which, between men who are bound together by a secret, can be more eloquent than speech.

I was reflecting, with a bitterness that surprised even myself, upon the irony of my situation. The very qualities that had made Korom invaluable to me—his reliability, his centrality to the network, the fact that he was known and trusted by figures whose names appeared in police files—were now the very qualities that made him the only candidate for Voss’s demanded arrest. He was plausible. He was foreign. He was connected. And because he was my informant, I knew precisely where he would be at any given hour, and precisely what evidence could be assembled against him, for I had, in a sense, manufactured that evidence myself through the reports I had filed over the years—reports that documented his associations, his presence at meetings, his proximity to declarations that, taken out of the context of the cooperation he was providing, assumed the aspect of conspiracy.

I knocked the ash from my pipe with a deliberation that was, I suppose, a form of procrastination, and I said to him, in that oblique manner which the life compels a man to adopt, that the climate of the city was changing. That there were pressures from above. That certain persons had been named. He watched me with his dark, intelligent eyes—eyes that had seen, I knew, things far worse than anything this city could produce—and I observed in their depths a slow alteration, a darkening, as if a cloud had passed across the light of comprehension within him. He said nothing for a long time. Then he asked me, in that halting English of his, with its curious formalities and its foreign constructions, whether I was advising him to leave.

The word struck me with the force of a physical blow. To leave. The simplicity of it. The reasonableness. And yet I knew, with a certainty that lay upon my chest like a stone, that I could not permit it. If he vanished, the arrest would not be made. Voss would demand an explanation. My network would be exposed. And the consequences would fall, not upon me alone, but upon others—upon informants I had not yet identified, upon operations that were still in their delicate, nascent stages. The machinery required its sacrifice, and Korom was to be that sacrifice, because the machinery could not conceive of any other form of resolution.

I told him that I was not advising him to leave. I told him that I was advising nothing. I told him that the situation was as I had described it, and that he must draw his own conclusions. The words left my mouth with the hollow, ceremonial sound of phrases uttered at a funeral—phrases which signify nothing, which comfort no one, and which serve only to mark the passage of a soul from one state of being to another, irrevocably.

He understood. I saw it in the way his hands, which had been resting on the workbench with the stillness of a man accustomed to precision, became very slightly tremulous, and then were still again, with a stillness that was deliberate, controlled, the stillness of a man who has determined upon a course of action and will not be moved from it by any expression of feeling. He said, at last, that he had always known this moment would come. He said it without bitterness, without reproach, with only a kind of weary fatalism that I found more unbearable than any accusation could have been. He said that he had placed his trust in me, and that the trust had, in its own way, been honoured—for had I not come to warn him? Had I not, by my very presence in that room, acknowledged the debt that existed between us?

I could not look at him. I sat there, in that yellowish light, with the smell of brass and tobacco in my nostrils, and I felt upon me the full, crushing weight of that moral solitude which is the inevitable inheritance of a man who has made of deception a profession and of fidelity an impossibility. I was preserving the safety of the many by sacrificing the one who had made that safety possible. And the one, in his terrible, quiet comprehension, was offering me, in his restraint, an absolution I had not earned and could not accept.

When at last I rose to go, he extended his hand. I took it. The palm was dry, the grip firm, the clasp brief—the handshake of men who part with the understanding that they will not meet again, and who are determined that the parting shall carry no stain of theatrical emotion. I descended the stairs into the street, where the November rain fell in a fine, persistent drizzle that seemed to dissolve the very outlines of the buildings, so that the city appeared as a mirage, a phantom of brick and gaslight, trembling on the edge of dissolution. And I walked back through those streets, beneath the lampposts that haloed in the wet air, carrying with me the knowledge that I had set in motion a process which would end, as such processes always end, in a courtroom, in a sentence, in the slow, grinding obliteration of a life that had been, in its own obscure and melancholy fashion, a life of honour.

Not till that was done did he break the silence, to the effect that most likely Stevie would profit greatly by being sent out of town for a while; only he supposed his wife could not get on without him.

“Could not get on without him!” repeated Mrs Verloc slowly.  “I couldn’t
get on without him if it were for his good!  The idea!  Of course, I can
get on without him.  But there’s nowhere for him to go.”

Mr Verloc got out some brown paper and a ball of string; and meanwhile he
muttered that Michaelis was living in a little cottage in the country.
Michaelis wouldn’t mind giving Stevie a room to sleep in.  There were no
visitors and no talk there.  Michaelis was writing a book.

Mrs Verloc declared her affection for Michaelis; mentioned her abhorrence
of Karl Yundt, “nasty old man”; and of Ossipon she said nothing.  As to
Stevie, he could be no other than very pleased.  Mr Michaelis was always
so nice and kind to him.  He seemed to like the boy.  Well, the boy was a
good boy.

“You too seem to have grown quite fond of him of late,” she added, after
a pause, with her inflexible assurance.

Mr Verloc tying up the cardboard box into a parcel for the post, broke
the string by an injudicious jerk, and muttered several swear words
confidentially to himself.  Then raising his tone to the usual husky
mutter, he announced his willingness to take Stevie into the country
himself, and leave him all safe with Michaelis.

He carried out this scheme on the very next day.  Stevie offered no
objection.  He seemed rather eager, in a bewildered sort of way.  He
turned his candid gaze inquisitively to Mr Verloc’s heavy countenance at
frequent intervals, especially when his sister was not looking at him.
His expression was proud, apprehensive, and concentrated, like that of a
small child entrusted for the first time with a box of matches and the
permission to strike a light.  But Mrs Verloc, gratified by her brother’s
docility, recommended him not to dirty his clothes unduly in the country.
At this Stevie gave his sister, guardian and protector a look, which for
the first time in his life seemed to lack the quality of perfect
childlike trustfulness.  It was haughtily gloomy.  Mrs Verloc smiled.

“Goodness me!  You needn’t be offended.  You know you do get yourself
very untidy when you get a chance, Stevie.”

Mr Verloc was already gone some way down the street.

Thus in consequence of her mother’s heroic proceedings, and of her
brother’s absence on this villegiature, Mrs Verloc found herself oftener
than usual all alone not only in the shop, but in the house.  For Mr
Verloc had to take his walks.  She was alone longer than usual on the day
of the attempted bomb outrage in Greenwich Park, because Mr Verloc went
out very early that morning and did not come back till nearly dusk.  She
did not mind being alone.  She had no desire to go out.  The weather was
too bad, and the shop was cosier than the streets.  Sitting behind the
counter with some sewing, she did not raise her eyes from her work when
Mr Verloc entered in the aggressive clatter of the bell.  She had
recognised his step on the pavement outside.

She did not raise her eyes, but as Mr Verloc, silent, and with his hat
rammed down upon his forehead, made straight for the parlour door, she
said serenely:

“What a wretched day.  You’ve been perhaps to see Stevie?”

“No!  I haven’t,” said Mr Verloc softly, and slammed the glazed parlour
door behind him with unexpected energy.

For some time Mrs Verloc remained quiescent, with her work dropped in her
lap, before she put it away under the counter and got up to light the
gas.  This done, she went into the parlour on her way to the kitchen.  Mr
Verloc would want his tea presently.  Confident of the power of her
charms, Winnie did not expect from her husband in the daily intercourse
of their married life a ceremonious amenity of address and courtliness of
manner; vain and antiquated forms at best, probably never very exactly
observed, discarded nowadays even in the highest spheres, and always
foreign to the standards of her class.  She did not look for courtesies
from him.  But he was a good husband, and she had a loyal respect for his
rights.

Mrs Verloc would have gone through the parlour and on to her domestic
duties in the kitchen with the perfect serenity of a woman sure of the
power of her charms.  But a slight, very slight, and rapid rattling sound
grew upon her hearing.  Bizarre and incomprehensible, it arrested Mrs
Verloc’s attention.  Then as its character became plain to the ear she
stopped short, amazed and concerned.  Striking a match on the box she
held in her hand, she turned on and lighted, above the parlour table, one
of the two gas-burners, which, being defective, first whistled as if
astonished, and then went on purring comfortably like a cat.

Mr Verloc, against his usual practice, had thrown off his overcoat.  It
was lying on the sofa.  His hat, which he must also have thrown off,
rested overturned under the edge of the sofa.  He had dragged a chair in
front of the fireplace, and his feet planted inside the fender, his head
held between his hands, he was hanging low over the glowing grate.  His
teeth rattled with an ungovernable violence, causing his whole enormous
back to tremble at the same rate.  Mrs Verloc was startled.

[Scenario]
An English railway engineer surveying a line through the mountains of a small republic is caught between the government that hired him and a rebel general who controls the passes. Both demand his loyalty, and each promises that the railway will bring civilisation.
Setting: A South American republic, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

The heat of the valley below was an oppression, but up here in the Cordilleras the air possessed a thin, biting quality that seemed to cut at the lungs, and the silence of the peaks lay upon the mind like a weight of ancient stone. I had been gazing through the heavy brass theodolite at the distant smudge of Santa Maria, the capital, a place of white walls and dark treacheries, when the sound of hooves, striking sharp and hard against the loose shale of the path, broke the profound stillness of the heights. It was a sound that carried an abruptness, a hostile interruption, as if the very crust of the earth were being struck by an impatient and remorseless fate. 

I lowered my eye from the instrument. The sun beat down upon the barren slopes with a blinding, cruel persistence. Below me, the proposed line of the railway—a scratch upon the earth that was to bind the restless provinces to the sea—wound its tentative way through a deep gorge. It was a line of progress, of iron and fire, drawn through a land of primeval shadow and sudden blood. And I, an Englishman, a man of precise calculations and honest levels, found myself standing at the very hinge of their violent illusions.

The rider pulled up in a cloud of pale dust. It was not one of President Mendoza’s gaudy lancers, with their cocked hats and absurd silver trappings, but a man in a serape of dark wool, his face shadowed by a broad, weather-beaten hat. He sat his horse with the careless, dangerous ease of one who had spent his life looking over his shoulder at death. He did not dismount. He looked down at me, at my tripod, at the chainmen standing idly by the blackened rocks, with a gaze that was heavy with a profound and sardonic melancholy.

“Senor Engineer,” he said, in a voice that was soft, almost caressing, yet carrying the intimate menace of a drawn blade, “you carry the line of the rails very high. The passes are treacherous. A man might lose his way up here, or find it, depending on the company he keeps.”

I made no answer at once. I was struck by the singular futility of his observation, and by the realization that this must be one of General Vargas’s men—the general who held the eastern valleys in a grip of terror and defiance. I wiped the sweat from my brow with a hand that was not entirely steady, the heat of the sun and the sudden chill of the altitude mingling in my blood.

“I am carrying the line where the surveys dictate,” I said, with a stiff formality that sounded absurd even to my own ears in that vast, empty wilderness. “The gradients will not allow of a lower passage. I have my instructions from the Government.”

“The Government,” he repeated, the words falling from his lips with a slow, deliberate emphasis, as if tasting the bitter irony of the phrase. “A Government of clerks and shopkeepers in Santa Maria, who believe that a strip of iron will bring them civilization. They think it will make them European. They do not understand that civilization is a terrible thing, a fire that burns the hands of those who handle it. General Vargas sends his compliments, Senor. He suggests that the line might run lower, through the valley of Rio Seco, where the people are many and the soil is rich. He promises you his protection, and his friendship. He asks only for your loyalty.”

“My loyalty,” I said, a sudden anger flaring up within me, a reaction against the brooding atmosphere of menace that seemed to emanate from the man, from the very rocks around us, “is not a commodity to be bargained for in the wilderness. I am here to build a railway, not to take part in your political squabbles. I serve the contract I signed.”

The rider smiled, a mere twitch of the lips beneath the dark mustache, a smile that held no mirth, but only a weary knowledge of the world’s futile obstinacy. “A contract, Senor, is a scrap of paper. It is the loyalty of the gun that makes the steel move. The Government in Santa Maria promises you the military, but the military is corrupt, and the soldiers are barefoot. The general promises you the mountains. You will find, perhaps, that the mountains are more enduring.” 

He turned his horse with a sudden pressure of the knee, the animal pivoting on the loose stones with a grace that seemed a mockery of human clumsiness. “Consider the valley of Rio Seco, Senor Engineer. The general will expect your answer by the time the sun touches the highest peak tomorrow.” 

He rode away, leaving me standing by my theodolite, the dust of his passage settling slowly over the brass and the white-painted staves of my surveying party. The silence closed in again, but it was no longer the silence of an empty land; it was a silence heavy with the unspoken, with the obscure and menacing possibilities of a choice I had no wish to make.

I thought of President Mendoza’s minister, a stout man with a diamond pin and a greasy smile, who had pressed a glass of aguardiente upon me in a stifling office in Santa Maria, speaking of the railway as the great artery of progress, of the light of science piercing the dark ignorance of the interior. “You are bringing us life, my dear friend,” he had said, his small eyes glistening with an enthusiasm that did not extend beyond the immediate prospect of personal gain. “You are the apostle of a new era.” 

And now, on the other side of the scale, there was General Vargas, a man I had never seen, but whose name was whispered with a shudder even by my peons, a man who also spoke of progress, but of a different kind—a progress bought with rifles, a civilization that marched hand in hand with rebellion. Both demanded the line; both promised peace; and both, I knew with a cold, sinking certainty, would not hesitate to bury me under the rubble of my own cuttings if I failed to serve their turn.

I walked slowly along the proposed route, the crunch of my boots on the loose shale sounding hollow and insignificant in the vast amphitheater of the mountains. The sun was sinking, and the shadows of the peaks stretched out across the valley like the long, dark fingers of a closing fate. The sky to the east was a deep, bruised purple, against which the jagged outlines of the Cordilleras stood out with a hard, metallic sharpness. 

What was this civilization I was bringing? A means to transport troops more swiftly to their slaughter, or to carry the spoils of a plundered province to the idle tyrants of the coast? I thought of the sleek iron rails, gleaming with a cold, industrial light, laid across a land that still worshipped the ancient, terrible gods of blood and stone. The railway would come, undoubtedly; the line would be built; the engines would puff their smoke into the pure, thin air of the passes. But would it bring peace? Or would it merely hasten the pace of destruction, turning the slow, patient cruelty of the old days into a swift and relentless modern horror?

I stopped by a deep cutting that my men had begun in the side of the hill. The raw earth, red and wet, looked like a wound in the side of the mountain. The peons had left their tools lying about—picks, shovels, a broken wheelbarrow—abandoned in a sudden access of fear or laziness. A faint, acrid smell of powder hung in the air from a recent blast. 

As I stood there, gazing down into the cutting, the full weight of my isolation pressed upon me. I was a foreigner, a man of a different breed, caught in the toils of a land I did not understand, and a people whose passions were as dark and unfathomable as the shadows that were now gathering in the gorges. The Government would not protect me; they were too busy plotting against their own shadows. The rebels would not spare me; they were too intent on their own savage justice. I was a mere instrument, a pawn in a game that was played with human lives and iron rails.

The first stars began to appear in the darkening sky, cold and remote, looking down with an ironic indifference upon the petty strivings of men. The wind rose, sighing through the loose stones with a sound like the murmur of a vast, invisible multitude. I wrapped my coat tighter about me, shivering slightly in the sudden chill. 

Tomorrow I would have to give an answer. I would have to choose between the valley of Rio Seco and the high pass, between General Vargas and President Mendoza, between two lies that both called themselves civilization. I looked again at the raw wound in the hillside, at the scattered tools, the symbols of my futile endeavor. The railway would not bring peace to this tortured land. It would only bring a swifter passage to death. And I, who had come here with such high hopes, such a clear conscience, would be the one to lay the iron track of their ruin.

I turned my back on the cutting and began the long, slow descent to the camp. The darkness closed in behind me, swallowing the mountains, the gorge, and the ghostly line of my survey, leaving nothing but the cold, pitiless stars and the heavy, brooding silence of the Cordilleras.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.

how little I do claim, but I will go that length. You have done so much for him, you are so fond of him; your whole life, Mrs. Bounderby, expresses such charming self-forgetfulness on his account—pardon me again—I am running wide of the subject. I am interested in him for his own sake.’

She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in
a hurry and gone away.  He had turned the course of what he said at that
instant, and she remained.

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ he resumed, in a lighter manner, and yet with a show of
effort in assuming it, which was even more expressive than the manner he
dismissed; ‘it is no irrevocable offence in a young fellow of your
brother’s years, if he is heedless, inconsiderate, and expensive—a little
dissipated, in the common phrase.  Is he?’

‘Yes.’

‘Allow me to be frank.  Do you think he games at all?’

‘I think he makes bets.’  Mr. Harthouse waiting, as if that were not her
whole answer, she added, ‘I know he does.’

‘Of course he loses?’

‘Yes.’

‘Everybody does lose who bets.  May I hint at the probability of your
sometimes supplying him with money for these purposes?’

She sat, looking down; but, at this question, raised her eyes searchingly
and a little resentfully.

‘Acquit me of impertinent curiosity, my dear Mrs. Bounderby.  I think Tom
may be gradually falling into trouble, and I wish to stretch out a
helping hand to him from the depths of my wicked experience.—Shall I say
again, for his sake?  Is that necessary?’

She seemed to try to answer, but nothing came of it.

‘Candidly to confess everything that has occurred to me,’ said James
Harthouse, again gliding with the same appearance of effort into his more
airy manner; ‘I will confide to you my doubt whether he has had many
advantages.  Whether—forgive my plainness—whether any great amount of
confidence is likely to have been established between himself and his
most worthy father.’

‘I do not,’ said Louisa, flushing with her own great remembrance in that
wise, ‘think it likely.’

‘Or, between himself, and—I may trust to your perfect understanding of my
meaning, I am sure—and his highly esteemed brother-in-law.’

She flushed deeper and deeper, and was burning red when she replied in a
fainter voice, ‘I do not think that likely, either.’

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ said Harthouse, after a short silence, ‘may there be a
better confidence between yourself and me?  Tom has borrowed a
considerable sum of you?’

‘You will understand, Mr. Harthouse,’ she returned, after some
indecision: she had been more or less uncertain, and troubled throughout
the conversation, and yet had in the main preserved her self-contained
manner; ‘you will understand that if I tell you what you press to know,
it is not by way of complaint or regret.  I would never complain of
anything, and what I have done I do not in the least regret.’

‘So spirited, too!’ thought James Harthouse.

‘When I married, I found that my brother was even at that time heavily in
debt.  Heavily for him, I mean.  Heavily enough to oblige me to sell some
trinkets.  They were no sacrifice.  I sold them very willingly.  I
attached no value to them.  They were quite worthless to me.’

Either she saw in his face that he knew, or she only feared in her
conscience that he knew, that she spoke of some of her husband’s gifts.
She stopped, and reddened again.  If he had not known it before, he would
have known it then, though he had been a much duller man than he was.

‘Since then, I have given my brother, at various times, what money I
could spare: in short, what money I have had.  Confiding in you at all,
on the faith of the interest you profess for him, I will not do so by
halves.  Since you have been in the habit of visiting here, he has wanted
in one sum as much as a hundred pounds.  I have not been able to give it
to him.  I have felt uneasy for the consequences of his being so
involved, but I have kept these secrets until now, when I trust them to
your honour.  I have held no confidence with any one, because—you
anticipated my reason just now.’  She abruptly broke off.

He was a ready man, and he saw, and seized, an opportunity here of
presenting her own image to her, slightly disguised as her brother.

‘Mrs. Bounderby, though a graceless person, of the world worldly, I feel
the utmost interest, I assure you, in what you tell me.  I cannot
possibly be hard upon your brother.  I understand and share the wise
consideration with which you regard his errors.  With all possible
respect both for Mr. Gradgrind and for Mr. Bounderby, I think I perceive
that he has not been fortunate in his training.  Bred at a disadvantage
towards the society in which he has his part to play, he rushes into
these extremes for himself, from opposite extremes that have long been
forced—with the very best intentions we have no doubt—upon him.  Mr.
Bounderby’s fine bluff English independence, though a most charming
characteristic, does not—as we have agreed—invite confidence.  If I might
venture to remark that it is the least in the world deficient in that
delicacy to which a youth mistaken, a character misconceived, and
abilities misdirected, would turn for relief and guidance, I should
express what it presents to my own view.’

As she sat looking straight before her, across the changing lights upon

‘All allowance,’ he continued, ‘must be made.  I have one great fault to

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
If any honest traveller, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and thirty-something, had found himself wandering down the cramped and crooked thoroughfare of Grimbal's Passage, near unto Holborn, he might have supposed that the narrow street had been built by some misanthropic architect expressly for the purpose of being avoided by the cheerful sun. It was a place where the very houses seemed to have stooped their shoulders against the weather, leaning across the slippery cobblestones to whisper miserable secrets into one another's damp and crumbling ears.

At the very bottom of this gloomy ravine, pressed into the darkest corner like a spider hiding in the recesses of a cracked teacup, stood the shut-up premises of Mr. Ebenezer Grittle. The shutters were of the heaviest, knottiest, and most uncompromising oak, bolted and barred with a severity that suggested Mr. Grittle expected the entire population of London to make a concerted assault upon his front window before teatime. Above this fortress, in a set of chambers that smelt pervasively of cold dust, stale tallow, and the slow decay of forgotten things, dwelt the old man himself; and it was to this uninviting sanctuary that Master Timothy Trundle, a small boy of exactly ten years of age, was abruptly and irrevocably dispatched.

Timothy had known neither father nor mother for very long, they having departed this mortal coil with a haste that left him chiefly in the care of parish beadle, and ultimately, by some obscure genealogical twist, at the mercy of his maternal grandfather. Timothy was a small child, possessing a pair of extraordinarily large, wistful eyes, which seemed perpetually engaged in trying to understand a world that went to a great deal of trouble to be misunderstood. He stood upon the slimy threshold of Grimbal's Passage, clutching a single and somewhat battered leather trunk, and looking up at the iron-knocker upon Mr. Grittle's door as if it were the jawbone of some fabulous beast prepared to swallow him whole.

The door was opened eventually, and with a prodigious grinding of rusty hinges, by Mr. Grittle himself. He was a man of a very shrivelled and dusty aspect, possessing a nose that seemed to have been sharpened expressly for the purpose of poking itself into other people's affairs, and a pair of small, red-rimmed eyes that twinkled with a hard, metallic distrust, like the reflection of a farthing candle in a brass saucepan. He wore a waistcoat that had once been of a flowery pattern, but which age and usage had reduced to a dim and ghostly landscape, and he carried his chin so tucked into his cravat that he appeared to be perpetually attempting to swallow his own collar.

"Umph!" said Mr. Grittle, surveying the boy as if he were an unwanted parcel of damaged goods. "So you are the boy."

"Yes, Grandfather," replied Timothy, trembling slightly.

"Don't 'Grandfather' me, till you've earned the right to the word," snapped the old man, with a suspicious hitch of his sharp shoulders. "Blood is thin, boy, very thin; and water is thicker, and a good sight cheaper. Come in, come in! Don't let the damp air get into the house; I can't afford to heat the atmosphere of all Holborn!"

Timothy stepped into the gloomy hall, and the door clapped-to behind him with a sound of final and dismal conviction. The interior of the dwelling exactly matched its outward promise. It was a cavern of shadows, crowded with the ghosts of departed commerce. Old garments dangled from pegs like the flayed skins of ancient martyrs, and stacks of obsolete brass instruments seemed to have grown out of the wainscoting, spreading their tarnished mouths in silent protest against the neglect of their owner.

"Mind your step, mind your step!" cried Mr. Grittle, leading the way up a staircase that groaned at every footfall as if lamenting the burden of humanity it was forced to bear. "I have no money to repair broken shins, and less patience to hear them whined about. You'll sleep in the back room. You'll earn your keep, or out you go upon the stones, where the parish may have the hauling of you!"

"I will work very hard, sir," said Timothy, earnestly.

"Work, umph! Everybody says they will work," muttered the old man, unlocking a door at the top of the stairs and revealing a sitting-room that was almost as forbidding as the shop below. "Talk is the cheapest thing in London, cheaper even than the lies that are told in the pawnbrokers' shops. Sit down, and don't fidget! Fidgeting wears out the furniture, and furniture costs money."

The boy sat down upon the very edge of a horsehair chair, which crackled under him with a threatening and reproachful sound. He cast his large eyes about the room, and observed, pinned above the mantelpiece, a small, faded silhouette of a young woman, drawn in profile. The nose was rather sharp, and the chin rather combative, but there was a certain softness about the setting of the head which somehow contradicted the severity of the features.

Mr. Grittle, catching the direction of the boy's gaze, snorted violently, marched to the mantelpiece, and turned the silhouette with its face to the wall. "Eyes off!" he barked. "That's no concern of yours! The dead are dead, and the living must look to their own pennies. Now, you are to fetch the water, sweep the floors, black the grate, and mind that you never, upon any pretext whatsoever, set foot in the shop below. Do you hear me?"

"Yes, sir. But, if you please—"

"But me no buts, boy! The shop is locked. The shop stays locked. The pledges are mine, bought and paid for, and I keep what is mine!" cried the old man, working himself into a sudden lather of indignation. "What is pledged to Grittle, stays with Grittle! Thirty years I've kept 'em, and thirty years more I'll keep 'em, if I live to be a hundred, which I don't intend to, just to spite the doctors!"

This was a puzzle that sat very heavily upon Timothy's young mind. He knew, from the general gossip of the parish authorities, that his grandfather had been a pawnbroker of some repute, but that he had shut up his business three decades ago, retaining every single article that had been left in pledge. The lower shop was a great, shuttered tomb of unredeemed humanity, filled with the sad belongings of people who had long since vanished into the poorer gutters of London.

In the days that followed, Timothy applied himself to his tasks with a desperate diligence. He blacked the grate until it shone like a mirror reflecting a coal-mine; he swept the floors until the very broom seemed to have acquired a nervous exhaustion; and he fetched the water from the street pump with a regularity that would have done credit to a mechanical automaton. All the while, Mr. Grittle sat in his armchair, watching the boy with his hard, red eyes, and demanding to know how much the coals cost, and why the candle was burning so high, and whether Timothy thought he was made of money.

"Everything costs, boy, everything!" the old man would croak, rubbing his knobby hands together. "Affection costs! Trust costs! And when you give 'em out, they never come back. They go into the dark, like the things in my shop, and they are never redeemed!"

But Timothy, being a boy of a persevering and affectionate nature, refused to be chilled by this perpetual frost. He began to leave little wildflowers—he had found a few stubborn dandelions pushing through the stones of a nearby courtyard—upon the old man's breakfast tray. He mended Mr. Grittle's slippers with a needle and thread borrowed from a neighboring charwoman, and he learned to anticipate the old man's querulous demands before they had fully formed upon his peevish lips.

One evening, when the rain was beating against the windows with a melancholy rattle, Timothy found his grandfather sitting before a meagre fire, holding the faded silhouette in his hands. The old man's face was not hard and metallic now, but deeply lined and unutterably weary. He looked up, and seeing the boy standing in the doorway, did not immediately bid him begone.

"She was my daughter," said Mr. Grittle, in a voice that seemed to have lost its accustomed sharpness, and to have crumbled into dust at the corners. "Your mother, boy. She ran away from me. Ran away, and married a feckless, penniless scamp of a Trundle, and left me alone with my ledgers and my pledges."

Timothy did not speak, but drew nearer, laying a small, grubby hand upon the old man's sleeve.

"I shut up the shop," Mr. Grittle continued, glaring into the fire as if it were the gateway to a haunted past. "I shut it up, the very week she left. I wouldn't redeem anything. I wouldn't let anything go. Every ring, and every watch, and every poor shawl that was left in my keeping, I kept! I clutched 'em to me! They were pledges of human trust, and I'd been robbed of mine, so I robbed the world of its belongings! I would hold onto what was left, and let the world come begging to my door, as I had to beg for her to come back!"

He paused, and his breath caught in his throat. "She never came back," he whispered. "Not till she was dead, and they brought her boy to my door."

Timothy squeezed the thin arm. "I am here, Grandfather," he said, softly.

The old man looked down at the boy, and for the first time, something in the hard, red eyes seemed to melt, like a long-frozen icicle dropping into a puddle of warm rain. If any honest traveller, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and thirty-something, had found himself wandering down the cramped and crooked thoroughfare of Grimbal's Passage, near unto Holborn, he might have supposed that the narrow street had been built by some misanthropic architect expressly for the purpose of being avoided by the cheerful sun. It was a place where the very houses seemed to have stooped their shoulders against the weather, leaning across the slippery cobblestones to whisper miserable secrets into one another's damp and crumbling ears.

At the very bottom of this gloomy ravine, pressed into the darkest corner like a spider hiding in the recesses of a cracked teacup, stood the shut-up premises of Mr. Ebenezer Grittle. The shutters were of the heaviest, knottiest, and most uncompromising oak, bolted and barred with a severity that suggested Mr. Grittle expected the entire population of London to make a concerted assault upon his front window before teatime. Above this fortress, in a set of chambers that smelt pervasively of cold dust, stale tallow, and the slow decay of forgotten things, dwelt the old man himself; and it was to this uninviting sanctuary that Master Timothy Trundle, a small boy of exactly ten years of age, was abruptly and irrevocably dispatched.

Timothy had known neither father nor mother for very long, they having departed this mortal coil with a haste that left him chiefly in the care of parish beadle, and ultimately, by some obscure genealogical twist, at the mercy of his maternal grandfather. Timothy was a small child, possessing a pair of extraordinarily large, wistful eyes, which seemed perpetually engaged in trying to understand a world that went to a great deal of trouble to be misunderstood. He stood upon the slimy threshold of Grimbal's Passage, clutching a single and somewhat battered leather trunk, and looking up at the iron-knocker upon Mr. Grittle's door as if it were the jawbone of some fabulous beast prepared to swallow him whole.

The door was opened eventually, and with a prodigious grinding of rusty hinges, by Mr. Grittle himself. He was a man of a very shrivelled and dusty aspect, possessing a nose that seemed to have been sharpened expressly for the purpose of poking itself into other people's affairs, and a pair of small, red-rimmed eyes that twinkled with a hard, metallic distrust, like the reflection of a farthing candle in a brass saucepan. He wore a waistcoat that had once been of a flowery pattern, but which age and usage had reduced to a dim and ghostly landscape, and he carried his chin so tucked into his cravat that he appeared to be perpetually attempting to swallow his own collar.

"Umph!" said Mr. Grittle, surveying the boy as if he were an unwanted parcel of damaged goods. "So you are the boy."

"Yes, Grandfather," replied Timothy, trembling slightly.

"Don't 'Grandfather' me, till you've earned the right to the word," snapped the old man, with a suspicious hitch of his sharp shoulders. "Blood is thin, boy, very thin; and water is thicker, and a good sight cheaper. Come in, come in! Don't let the damp air get into the house; I can't afford to heat the atmosphere of all Holborn!"

Timothy stepped into the gloomy hall, and the door clapped-to behind him with a sound of final and dismal conviction. The interior of the dwelling exactly matched its outward promise. It was a cavern of shadows, crowded with the ghosts of departed commerce. Old garments dangled from pegs like the flayed skins of ancient martyrs, and stacks of obsolete brass instruments seemed to have grown out of the wainscoting, spreading their tarnished mouths in silent protest against the neglect of their owner.

"Mind your step, mind your step!" cried Mr. Grittle, leading the way up a staircase that groaned at every footfall as if lamenting the burden of humanity it was forced to bear. "I have no money to repair broken shins, and less patience to hear them whined about. You'll sleep in the back room. You'll earn your keep, or out you go upon the stones, where the parish may have the hauling of you!"

"I will work very hard, sir," said Timothy, earnestly.

"Work, umph! Everybody says they will work," muttered the old man, unlocking a door at the top of the stairs and revealing a sitting-room that was almost as forbidding as the shop below. "Talk is the cheapest thing in London, cheaper even than the lies that are told in the pawnbrokers' shops. Sit down, and don't fidget! Fidgeting wears out the furniture, and furniture costs money."

The boy sat down upon the very edge of a horsehair chair, which crackled under him with a threatening and reproachful sound. He cast his large eyes about the room, and observed, pinned above the mantelpiece, a small, faded silhouette of a young woman, drawn in profile. The nose was rather sharp, and the chin rather combative, but there was a certain softness about the setting of the head which somehow contradicted the severity of the features.

Mr. Grittle, catching the direction of the boy's gaze, snorted violently, marched to the mantelpiece, and turned the silhouette with its face to the wall. "Eyes off!" he barked. "That's no concern of yours! The dead are dead, and the living must look to their own pennies. Now, you are to fetch the water, sweep the floors, black the grate, and mind that you never, upon any pretext whatsoever, set foot in the shop below. Do you hear me?"

"Yes, sir. But, if you please—"

"But me no buts, boy! The shop is locked. The shop stays locked. The pledges are mine, bought and paid for, and I keep what is mine!" cried the old man, working himself into a sudden lather of indignation. "What is pledged to Grittle, stays with Grittle! Thirty years I've kept 'em, and thirty years more I'll keep 'em, if I live to be a hundred, which I don't intend to, just to spite the doctors!"

This was a puzzle that sat very heavily upon Timothy's young mind. He knew, from the general gossip of the parish authorities, that his grandfather had been a pawnbroker of some repute, but that he had shut up his business three decades ago, retaining every single article that had been left in pledge. The lower shop was a great, shuttered tomb of unredeemed humanity, filled with the sad belongings of people who had long since vanished into the poorer gutters of London.

In the days that followed, Timothy applied himself to his tasks with a desperate diligence. He blacked the grate until it shone like a mirror reflecting a coal-mine; he swept the floors until the very broom seemed to have acquired a nervous exhaustion; and he fetched the water from the street pump with a regularity that would have done credit to a mechanical automaton. All the while, Mr. Grittle sat in his armchair, watching the boy with his hard, red eyes, and demanding to know how much the coals cost, and why the candle was burning so high, and whether Timothy thought he was made of money.

"Everything costs, boy, everything!" the old man would croak, rubbing his knobby hands together. "Affection costs! Trust costs! And when you give 'em out, they never come back. They go into the dark, like the things in my shop, and they are never redeemed!"

But Timothy, being a boy of a persevering and affectionate nature, refused to be chilled by this perpetual frost. He began to leave little wildflowers—he had found a few stubborn dandelions pushing through the stones of a nearby courtyard—upon the old man's breakfast tray. He mended Mr. Grittle's slippers with a needle and thread borrowed from a neighboring charwoman, and he learned to anticipate the old man's querulous demands before they had fully formed upon his peevish lips.

One evening, when the rain was beating against the windows with a melancholy rattle, Timothy found his grandfather sitting before a meagre fire, holding the faded silhouette in his hands. The old man's face was not hard and metallic now, but deeply lined and unutterably weary. He looked up, and seeing the boy standing in the doorway, did not immediately bid him begone.

"She was my daughter," said Mr. Grittle, in a voice that seemed to have lost its accustomed sharpness, and to have crumbled into dust at the corners. "Your mother, boy. She ran away from me. Ran away, and married a feckless, penniless scamp of a Trundle, and left me alone with my ledgers and my pledges."

Timothy did not speak, but drew nearer, laying a small, grubby hand upon the old man's sleeve.

"I shut up the shop," Mr. Grittle continued, glaring into the fire as if it were the gateway to a haunted past. "I shut it up, the very week she left. I wouldn't redeem anything. I wouldn't let anything go. Every ring, and every watch, and every poor shawl that was left in my keeping, I kept! I clutched 'em to me! They were pledges of human trust, and I'd been robbed of mine, so I robbed the world of its belongings! I would hold onto what was left, and let the world come begging to my door, as I had to beg for her to come back!"

He paused, and his breath caught in his throat. "She never came back," he whispered. "Not till she was dead, and they brought her boy to my door."

Timothy squeezed the thin arm. "I am here, Grandfather," he said, softly.

The old man looked down at the boy, and for the first time, something in the hard, red eyes seemed to melt, like a long-frozen icicle dropping into a puddle of warm rain. "You are here," he repeated, slowly. "Umph! And I suppose you'll want your supper. It's in the cupboard. Don't waste the bread, boy!"

But Timothy, knowing the old man's peculiar grammar of affection, recognized the tender concession in the gruff command, and went to fetch his supper, feeling that the great, shuttered tomb below was, perhaps, not quite so hopeless a place as it had been the day before.

An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
It was upon a certain dreary afternoon in November—when the fog, that great unwashed linen of the London sky, hung so low over the pavement of Cursitor Street that the very chimney-pots seemed to be coughing up soot into the eyes of Providence—that Master Timothy Twigg, aged ten years and three months, was deposited by a hackney-coachman at the door of number fourteen, Thessaly Court. He was a small, sharp-featured boy, with a countenance that seemed already to have taken a premature lease upon the cares of manhood, and he carried a bundle wrapped in a red handkerchief which contained the entire worldly wealth of his future.

The house before which he stood was a narrow, high-shouldered building, wedged between a print-shop and a chandler’s like a bone stuck in the throat of the street. Its upper stories bulged forward with a singular malignity, as if they were frowning at the pedestrians below; and its lower story was a shop of such profound darkness and shuttered seclusion that it might have been the tomb of commerce itself. Over the door, in faded gold letters that flaked away like dried skin, were the words: A. MUMBLE, PAWNBROKER. And in the window, behind iron bars that looked like the teeth of a trap, there hung a placard, written in a hand so crabbed and angular it resembled a nest of spiders: *Closed for Business. Closed for Trust. Closed for Good.*

Timothy pulled the bell—a bell that gave forth a sound not of ringing, but of a feeble, asthmatic rattle—and waited. The door was opened at last by a man who seemed to have been constructed entirely out of the dust and cobwebs of the shop he inhabited. This was Mr. Obadiah Mumble, the grandfather, the retired trader in pledges, the man who trusted nobody, and who was at present regarding his grandson with an expression of such intense and calculating suspicion that Timothy felt as though he were being appraised not as a relation, but as a doubtful article of wearing apparel left in pawn.

‘You are late,’ said Mr. Mumble. His voice was dry, like the rustling of old banknotes.

‘The coachman said the fog—’ Timothy began, with the timid hesitation of a small creature in the presence of a large predator.

‘The coachman is a liar, as all men are liars,’ retorted the old man, seizing the boy by the collar and drawing him into the gloom. ‘The fog is an excuse; the fog is a convenience; the fog is the cloak under which the idle steal the hours. Come in, and wipe your feet, and do not touch the walls, for the walls have ears and the ears have grudges.’

The interior of number fourteen was a labyrinth of shadows. The shop, which had not seen a customer in thirty years, was a forest of dusty articles. Here lay a silver teapot, tarnished to the colour of a storm cloud; there stood a fiddle, mute and stringless, which seemed to be weeping silently for the music it had lost; and everywhere, on shelves that reached to the ceiling, were bundles, and boxes, and parcels, and trinkets, and watches, and rings, all of them sleeping under a thick grey counterpane of dust. It was a museum of broken promises, a warehouse of departed joys. The air was heavy with the smell of mildew and stagnant time.

‘Thirty years,’ said Mr. Mumble, observing the direction of the boy’s gaze. He did not say this as a statement of fact, but as a challenge, a riddle, a thorn in the side of the universe. ‘Thirty years I have kept them. Not sold. Not returned. Kept. Why?’

Timothy, who had been taught by his late mother to be seen and not heard, and preferably neither, merely stared.

‘Because!’ shouted the old man, startling a pigeon that had somehow found its way into the rafters. ‘Because the world is a thief, and the people in it are the fences! They come with their trinkets and their tears. “Oh, Mr. Mumble, keep it safe, Mr. Mumble, I shall return on Tuesday!” Tuesday comes, and Tuesday goes, and the Tuesday after that, and they are gone to the devil, and I am left with the corpse of their collateral! I keep them as a monument to their perfidy! I keep them as a lesson to you, boy! Trust no one! Not even your own grandfather! Especially not your own grandfather!’

He led the boy up a staircase that creaked and groaned with every step, like a ship in a gale, to the living quarters above. The room was as spare and hard as the man himself. There was a table, two chairs, a cold fireplace, and a clock that ticked with a slow, heavy deliberation, measuring out the seconds of a life lived in solitude.

‘You will sleep there,’ said Mr. Mumble, pointing to a cupboard under the stairs. ‘You will eat what I eat, which is bread and broth, and you will work for your keep. I am not a charity, boy. I am a fortress, and you are the garrison.’

And so began the strange, silent siege of Timothy Twigg’s heart against the cold stone of Mr. Mumble’s breast. The days passed in a grey routine. Timothy swept the floors of the shuttered shop, removing the dust only to have it settle again like a curse. He polished the brass of the gas-lamps that were never lit. He read the labels of the pledges—*A Wedding Ring, 1804; A Soldier’s Medal, 1815; A Child’s Locket, date unknown*—and wondered at the stories that lay behind them, stories that the old man refused to tell.

Yet, as the winter deepened and the frost etched ferns upon the windowpanes, a subtle change began to occur, as imperceptible as the turning of the tide. It happened one evening when Timothy, in a fit of childish boldness, had rescued a small wooden bird from a high shelf where it had been gathering dust for decades. He cleaned it carefully and placed it upon the mantelpiece.

Mr. Mumble entered the room, stopped, and stared at the bird. His hand trembled, just for an instant.

‘That was a pledge,’ he whispered. ‘A gentleman brought it. A man of feeling. He pawned it to buy medicine for his wife. He never came back.’

‘Did the wife get better?’ asked Timothy.

‘The wife died,’ said Mr. Mumble, and his voice cracked, just a little, like the varnish on an old painting. ‘He kept the bird. I kept the memory. It is the only currency that does not devalue, boy.’

From that moment, the ice did not break, but it began to melt. Mr. Mumble began to talk—not of trust, which he still despised, but of the things themselves. He showed Timothy the watch that had stopped at midnight, the ring that had been worn smooth by a nervous thumb, the letters that were never sent. He explained that he had not kept them out of greed, but out of a strange, miserly love for the humanity that had abandoned them. He could not bear to let the objects go, because to let them go would be to admit that the people who left them were truly gone.

One night, as the wind howled around the chimneys of Thessaly Court, Mr. Mumble sat by the fire, and Timothy sat at his feet.

‘You are a sharp boy,’ said the old man, looking into the flames. ‘Sharper than the fog. Sharper than the lies.’

‘I try to be good, Grandfather,’ said Timothy.

‘Goodness is a luxury,’ muttered Mr. Mumble, though he placed a gnarled hand upon the boy’s shoulder. ‘But perhaps... perhaps it is a luxury I can afford to keep. Like the bird. Like the watch.’

He looked around the room, at the shuttered shop below, at the dust and the silence.

‘Thirty years I have been alone,’ he said. ‘Thirty years of guarding the ghosts. I think... I think the garrison has grown by one. Do not make me regret it, Timothy. Do not make me put you in pawn.’

‘I shall never leave,’ said Timothy.

‘We shall see,’ said Mr. Mumble. ‘We shall see.’

And outside, the fog rolled on over Holborn, covering the city in its grey, mysterious shroud, while inside number fourteen, the clock ticked on, not measuring the passing of time now, but the beating of two hearts, bound together in the dusty, silent shop of a man who had finally found something worth keeping.

‘Goodness is a luxury,’ muttered Mr. Mumble, though he placed a gnarled hand upon the boy’s shoulder. ‘But perhaps... perhaps it is a luxury I can afford to keep. Like the bird. Like the watch.’

He looked around the room, at the shuttered shop below, at the dust and the silence.

‘Thirty years I have been alone,’ he said. ‘Thirty years of guarding the ghosts. I think... I think the garrison has grown by one. Do not make me regret it, Timothy. Do not make me put you in pawn.’

‘I shall never leave,’ said Timothy.

‘We shall see,’ said Mr. Mumble. ‘We shall see.’

And outside, the fog rolled on over Holborn, covering the city in its grey, mysterious shroud, while inside number fourteen, the clock ticked on, not measuring the passing of time now, but the beating of two hearts, bound together in the dusty, silent shop of a man who had finally found something worth keeping.

[Scenario]
A police inspector who has spent years cultivating informers among London's foreign revolutionaries is ordered by a new superior to make an arrest that will please the newspapers. The only man he can plausibly arrest is the informer who has kept him safe.
Setting: Soho and Scotland Yard, London, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The rain in London did not fall; it seeped, a persistent, grey moisture that found its way into the bones of the city and the souls of the men who moved through it. Inspector Arthur Vane stood by the window of his office in the basement of the old building on Great Pulteney Street, watching the wet cobblestones of the street below glisten like the scales of some dead, silver fish. The gaslight from the streetlamp across the way cast a sickly, yellow halo on the glass, distorting the shapes of the pedestrians into blurs of charcoal and shadow. He had been in this line of work for twenty years, a time long enough to learn that the world was not divided into the clean lines of law and disorder, but into shades of grey, into the murky, breathing fog of compromise.

His new superior, a man named Comber who had arrived from the countryside with a fresh, bloodless optimism and a hatred for anything that smelled of the old, dirty methods, had summoned him that morning. Comber spoke with a precision that was almost violent, his words clipped and sharp as a razor. He wanted a name. He wanted a head in the papers, a scandal that would justify the extra budget for surveillance, a triumph over the "foreign element" that haunted the dreams of the Home Office. He did not care about the intricate web of loyalties and betrayals that Vane had woven over the years; he cared only about the spectacle. And so, the choice had been laid before Vane, not as a question, but as a fact.

The name was Elias Thorne.

To arrest Thorne was to destroy the very foundation upon which Vane’s career rested. Thorne was not merely an informer; he was the lens through which Vane saw the world. He was a man of quiet, intellectual demeanor, a former professor of history who had been driven into the revolutionary circles by a kind of romantic despair, and then driven back into the arms of the police by a colder, more practical fear. Thorne had kept Vane safe, had fed him intelligence that allowed him to anticipate moves, to step aside from the path of danger with the grace of a dancer. In return, Vane had given Thorne protection, a quiet existence, a sense of purpose. It was a transaction of souls, a dark pact made in the shadows of Soho, far from the bright, judgmental light of the public square.

Vane turned from the window. The room was dim, the air thick with the smell of stale tobacco and damp wool. On the desk lay the warrant, signed by Comber’s hand, the ink still wet, a fresh wound in the paper. He picked it up, feeling its weight. It was a small piece of paper, yet it felt heavier than any chain. He thought of Thorne’s face, pale and thin, with eyes that held a constant, watchful sadness. Thorne had never spoken of his motives, not truly. He had only said, once, in a low voice, that he had seen the future, and that it was a future of fire and ash, and that he could not bear to watch it burn. Vane had not asked if Thorne’s future was one of destruction or of creation. It did not matter. In the end, men were defined not by their intentions, but by their actions, and actions, once set in motion, carried their own terrible momentum.

He put on his coat, a heavy thing of black wool, and buttoned it to the chin. The street was empty, the rain continuing its slow, rhythmic tapping against the pavement. He walked towards Soho, the district that had become his second home, a place of foreign tongues and foreign faces, a labyrinth of narrow streets and high, dark windows. He walked with a deliberate slowness, trying to clear his mind, trying to find a justification for what he was about to do. But the mind is a treacherous servant; it offers up reasons, but it does not offer up peace.

He found Thorne in his usual place, a small, dimly lit cafe near Charing Cross Road. The place was empty, save for a few students huddled over their books, their faces illuminated by the flickering light of the gas. Thorne sat in the corner, his back to the wall, a book open on the table before him. He did not look up as Vane approached. He had known that Vane would come. He had always known.

Vane sat down across from him. The silence between them was heavy, charged with a tension that was almost physical. Thorne turned a page, his fingers pale and steady.

"You are late," Thorne said, his voice quiet, devoid of surprise.

"The rain," Vane replied, though the rain had stopped, or at least had receded into a thin mist.

Thorne looked up then, his eyes meeting Vane’s. There was no anger in them, no fear. Only a deep, weary understanding. He had known, Vane realized, that this day would come. It was the price of their agreement, the inevitable consequence of living in the shadows.

"I have the warrant," Vane said, placing it on the table between them. The paper lay there, white and stark against the dark wood.

Thorne looked at it, then at Vane. He smiled, a faint, sad curve of the lips. "You have done your duty, Arthur. I suppose I must do mine."

"Is there nothing to say?" Vane asked, his voice cracking, a sound of raw emotion that he had long since learned to suppress.

Thorne closed the book. "There is always something to say. But words are like the rain, Arthur. They fall, and they leave a mark, but they do not change the ground."

Vane reached for the warrant. His hand trembled, a slight, involuntary movement that betrayed the turmoil within him. He had spent years building a relationship based on trust, on the unspoken understanding that they were, in their own way, allies against the chaos of the world. Now, he was the enemy. He was the hand that would reach out and drag Thorne into the light, into the judgment of the courts, into the humiliation of the newspapers.

As he reached for the paper, Thorne placed his hand over it. His grip was firm, but not aggressive. "Wait," he said.

Vane froze. The cafe was silent, the students unaware of the drama unfolding in the corner. The rain had begun again, a soft patter on the windows, a sound that seemed to come from a great distance.

"Let me finish the chapter," Thorne said softly. "It is the end of the book. I have been working on it for years."

Vane looked at him, at this man who had been his guide, his confidant, his shadow. He saw in Thorne’s face a kind of dignity, a quiet acceptance of fate that was more terrifying than any act of violence. He wanted to pull his hand away, to snatch the warrant, to fulfill the order. But something held him back, a force that was stronger than duty, stronger than fear. It was the weight of the years they had shared, the silence they had built, the dark, intricate tapestry of their lives.

He withdrew his hand.

"Finish," Vane said, his voice barely a whisper.

Thorne nodded. He opened the book again, his eyes returning to the page. Vane sat back, his heart pounding in his chest, a drumbeat in the silence. He watched Thorne’s face, the light from the gas lamp flickering on his features, casting long, dancing shadows. He thought of Comber, waiting for the news, waiting for the triumph. He thought of the newspapers, the headlines, the public outrage. He thought of himself, standing in the rain, a man who had lost everything in the name of nothing.

The rain fell on the street outside, washing the city clean, or perhaps just making it shine with a cold, indifferent brilliance. In the corner of the cafe, two men sat in silence, bound by a secret that would never be spoken, a silence that was louder than any shout, a darkness that was deeper than any night. Vane knew that he would never arrest Thorne. He knew that he would have to find another way, a way to satisfy Comber, a way to save himself. But for now, in this moment, there was only the rain, the light, and the weight of the unsaid.

motionless ship that floated quietly in the silence of a world asleep, fighting against time for the freeing of that boat, grovelling on all-fours, standing up in despair, tugging, pushing, snarling at each other venomously, ready to kill, ready to weep, and only kept from flying at each other’s throats by the fear of death that stood silent behind them like an inflexible and cold-eyed taskmaster. Oh yes! It must have been a pretty sight. He saw it all, he could talk about it with scorn and bitterness; he had a minute knowledge of it by means of some sixth sense, I conclude, because he swore to me he had remained apart without a glance at them and at the boat--without one single glance. And I believe him. I should think he was too busy watching the threatening slant of the ship, the suspended menace discovered in the midst of the most perfect security--fascinated by the sword hanging by a hair over his imaginative head.

‘Nothing in the world moved before his eyes, and he could depict to
himself without hindrance the sudden swing upwards of the dark sky-line,
the sudden tilt up of the vast plain of the sea, the swift still rise,
the brutal fling, the grasp of the abyss, the struggle without hope, the
starlight closing over his head for ever like the vault of a tomb--the
revolt of his young life--the black end. He could! By Jove! who
couldn’t? And you must remember he was a finished artist in that
peculiar way, he was a gifted poor devil with the faculty of swift and
forestalling vision. The sights it showed him had turned him into cold
stone from the soles of his feet to the nape of his neck; but there
was a hot dance of thoughts in his head, a dance of lame, blind, mute
thoughts--a whirl of awful cripples. Didn’t I tell you he confessed
himself before me as though I had the power to bind and to loose? He
burrowed deep, deep, in the hope of my absolution, which would have been
of no good to him. This was one of those cases which no solemn deception
can palliate, where no man can help; where his very Maker seems to
abandon a sinner to his own devices.

‘He stood on the starboard side of the bridge, as far as he could get
from the struggle for the boat, which went on with the agitation
of madness and the stealthiness of a conspiracy. The two Malays had
meantime remained holding to the wheel. Just picture to yourselves
the actors in that, thank God! unique, episode of the sea, four beside
themselves with fierce and secret exertions, and three looking on in
complete immobility, above the awnings covering the profound ignorance
of hundreds of human beings, with their weariness, with their dreams,
with their hopes, arrested, held by an invisible hand on the brink of
annihilation. For that they were so, makes no doubt to me: given the
state of the ship, this was the deadliest possible description of
accident that could happen. These beggars by the boat had every reason
to go distracted with funk. Frankly, had I been there, I would not have
given as much as a counterfeit farthing for the ship’s chance to keep
above water to the end of each successive second. And still she
floated! These sleeping pilgrims were destined to accomplish their
whole pilgrimage to the bitterness of some other end. It was as if the
Omnipotence whose mercy they confessed had needed their humble testimony
on earth for a while longer, and had looked down to make a sign,
“Thou shalt not!” to the ocean. Their escape would trouble me as a
prodigiously inexplicable event, did I not know how tough old iron can
be--as tough sometimes as the spirit of some men we meet now and then,
worn to a shadow and breasting the weight of life. Not the least
wonder of these twenty minutes, to my mind, is the behaviour of the two
helmsmen. They were amongst the native batch of all sorts brought over
from Aden to give evidence at the inquiry. One of them, labouring under
intense bashfulness, was very young, and with his smooth, yellow,
cheery countenance looked even younger than he was. I remember perfectly
Brierly asking him, through the interpreter, what he thought of it at
the time, and the interpreter, after a short colloquy, turning to the
court with an important air--

‘“He says he thought nothing.”

‘The other, with patient blinking eyes, a blue cotton handkerchief, faded with much washing, bound with a smart twist over a lot of grey wisps, his face shrunk into grim hollows, his brown skin made darker by a mesh of wrinkles, explained that he had a knowledge of some evil thing befalling the ship, but there had been no order; he could not remember an order; why should he leave the helm? To some further questions he jerked back his spare shoulders, and declared it never came into his mind then that the white men were about to leave the ship through fear of death. He did not believe it now. There might have been secret reasons. He wagged his old chin knowingly. Aha! secret reasons. He was a man of great experience, and he wanted _that_ white Tuan to know--he turned towards Brierly, who didn’t raise his head--that he had acquired a knowledge of many things by serving white men on the sea for a great number of years--and, suddenly, with shaky excitement he poured upon our spellbound attention a lot of queer-sounding names, names of dead-and-gone skippers, names of forgotten country ships, names of familiar and distorted sound, as if the hand of dumb time had been at work on them for ages. They stopped him at last. A silence fell upon the court,--a silence that remained unbroken for at least a minute, and passed gently into a deep murmur.
