[Scenario]
A young second mate, on his first voyage with the rank, freezes during a squall and the captain takes the deck in his place. Nobody speaks of it afterwards. For the rest of the passage the mate watches the crew for any sign that they saw, and the captain for any sign that he will report it.
Setting: A barque in the Indian Ocean, 1880s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The wind did not howl; it screamed, a thin, high-pitched shriek that seemed to tear the fabric of the night apart, exposing the raw, wet bones of the ocean. It was a squall of that peculiar, vicious kind that the old sailors in the lower quarters spoke of with a mixture of dread and superstitious respect, a storm that did not merely batter the ship but sought to unmake it, to strip the iron and wood down to their essential, fragile state. I remember the sensation of the deck tilting beneath my feet, a sickening lurch that turned my stomach into a void, and the rain, which was not rain but a horizontal spray of ice-cold needles, stinging the exposed skin of my face until I could no longer distinguish where the sea ended and the sky began. I was the second mate, newly appointed, a title that felt less like a rank and more like a heavy, invisible stone around my neck, a burden of expectation that I had not yet learned how to carry.

I stood at the starboard rail, my hands gripping the wet iron so tightly that my knuckles were white, my breath coming in short, sharp gasps that tasted of salt and fear. The barque, the *St. Jude*, was a solid vessel, old but sturdy, yet in the teeth of that gale she seemed to be a living thing in agony, groaning in her timbers, heaving against the invisible hand that sought to drag her down. The helm was manned by a Malay helmsman, a young lad with eyes wide as saucers, his face a mask of terrified concentration. He was steering by feel, by the instinct that runs deeper than reason, but I could see in the tremor of his hands that the authority of the ship, the quiet command that keeps a crew from dissolving into chaos, was missing. It was my duty to be there, to stand at his shoulder, to issue the orders, to be the anchor of the vessel’s stability. But I was frozen. Not by the cold, though the cold was a physical presence, a biting claw at my spine, but by a paralysis of the spirit, a sudden, terrifying awareness of my own inadequacy. I was a ghost in the flesh, a hollow shell wearing the clothes of a man who did not exist. I watched the waves break over the bow, huge, black mountains of water that rose and fell with a rhythm that was both beautiful and deadly, and I knew, with a certainty that was more profound than thought, that I was not equal to this moment. I was a boy playing at men, and the sea, that ancient, indifferent god, had seen through me.

Then, a shadow fell across me. It was not the captain’s shadow, not the broad, commanding presence I had come to expect from him, but the quick, silent step of a man who had moved without making a sound. I turned, and there was Captain Thorne. He did not shout. He did not curse. He simply moved to the helm, his hand resting lightly on the helmsman’s shoulder, a touch that was more forceful than any command could have been. His face was obscured by the brim of his oilskin cap, but I could see the set of his jaw, the rigid line of his mouth. He took the wheel in his own hands, and in that single, effortless motion, the panic in the helmsman’s eyes subsided, replaced by a calm that was contagious, a stillness that spread through the crew like a wave of relief. The ship steadied. The wind still screamed, the rain still lashed, but the chaos in my mind receded, pushed back by the sheer, quiet authority of the man who had taken the deck from me.

I stood aside, a spectator to my own failure, watching Thorne as he guided the ship through the worst of the storm. He was a figure carved out of the darkness, solid and unyielding, a man who had lived with the sea for so long that he had become part of its rhythm. I saw him adjust the sails, his movements precise and economical, wasting no energy, expressing no emotion. He was not angry. That was the worst part. Anger would have been a sign that I had offended him, a sign that he saw me as a rival or a fool. But there was only a cold, professional detachment, a look that passed over me as if I were a piece of rigging, a thing that was there but not important. I was invisible. I was nothing.

The storm passed as quickly as it had come, leaving behind a sky washed clean of clouds, a sky that was so bright and empty it seemed to hurt the eyes. The sun rose, weak and pale, casting long, gray shadows across the deck. The crew went about their duties, mending the rigging, bailing the water, their voices low and subdued, as if speaking above a whisper would break the fragile peace. I went below to my cabin, a small, cramped space that smelled of damp wood and tar. I sat on the edge of my bunk, my hands still trembling, and I tried to make sense of what had happened. I told myself it was the cold, the exhaustion, the novelty of the situation. I told myself that Thorne had only taken the helm because he knew I was not ready, that it was a kindness, a lesson. But deep down, in that dark place where true fears reside, I knew that was a lie. He had taken the helm because he saw that I was failing, and he had corrected it with a silence that was more damning than any rebuke.

For the rest of the passage, which lasted three weeks, I lived in a state of suspended animation. I watched the crew, every one of them, looking for a sign, a glance, a whispered word that would confirm that they had seen me freeze. The Malay helmsman, young and eager, would sometimes look at me with a mixture of respect and pity, a look that I could not bear. The other officers, the first mate, the steward, they moved around me like ghosts, their eyes avoiding mine, their conversations cut short when I entered the room. I was the center of a conspiracy of silence, a secret that they all shared and none would speak. And I watched Thorne. I watched him every moment I could, looking for a sign that he would report me, that he would bring my failure to the attention of the owners, that he would strip me of my rank and send me back to the shore in disgrace. But he never did. He continued to give his orders, to inspect the ship, to eat his meals in the officers’ mess, his face a mask of professional indifference. He never mentioned the squall. He never mentioned the helm. He treated me as if I had not existed in that moment, as if I were a new man, a man who had not yet failed.

It was a mercy, I thought, but it was also a curse. If he had scolded me, I could have apologized, I could have learned from the lesson. But by ignoring it, by refusing to acknowledge the failure, he had left me in a state of perpetual doubt, a man walking on thin ice, never knowing if I was safe, never knowing if I was forgiven. I began to doubt my own memory, to wonder if I had imagined the paralysis, if I had merely been slow to act, if the captain had taken the helm for reasons that had nothing to do with me. But the memory was too vivid, too real, to be dismissed. I could still feel the cold in my bones, the terror in my heart, the weight of the ship on my shoulders. I was a man who had seen his own reflection in the dark water, and I did not like what I had seen.

As the ship approached the port of Callao, the silence grew heavier. The crew was restless, eager to be ashore, to breathe air that did not taste of salt and fear. I stood on the deck, watching the coastline appear in the distance, a thin line of land against the horizon. Thorne was beside me, his hands clasped behind his back, his eyes fixed on the shore. He said nothing. He did not need to. The silence between us was a wall, a barrier that no words could penetrate. I knew that I would never be the same again. I was no longer the young second mate who had come to the sea with dreams of adventure and glory. I was a man who had known the weight of his own failure, and who carried that weight with him, a stone in his pocket, a secret in his heart. And I knew, with a certainty that was more profound than thought, that Thorne knew it too. And that was enough. That was more than enough. It was a verdict that no court could pass, a judgment that no appeal could overturn. We were two men who had seen each other’s souls, and we had said nothing. And in that silence, we were bound together by a chain that no amount of time or distance could break.

messages.content:
Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.
<<<
flames burst forth, and the stone faces awakened, stared out of fire.

A faint murmur arose about the house from the few people who were left
there, and there was a saddling of a horse and riding away. There was
spurring and splashing through the darkness, and bridle was drawn in the
space by the village fountain, and the horse in a foam stood at Monsieur
Gabelle’s door. “Help, Gabelle! Help, every one!” The tocsin rang
impatiently, but other help (if that were any) there was none. The
mender of roads, and two hundred and fifty particular friends, stood
with folded arms at the fountain, looking at the pillar of fire in the
sky. “It must be forty feet high,” said they, grimly; and never moved.

The rider from the chateau, and the horse in a foam, clattered away
through the village, and galloped up the stony steep, to the prison on
the crag. At the gate, a group of officers were looking at the fire;
removed from them, a group of soldiers. “Help, gentlemen--officers! The
chateau is on fire; valuable objects may be saved from the flames by
timely aid! Help, help!” The officers looked towards the soldiers who
looked at the fire; gave no orders; and answered, with shrugs and biting
of lips, “It must burn.”

As the rider rattled down the hill again and through the street, the
village was illuminating. The mender of roads, and the two hundred and
fifty particular friends, inspired as one man and woman by the idea of
lighting up, had darted into their houses, and were putting candles in
every dull little pane of glass. The general scarcity of everything,
occasioned candles to be borrowed in a rather peremptory manner of
Monsieur Gabelle; and in a moment of reluctance and hesitation on
that functionary’s part, the mender of roads, once so submissive to
authority, had remarked that carriages were good to make bonfires with,
and that post-horses would roast.

The chateau was left to itself to flame and burn. In the roaring and
raging of the conflagration, a red-hot wind, driving straight from the
infernal regions, seemed to be blowing the edifice away. With the rising
and falling of the blaze, the stone faces showed as if they were in
torment. When great masses of stone and timber fell, the face with the
two dints in the nose became obscured: anon struggled out of the smoke
again, as if it were the face of the cruel Marquis, burning at the stake
and contending with the fire.

The chateau burned; the nearest trees, laid hold of by the fire,
scorched and shrivelled; trees at a distance, fired by the four fierce
figures, begirt the blazing edifice with a new forest of smoke. Molten
lead and iron boiled in the marble basin of the fountain; the water ran
dry; the extinguisher tops of the towers vanished like ice before the
heat, and trickled down into four rugged wells of flame. Great rents and
splits branched out in the solid walls, like crystallisation; stupefied
birds wheeled about and dropped into the furnace; four fierce figures
trudged away, East, West, North, and South, along the night-enshrouded
roads, guided by the beacon they had lighted, towards their next
destination. The illuminated village had seized hold of the tocsin, and,
abolishing the lawful ringer, rang for joy.

Not only that; but the village, light-headed with famine, fire, and
bell-ringing, and bethinking itself that Monsieur Gabelle had to do with
the collection of rent and taxes--though it was but a small instalment
of taxes, and no rent at all, that Gabelle had got in those latter
days--became impatient for an interview with him, and, surrounding his
house, summoned him to come forth for personal conference. Whereupon,
Monsieur Gabelle did heavily bar his door, and retire to hold counsel
with himself. The result of that conference was, that Gabelle again
withdrew himself to his housetop behind his stack of chimneys; this time
resolved, if his door were broken in (he was a small Southern man
of retaliative temperament), to pitch himself head foremost over the
parapet, and crush a man or two below.

Probably, Monsieur Gabelle passed a long night up there, with the
distant chateau for fire and candle, and the beating at his door,
combined with the joy-ringing, for music; not to mention his having an
ill-omened lamp slung across the road before his posting-house gate,
which the village showed a lively inclination to displace in his favour.
A trying suspense, to be passing a whole summer night on the brink of
the black ocean, ready to take that plunge into it upon which Monsieur
Gabelle had resolved! But, the friendly dawn appearing at last, and the
rush-candles of the village guttering out, the people happily dispersed,
and Monsieur Gabelle came down bringing his life with him for that
while.

Within a hundred miles, and in the light of other fires, there were
other functionaries less fortunate, that night and other nights, whom
the rising sun found hanging across once-peaceful streets, where they
had been born and bred; also, there were other villagers and townspeople
less fortunate than the mender of roads and his fellows, upon whom the
functionaries and soldiery turned with success, and whom they strung up
in their turn. But, the fierce figures were steadily wending East, West,
North, and South, be that as it would; and whosoever hung, fire burned.
The altitude of the gallows that would turn to water and quench it,
no functionary, by any stretch of mathematics, was able to calculate
successfully.

In such risings of fire and risings of sea--the firm earth shaken by the rushes of an angry ocean which had now no ebb, but was always on the flow, higher and higher, to the terror and wonder of the beholders on the shore--three years of tempest were consumed. [Scenario]
A pompous alderman who has organised a banquet to celebrate a new town hall discovers on the morning of the feast that the contractor has run off with the funds and the roof is unfinished. He must preside over the banquet in the rain without admitting anything is wrong.
Setting: A Midlands market town, 1850s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
Mr. Alderman Pumblechook—for so he was universally styled, though the christening register had it Pumblechook *cum* Puddingcome, his mother having married twice and being a woman of an economical turn that sought to bury the one name decently within the other—Mr. Alderman Pumblechook rose from his bed on the morning of the great banquet with the sun upon his counterpane and a psalm of thanksgiving upon his lips. The day was come. The new Town Hall of Cinderbury—the pride of the Midlands, the wonder of the age, the edifice that was to have a clock in its tower and a fountain before its door and a cornice that should make the neighbouring boroughs bite their nails with envy—was to be opened that very afternoon with a public dinner of one hundred and forty covers, and Mr. Alderman Pumblechook was to preside.

He shaved himself with a hand that trembled with anticipated glory. He rehearsed his speech before the looking-glass, addressing the soap-dish as the assembled company and the shaving-brush as the Mayor of Thrapston, who was known to be coming with a deputation and an appetite. He was in the very middle of a rolling period concerning the commercial greatness of Cinderbury and the imperishable fame of its founders, when there came a knocking at his door so hurried, so peremptory, so entirely out of keeping with the solemnity of the occasion, that he cut himself upon the chin and answered in a voice of thunder.

The knocker was his clerk, one Nathaniel Winks, a small man with a large conscience, who stood upon the mat in a condition of agitation that had disordered his neckcloth and his grammar together. "Sir," says he, "the roof—"

"The roof, you jackanapes?"

"The roof, sir, is not on."

Mr. Alderman Pumblechook laid down his razor with the gravity of a man laying down the seals of office. "Not on," says he. "Not on? What do you mean, sir, that the roof is not on? Roofs, sir, are on. It is the nature of a roof to be on. It is the office, the function, the very definition of a roof to be on. If it were not on, sir, it would be a floor."

Mr. Winks, who had a great respect for his master and a greater for the truth, submitted, with the humility of one who knows that the facts are against him, that the contractor, Mr. Bartholomew Gudge, had been seen at the railway station at six of the clock that morning with a carpet-bag and the funds of the Building Committee, and that the roof of the new Town Hall consisted at present of a quantity of scaffolding, a quantity of rain, and a quantity of sky, in about equal proportions.

Mr. Alderman Pumblechook sat down upon the edge of his bed, and for the space of a minute and a half was silent. Then he arose, and putting on his coat with a slow and awful dignity, observed that the banquet would proceed.

"Proceed, sir!" cried Mr. Winks. "With the roof off, and the rain coming down in—in cataracts, sir, and the Mayor of Thrapston coming with a deputation!"

"The banquet," repeated Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, "will proceed. The roof, sir, is a detail. The roof, sir, is a matter for the Building Committee, and the Building Committee is—is otherwise engaged. The dignity of Cinderbury, sir, is not to be measured by slates and plaster. The dignity of Cinderbury, sir, is imperishable. Let the banquet proceed."

Now the new Town Hall of Cinderbury stood in the market-place, and was a building of the Corinthian order, or of an order so nearly approaching the Corinthian that the difference was not to be discerned by the naked eye of Cinderbury. Its portico was supported by six columns of a whiteness that had cost the committee dear, and its great hall was capable of seating one hundred and forty persons at a long table, with the chairman at the head of it, and the Mayor of Thrapston at his right hand. And it was into this great hall, at the hour appointed, that the company came, shaking the rain from their hats and their umbrellas, and looking about them with an air of wonder that was not entirely admiration.

For the rain, which had begun at daybreak, had by four of the clock settled into a steady, methodical, uncompromising downpour, such as only the Midlands can produce, and it fell through the unfinished roof of the great hall in a manner that suggested the deliberate malice of Providence. It fell upon the long table in a hundred little pattering streams. It fell upon the napery, and the napery, being of a quality that had been warranted to the committee as damask, revealed itself in its true character as a species of painted canvas that ran like a water-colour. It fell upon the great chandelier, and the great chandelier, being of a substance that was not precisely ormolu, gave out a sound as of a hundred small kettles. It fell, in fine, upon the assembled company, and the assembled company, being of the commercial and municipal classes, and having paid for their tickets, bore it with the fortitude of men who intend to have their money's worth or to know the reason why.

Mr. Alderman Pumblechook took his seat at the head of the table with the rain upon his bald head and the Mayor of Thrapston upon his right hand. The Mayor of Thrapston, a man of a dry and waggish turn, observed that the ventilation was excellent, and that he had never seen a room so open to conviction. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook replied, with a smile of ineffable sweetness, that the committee had given particular attention to the ventilation, and that he was gratified to find it appreciated.

The soup was served. It was a soup of a brown and noble complexion, and it was served in plates, and the plates contained, in addition to the soup, a quantity of the rain of Cinderbury, which had found its way through the roof and into the tureen, and which gave to the soup a certain freshness, a certain sparkle, a certain—as the Mayor of Thrapston observed—riverine quality. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, lifting his spoon, declared that he had never tasted a soup so—so—so suggestive of the element from which it came.

The fish was served, and the rain fell upon the fish. The entrées were served, and the rain fell upon the entrées. The Mayor of Thrapston, whose humour was of a persistent and a penetrating kind, remarked that the banquet was, in a manner of speaking, a baptism, and that he hoped the Town Hall would grow up a good and honest building. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook replied that the Town Hall was already grown up, and that it was the finest Town Hall in the Midlands, and that he would maintain it against all comers.

Then came the moment for the speech. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook rose, with the rain upon his shirt-front and the rain upon his notes, and the rain, having soaked the notes, had reduced them to a pulp, and the speech that he delivered was a speech that he improvised upon the spur of the moment, and it was a speech that he never afterwards forgot. He spoke of the commercial greatness of Cinderbury. He spoke of the imperishable fame of its founders. He spoke of the new Town Hall, which he described as an edifice that would endure for ages, and he did not say that the roof was off. He spoke of the banquet, which he described as a repast that would be remembered for years, and he did not say that the soup had been diluted by the heavens. He spoke of the rain, which he described as a gracious dispensation of Providence, and the Mayor of Thrapston, who was a man of a dry and waggish turn, observed that Providence had been very gracious indeed.

And so the banquet proceeded, and the rain proceeded, and the night came on, and the candles were lit, and the candles, being lit, were immediately extinguished by the rain, and the company sat in a darkness that was rendered more impressive by the occasional flash of lightning. And Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, sitting at the head of the table with the water running off his nose, continued to speak of the commercial greatness of Cinderbury and the imperishable fame of its founders, and the company, who had paid for their tickets, listened with a respect that was not entirely admiration, and the Mayor of Thrapston, who had paid for nothing, enjoyed himself exceedingly.

It was past midnight when the last of the company departed, and Mr. Alderman Pumblechook stood alone in the great hall, with the rain falling upon his bald head and the darkness all about him, and the scaffolding of the unfinished roof looming above him like the ribs of a stranded ship. And as he stood there, he heard a voice, which was the voice of Mr. Nathaniel Winks, saying, "Sir, the Mayor of Thrapston has taken the opportunity to observe that the banquet was the most original he ever attended, and that he would not have missed it for a hundred pounds."

And Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, drawing himself up to his full height, and shaking the rain from his coat-tails, replied, "Winks, the dignity of Cinderbury is imperishable." And with that he walked out into the market-place, and the rain fell upon him, and the clock in the tower of the old church struck one, and the new Town Hall of Cinderbury stood in the darkness with its roof off, and the Mayor of Thrapston went home to Thrapston in a gig, laughing all the way.

It is the nature of a roof to be on. It is the office, the function, the very definition of a roof to be on. If it were not on, sir, it would be a floor."

Mr. Winks, who had a great respect for his master and a greater for the truth, submitted, with the humility of one who knows that the facts are against him, that the contractor, Mr. Bartholomew Gudge, had been seen at the railway station at six of the clock that morning with a carpet-bag and the funds of the Building Committee, and that the roof of the new Town Hall consisted at present of a quantity of scaffolding, a quantity of rain, and a quantity of sky, in about equal proportions.

Mr. Alderman Pumblechook sat down upon the edge of his bed, and for the space of a minute and a half was silent. Then he arose, and putting on his coat with a slow and awful dignity, observed that the banquet would proceed.

"Proceed, sir!" cried Mr. Winks. "With the roof off, and the rain coming down in—in cataracts, sir, and the Mayor of Thrapston coming with a deputation!"

"The banquet," repeated Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, "will proceed. The roof, sir, is a detail. The roof, sir, is a matter for the Building Committee, and the Building Committee is—is otherwise engaged. The dignity of Cinderbury, sir, is not to be measured by slates and plaster. The dignity of Cinderbury, sir, is imperishable. Let the banquet proceed."

Now the new Town Hall of Cinderbury stood in the market-place, and was a building of the Corinthian order, or of an order so nearly approaching the Corinthian that the difference was not to be discerned by the naked eye of Cinderbury. Its portico was supported by six columns of a whiteness that had cost the committee dear, and its great hall was capable of seating one hundred and forty persons at a long table, with the chairman at the head of it, and the Mayor of Thrapston at his right hand. And it was into this great hall, at the hour appointed, that the company came, shaking the rain from their hats and their umbrellas, and looking about them with an air of wonder that was not entirely admiration.

For the rain, which had begun at daybreak, had by four of the clock settled into a steady, methodical, uncompromising downpour, such as only the Midlands can produce, and it fell through the unfinished roof of the great hall in a manner that suggested the deliberate malice of Providence. It fell upon the long table in a hundred little pattering streams. It fell upon the napery, and the napery, being of a quality that had been warranted to the committee as damask, revealed itself in its true character as a species of painted canvas that ran like a water-colour. It fell upon the great chandelier, and the great chandelier, being of a substance that was not precisely ormolu, gave out a sound as of a hundred small kettles. It fell, in fine, upon the assembled company, and the assembled company, being of the commercial and municipal classes, and having paid for their tickets, bore it with the fortitude of men who intend to have their money's worth or to know the reason why.

Mr. Alderman Pumblechook took his seat at the head of the table with the rain upon his bald head and the Mayor of Thrapston upon his right hand. The Mayor of Thrapston, a man of a dry and waggish turn, observed that the ventilation was excellent, and that he had never seen a room so open to conviction. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook replied, with a smile of ineffable sweetness, that the committee had given particular attention to the ventilation, and that he was gratified to find it appreciated.

The soup was served. It was a soup of a brown and noble complexion, and it was served in plates, and the plates contained, in addition to the soup, a quantity of the rain of Cinderbury, which had found its way through the roof and into the tureen, and which gave to the soup a certain freshness, a certain sparkle, a certain—as the Mayor of Thrapston observed—riverine quality. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, lifting his spoon, declared that he had never tasted a soup so—so—so suggestive of the element from which it came.

The fish was served, and the rain fell upon the fish. The entrées were served, and the rain fell upon the entrées. The Mayor of Thrapston, whose humour was of a persistent and a penetrating kind, remarked that the banquet was, in a manner of speaking, a baptism, and that he hoped the Town Hall would grow up a good and honest building. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook replied that the Town Hall was already grown up, and that it was the finest Town Hall in the Midlands, and that he would maintain it against all comers.

Then came the moment for the speech. Mr. Alderman Pumblechook rose, with the rain upon his shirt-front and the rain upon his notes, and the rain, having soaked the notes, had reduced them to a pulp, and the speech that he delivered was a speech that he improvised upon the spur of the moment, and it was a speech that he never afterwards forgot. He spoke of the commercial greatness of Cinderbury. He spoke of the imperishable fame of its founders. He spoke of the new Town Hall, which he described as an edifice that would endure for ages, and he did not say that the roof was off. He spoke of the banquet, which he described as a repast that would be remembered for years, and he did not say that the soup had been diluted by the heavens. He spoke of the rain, which he described as a gracious dispensation of Providence, and the Mayor of Thrapston, who was a man of a dry and waggish turn, observed that Providence had been very gracious indeed.

And so the banquet proceeded, and the rain proceeded, and the night came on, and the candles were lit, and the candles, being lit, were immediately extinguished by the rain, and the company sat in a darkness that was rendered more impressive by the occasional flash of lightning. And Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, sitting at the head of the table with the water running off his nose, continued to speak of the commercial greatness of Cinderbury and the imperishable fame of its founders, and the company, who had paid for their tickets, listened with a respect that was not entirely admiration, and the Mayor of Thrapston, who had paid for nothing, enjoyed himself exceedingly.

It was past midnight when the last of the company departed, and Mr. Alderman Pumblechook stood alone in the great hall, with the rain falling upon his bald head and the darkness all about him, and the scaffolding of the unfinished roof looming above him like the ribs of a stranded ship. And as he stood there, he heard a voice, which was the voice of Mr. Nathaniel Winks, saying, "Sir, the Mayor of Thrapston has taken the opportunity to observe that the banquet was the most original he ever attended, and that he would not have missed it for a hundred pounds."

And Mr. Alderman Pumblechook, drawing himself up to his full height, and shaking the rain from his coat-tails, replied, "Winks, the dignity of Cinderbury is imperishable." And with that he walked out into the market-place, and the rain fell upon him, and the clock in the tower of the old church struck one, and the new Town Hall of Cinderbury stood in the darkness with its roof off, and the Mayor of Thrapston went home to Thrapston in a gig, laughing all the way.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Joseph Conrad (1857–1924).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
A brooding, morally searching voice; events are filtered through memory, interpretation and ironic distance. Long, rhythmic sentences layered with qualification, often rendering an impression before its meaning is understood. Dense atmospheric description of light, darkness, heat, water and silence, beside abstract moral vocabulary. Speech is halting, oblique or formal, with foreign idioms and much left unsaid.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Joseph Conrad. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.
<<<
motionless ship that floated quietly in the silence of a world asleep, fighting against time for the freeing of that boat, grovelling on all-fours, standing up in despair, tugging, pushing, snarling at each other venomously, ready to kill, ready to weep, and only kept from flying at each other’s throats by the fear of death that stood silent behind them like an inflexible and cold-eyed taskmaster. Oh yes! It must have been a pretty sight. He saw it all, he could talk about it with scorn and bitterness; he had a minute knowledge of it by means of some sixth sense, I conclude, because he swore to me he had remained apart without a glance at them and at the boat--without one single glance. And I believe him. I should think he was too busy watching the threatening slant of the ship, the suspended menace discovered in the midst of the most perfect security--fascinated by the sword hanging by a hair over his imaginative head.

‘Nothing in the world moved before his eyes, and he could depict to
himself without hindrance the sudden swing upwards of the dark sky-line,
the sudden tilt up of the vast plain of the sea, the swift still rise,
the brutal fling, the grasp of the abyss, the struggle without hope, the
starlight closing over his head for ever like the vault of a tomb--the
revolt of his young life--the black end. He could! By Jove! who
couldn’t? And you must remember he was a finished artist in that
peculiar way, he was a gifted poor devil with the faculty of swift and
forestalling vision. The sights it showed him had turned him into cold
stone from the soles of his feet to the nape of his neck; but there
was a hot dance of thoughts in his head, a dance of lame, blind, mute
thoughts--a whirl of awful cripples. Didn’t I tell you he confessed
himself before me as though I had the power to bind and to loose? He
burrowed deep, deep, in the hope of my absolution, which would have been
of no good to him. This was one of those cases which no solemn deception
can palliate, where no man can help; where his very Maker seems to
abandon a sinner to his own devices.

‘He stood on the starboard side of the bridge, as far as he could get
from the struggle for the boat, which went on with the agitation
of madness and the stealthiness of a conspiracy. The two Malays had
meantime remained holding to the wheel. Just picture to yourselves
the actors in that, thank God! unique, episode of the sea, four beside
themselves with fierce and secret exertions, and three looking on in
complete immobility, above the awnings covering the profound ignorance
of hundreds of human beings, with their weariness, with their dreams,
with their hopes, arrested, held by an invisible hand on the brink of
annihilation. For that they were so, makes no doubt to me: given the
state of the ship, this was the deadliest possible description of
accident that could happen. These beggars by the boat had every reason
to go distracted with funk. Frankly, had I been there, I would not have
given as much as a counterfeit farthing for the ship’s chance to keep
above water to the end of each successive second. And still she
floated! These sleeping pilgrims were destined to accomplish their
whole pilgrimage to the bitterness of some other end. It was as if the
Omnipotence whose mercy they confessed had needed their humble testimony
on earth for a while longer, and had looked down to make a sign,
“Thou shalt not!” to the ocean. Their escape would trouble me as a
prodigiously inexplicable event, did I not know how tough old iron can
be--as tough sometimes as the spirit of some men we meet now and then,
worn to a shadow and breasting the weight of life. Not the least
wonder of these twenty minutes, to my mind, is the behaviour of the two
helmsmen. They were amongst the native batch of all sorts brought over
from Aden to give evidence at the inquiry. One of them, labouring under
intense bashfulness, was very young, and with his smooth, yellow,
cheery countenance looked even younger than he was. I remember perfectly
Brierly asking him, through the interpreter, what he thought of it at
the time, and the interpreter, after a short colloquy, turning to the
court with an important air--

‘“He says he thought nothing.”

‘The other, with patient blinking eyes, a blue cotton handkerchief, faded with much washing, bound with a smart twist over a lot of grey wisps, his face shrunk into grim hollows, his brown skin made darker by a mesh of wrinkles, explained that he had a knowledge of some evil thing befalling the ship, but there had been no order; he could not remember an order; why should he leave the helm? To some further questions he jerked back his spare shoulders, and declared it never came into his mind then that the white men were about to leave the ship through fear of death. He did not believe it now. There might have been secret reasons. He wagged his old chin knowingly. Aha! secret reasons. He was a man of great experience, and he wanted _that_ white Tuan to know--he turned towards Brierly, who didn’t raise his head--that he had acquired a knowledge of many things by serving white men on the sea for a great number of years--and, suddenly, with shaky excitement he poured upon our spellbound attention a lot of queer-sounding names, names of dead-and-gone skippers, names of forgotten country ships, names of familiar and distorted sound, as if the hand of dumb time had been at work on them for ages. They stopped him at last. A silence fell upon the court,--a silence that remained unbroken for at least a minute, and passed gently into a deep murmur.
>>>

[Scenario]
A young second mate, on his first voyage with the rank, freezes during a squall and the captain takes the deck in his place. Nobody speaks of it afterwards. For the rest of the passage the mate watches the crew for any sign that they saw, and the captain for any sign that he will report it.
Setting: A barque in the Indian Ocean, 1880s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The squall came up out of the nor’-west with that stealth which is the peculiar treachery of the Indian Ocean—a blackening of the air rather than a cloud, a breathless hush that seemed to press upon the ear-drums, and then the wind, not as a gust but as a wall, solid and suffocating, that struck the barque *Lavinia* upon her starboard quarter and laid her over until her lee rail was buried in a smother of white. I was upon the poop, as it was my watch, and I remember—God knows I have had reason enough to remember—the precise quality of the light at that instant: a livid, greenish pallor, as though the sun had been drowned in the sea and its corpse-light lingered in the waste of waters. The rain followed, not drops but a deluge, a warm and blinding cataract that shut the world away and left me standing in a little circle of my own terror, solitary as a man in a tomb.

What happened in the next few minutes I have never been able to recover entire. There is a blank in my memory, a gap through which the wind screamed and the canvas thundered and the voices of the men came to me as from a great distance, distorted and meaningless. I know that I did not move. I stood with my hands upon the rail, and I felt the ship stagger and recover and stagger again, and I watched the topgallant sails tear themselves into ribbons with a kind of frozen fascination, and I did nothing—nothing at all—while the sea made fair to swallow us and the masts strained and groaned like creatures in torment. It was not fear, precisely, that held me. It was something colder and more shameful: a paralysis of the will, a sudden and complete abdication of that faculty which distinguishes the seaman from the landsman, and which I had believed—fool that I was—to be as much a part of me as the blood in my veins.

Then a hand fell upon my shoulder, and I turned to see the captain, Mr. Elias Grieve, standing at my elbow in his shirt-sleeves, bareheaded, the rain streaming from his grey beard and his eyes fixed upon me with an expression I could not read. He said nothing. He looked at me for what seemed an eternity, and then he stepped past me to the rail and began to give his orders in that flat, unhurried voice of his which had in it the quality of iron—not loud, but carrying, cutting through the roar of the elements as a knife cuts through silk. The men, who had been running wild, found their hands and their ears at once. The wheel was eased, the yards braced, the fore-topmast staysail got down and stowed, and in a space of time that I could not measure the *Lavinia* had come up to the wind and was riding it out, wet and battered but alive, while the squall passed over us and vanished into the darkness of the eastward with a last petulant flick of rain.

I stood where he had left me. I do not know how long. The stars came out, one by one, and the sea smoothed itself into that long, oily swell which follows a blow, and the ship found her rhythm again, and still I stood, my hands upon the rail, my heart a stone within me. At last I heard his step behind me, and I turned. He was lighting his pipe, shielding the match with his broad palm, and the flame illumined for an instant the deep seams of his face, the tight-shut mouth, the eyes that had seen too much to be surprised at anything—least of all at the failure of a young man upon whom he had deigned to confer the dignity of a mate’s berth.

“You had best get below,” he said, “and change your clothes. You are wet through.”

That was all. He did not speak of what had passed. He did not speak of it that night, nor the next day, nor ever. And I—I who had stood like a figurehead while the ship was in peril and the men looked to me for the word that would not come—I crept to my cabin like a whipped dog, and lay in my bunk with my face to the bulkhead, and listened to the water gurgling in the scuppers and the creak of the timbers, and wished that the sea had taken me.

In the days that followed I went about my duties with a careful and elaborate precision, as though by the mere performance of them I might somehow undo the thing that could not be undone. I watched the men. I watched them with a sickening intensity, searching their faces for that flicker of contempt which I knew must be there, for that half-smile of understanding which is worse than any open scorn. The Dutchman, Van Der Meer, who was the boatswain—a heavy, red-faced man with pale eyes and a way of looking at one sidewise—seemed to me to be always upon the point of speaking. I would catch his glance upon me in the dog-watches, and my blood would run cold, and I would turn away and busy myself with the log-line or the sand-glass, and when I looked again he would be chewing his quid and staring at the sea as though he had never had a thought of me in his life. The young fellow, Petersen, who was the other mate, a Dane with a fair, open countenance, treated me with a kindness that was worse than any cruelty. He would offer me his tobacco, or ask me to share his watch below, and I would refuse him curtly and go apart and hate him for his charity.

But it was the captain whom I watched most closely. I watched him as a man watches a judge, seeking for some sign of the sentence that is to come. He was a silent man at the best of times, given to standing apart with his pipe and his thoughts, and there was nothing in his manner that I could lay hold upon. He gave his orders as before, he took his sights and worked out his position, he walked the poop in the evening with his hands behind his back and his eyes upon the horizon. And yet I could not believe that he had forgotten. I would see him, sometimes, standing by the taffrail, looking down at the wake as it streamed away from us into the darkness, and I would fancy that he was turning over in his mind the words he would use when we came to port—the report he would make to the owners, the quiet, damning phrases that would strip me of my certificate and my livelihood and my name. I would lie awake at night and hear his voice in imagination, flat and unhurried, saying: “The second mate, sir, proved unequal to his responsibilities. Upon the night of the twelfth I was compelled to take the deck in his place.” And then the silence, and the scratching of a pen, and the end of all things.

I have heard men say that cowardice is a thing of the body only, that the spirit can rise above it. I do not believe them. I believe that what I felt in those days was a cowardice of the soul, a creeping and corrosive shame that ate into the very roots of my being and left me hollow. I had been so sure of myself—so sure of my seamanship, my nerve, my readiness to meet whatever the sea might send. And in the space of a few minutes, in the roar of a squall, I had learned that I was nothing—a man of straw, a broken reed, a creature whose will could be blown out like a candle by the first breath of danger.

We came to Aden on the twenty-third day out, and I went ashore with the captain to report to the agents. He said nothing to me on the way, and I walked beside him in a sweat of apprehension, waiting for the blow to fall. But when we were seated in the office, and the agent had asked his questions, and the captain had answered them in his flat, unemotional voice, he said nothing of the squall, nothing of my failure, nothing of the night when he had taken the deck from my hands. He spoke of the weather, of the cargo, of the run we had made, and then he rose and shook hands with the agent and we went out into the blinding sunlight, and I knew that I was saved—saved by his silence, which was more terrible than any words.

I never sailed with him again. I never asked him why he had spared me, and he never offered to tell. But I have thought of it often, in the years since, when I have walked my own quarterdeck and watched the young men under me and seen in their eyes the same fear that was in mine. And I have come to believe that he kept silent not out of mercy, but out of a deeper and more terrible knowledge—the knowledge that every man has his squall, his moment of darkness, and that the sea, which takes all things, takes also the memory of our shame and hides it in its own unfathomable silence.

shelf, peeped in to see that the contents were all right, and put it down gently on the counter. Not till that was done did he break the silence, to the effect that most likely Stevie would profit greatly by being sent out of town for a while; only he supposed his wife could not get on without him.

“Could not get on without him!” repeated Mrs Verloc slowly.  “I couldn’t
get on without him if it were for his good!  The idea!  Of course, I can
get on without him.  But there’s nowhere for him to go.”

Mr Verloc got out some brown paper and a ball of string; and meanwhile he
muttered that Michaelis was living in a little cottage in the country.
Michaelis wouldn’t mind giving Stevie a room to sleep in.  There were no
visitors and no talk there.  Michaelis was writing a book.

Mrs Verloc declared her affection for Michaelis; mentioned her abhorrence
of Karl Yundt, “nasty old man”; and of Ossipon she said nothing.  As to
Stevie, he could be no other than very pleased.  Mr Michaelis was always
so nice and kind to him.  He seemed to like the boy.  Well, the boy was a
good boy.

“You too seem to have grown quite fond of him of late,” she added, after
a pause, with her inflexible assurance.

Mr Verloc tying up the cardboard box into a parcel for the post, broke
the string by an injudicious jerk, and muttered several swear words
confidentially to himself.  Then raising his tone to the usual husky
mutter, he announced his willingness to take Stevie into the country
himself, and leave him all safe with Michaelis.

He carried out this scheme on the very next day.  Stevie offered no
objection.  He seemed rather eager, in a bewildered sort of way.  He
turned his candid gaze inquisitively to Mr Verloc’s heavy countenance at
frequent intervals, especially when his sister was not looking at him.
His expression was proud, apprehensive, and concentrated, like that of a
small child entrusted for the first time with a box of matches and the
permission to strike a light.  But Mrs Verloc, gratified by her brother’s
docility, recommended him not to dirty his clothes unduly in the country.
At this Stevie gave his sister, guardian and protector a look, which for
the first time in his life seemed to lack the quality of perfect
childlike trustfulness.  It was haughtily gloomy.  Mrs Verloc smiled.

“Goodness me!  You needn’t be offended.  You know you do get yourself
very untidy when you get a chance, Stevie.”

Mr Verloc was already gone some way down the street.

Thus in consequence of her mother’s heroic proceedings, and of her
brother’s absence on this villegiature, Mrs Verloc found herself oftener
than usual all alone not only in the shop, but in the house.  For Mr
Verloc had to take his walks.  She was alone longer than usual on the day
of the attempted bomb outrage in Greenwich Park, because Mr Verloc went
out very early that morning and did not come back till nearly dusk.  She
did not mind being alone.  She had no desire to go out.  The weather was
too bad, and the shop was cosier than the streets.  Sitting behind the
counter with some sewing, she did not raise her eyes from her work when
Mr Verloc entered in the aggressive clatter of the bell.  She had
recognised his step on the pavement outside.

She did not raise her eyes, but as Mr Verloc, silent, and with his hat
rammed down upon his forehead, made straight for the parlour door, she
said serenely:

“What a wretched day.  You’ve been perhaps to see Stevie?”

“No!  I haven’t,” said Mr Verloc softly, and slammed the glazed parlour
door behind him with unexpected energy.

For some time Mrs Verloc remained quiescent, with her work dropped in her
lap, before she put it away under the counter and got up to light the
gas.  This done, she went into the parlour on her way to the kitchen.  Mr
Verloc would want his tea presently.  Confident of the power of her
charms, Winnie did not expect from her husband in the daily intercourse
of their married life a ceremonious amenity of address and courtliness of
manner; vain and antiquated forms at best, probably never very exactly
observed, discarded nowadays even in the highest spheres, and always
foreign to the standards of her class.  She did not look for courtesies
from him.  But he was a good husband, and she had a loyal respect for his
rights.

Mrs Verloc would have gone through the parlour and on to her domestic
duties in the kitchen with the perfect serenity of a woman sure of the
power of her charms.  But a slight, very slight, and rapid rattling sound
grew upon her hearing.  Bizarre and incomprehensible, it arrested Mrs
Verloc’s attention.  Then as its character became plain to the ear she
stopped short, amazed and concerned.  Striking a match on the box she
held in her hand, she turned on and lighted, above the parlour table, one
of the two gas-burners, which, being defective, first whistled as if
astonished, and then went on purring comfortably like a cat.

Mr Verloc, against his usual practice, had thrown off his overcoat.  It
was lying on the sofa.  His hat, which he must also have thrown off,
rested overturned under the edge of the sofa.  He had dragged a chair in
front of the fireplace, and his feet planted inside the fender, his head
held between his hands, he was hanging low over the glowing grate.  His

[Scenario]
An English railway engineer surveying a line through the mountains of a small republic is caught between the government that hired him and a rebel general who controls the passes. Both demand his loyalty, and each promises that the railway will bring civilisation.
Setting: A South American republic, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The heat of the valley, a stagnant and oppressive weight, lay upon the town of Santa Rosa like a shroud, pressing the breath out of the very stones. It was a place of crumbling plaster and shuttered windows, where the silence of the siesta was broken only by the buzzing of flies in the stagnant air of the cantina, or the distant, hollow clang of a church bell marking the hours that seemed to have no beginning and no end. In the office of the Ministry of Public Works, a room high-ceilinged and vast, smelling of dust and damp leather, Mr. Arthur Pemberton sat before a map that represented not merely the topography of the land, but the intricate, treacherous web of his own existence.

Pemberton was a man of iron and calculation, an Englishman of the type that exports itself to the ends of the earth to impose order upon chaos, yet he found himself here, in the year of our Lord 1893, the object of a contest that had nothing to do with gradients or ballast. He was the pivot upon which the fate of the republic turned, and the knowledge of it sat heavy upon his soul, distinct from the physical heat. The government, represented by the sleek and sweating figure of the Minister, Don Rafael, demanded his loyalty, his signature, his genius for bridging chasms. They spoke of civilization, of progress, of the railway that would bind the coastal cities to the mineral wealth of the interior, a steel artery that would pump life into the dying body of the nation.

But the passes—the vital, narrow throats of the mountains where the line must go—were held by the General.

The General did not sit in offices. He existed in the mist and the rock, a shadow with a following of men who were less soldiers than brigands with a cause. He had sent a message, not written in ink but carried by a man with eyes like flint and a machete at his belt. The message was simple, devoid of the flowery rhetoric of the Ministry. The railway would be built, yes. But it would be built for the people, for the liberation of the valley, not for the coffers of the capital. The General, too, promised civilization—a civilization of the rifle and the shared loaf, perhaps, but a civilization nonetheless.

Pemberton looked at the map. The red line of the proposed survey snaked through the blue contortions of the Cordillera. It was a line of blood, he thought, or perhaps a line of ash. He picked up his pencil, the graphite tip hovering over the paper. To choose the route favored by the Ministry meant to invite the General’s wrath, to see his coolies shot in the ravines and his bridges blown to scrap metal before the first spike was driven. To favor the General’s pass, the difficult, jagged route through the *Quebrada del Diablo*, was to defy the men who paid his wages and held the title to the land.

He heard the door open behind him, the heavy, sweeping sound of a frock coat. It was Don Rafael. The Minister smelled of bay rum and anxiety.

“Mr. Pemberton,” Don Rafael said, his voice smooth as oil, yet quivering with a latent hysteria. “You have been staring at the mountains for an hour. They do not speak, do they? It is we who must give them a voice.”

“They speak loudly enough, Your Excellency,” Pemberton replied, not turning. His voice was dry, the English accent clipping the Spanish vowels into something hard and unyielding. “They speak of rockfalls and grades of one in forty. They speak of expense.”

“Expense is a matter for the treasury,” Don Rafael waved a hand, a gesture of magnificent, hollow indifference. “But the *morale* of the investor... ah, that is delicate. We must show that the Republic is master in its own house. We must go through the *Paso del Sol*. It is direct. It is... triumphant.”

“The *Paso del Sol* is held by the General’s nephew,” Pemberton said slowly. “If I send my surveyors there, I am sending them to their death. And if the line is cut there, the railway is a failure before it begins. It is a bad engineering decision, Don Rafael. It is a vanity.”

The Minister moved to the table, his shadow falling over the map, darkening the red line. “And the alternative? To skulk through the Devil’s Gorge? To concede that the bandit controls the arteries of the state? No, Mr. Pemberton. You English understand discipline. You understand that order must be imposed. You will go to the *Paso del Sol*. You will make the line go there.”

“And if the General objects?”

“The General is a fever,” Don Rafael said, his eyes darting to the window, as if expecting a bullet. “Fever passes. The railway remains. You have our protection. You have the army.”

“The army is in the barracks,” Pemberton muttered, turning at last to face the man. “The General is in the mountains. There is a difference between a map and a territory, Your Excellency.”

Don Rafael smiled, a thin stretching of the lips that did not reach his eyes. “Then make the map the territory, Mr. Pemberton. That is what we pay you for. Civilisation is not a gift, you know. It is an act of violence. It is the cutting away of the wilderness.”

He left then, leaving behind the scent of cologne and the crushing weight of the command. Pemberton sat back in his chair. The light in the room was failing, the shadows lengthening, turning the white plaster of the walls to a bruised purple. He felt a profound, weary disgust—not with the General, who was a savage with a code, nor with the Minister, who was a thief with a title, but with the iron rails themselves. He had thought them a force of logic, of geometry. Here, they were merely a rope for hanging men.

He rose and walked to the window, looking out at the darkening silhouette of the mountains. They were immense, indifferent, and terrible. Somewhere up there, in the cold air, the General was waiting. He would demand an answer soon. He would demand a signature on the ground, written in the dust of the trail.

Pemberton realized then that his loyalty was a currency that could not be spent in two markets. He had been hired to bring light to this dark place, but the light he carried was merely a lantern that illuminated the faces of the men who wanted to steal the oil. The railway would come, yes. It would snake its way through the rock, indifferent to the blood spilled to lay it. It would bring the trains, the clocks, the ledgers. But it would not bring justice. It would only bring the means to exploit the injustice more efficiently.

He picked up his heavy theodolite case, checking the brass fittings with a mechanical tenderness. It was the only honest thing in the room. It measured what was there, not what was desired. He would go out at dawn. He would not go to the *Paso del Sol*, nor to the Devil’s Gorge. He would go to the place where the earth demanded to be crossed, where the physics of the slope allowed it. He would let the mountain decide.

And if the General shot him, or the Minister dismissed him, it would be a small matter in the long, indifferent history of the Cordillera. The silence of the room pressed in again, heavy as the heat of the coming day. Pemberton lit the lamp, the small flame trembling in the glass, a fragile, solitary spark against the encroaching dark. He sat down to write his letter of resignation, or perhaps his letter of acceptance. He did not know which. He only knew that the line must be drawn, and that he was the hand holding the pencil.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.
<<<
flames burst forth, and the stone faces awakened, stared out of fire.

A faint murmur arose about the house from the few people who were left
there, and there was a saddling of a horse and riding away. There was
spurring and splashing through the darkness, and bridle was drawn in the
space by the village fountain, and the horse in a foam stood at Monsieur
Gabelle’s door. “Help, Gabelle! Help, every one!” The tocsin rang
impatiently, but other help (if that were any) there was none. The
mender of roads, and two hundred and fifty particular friends, stood
with folded arms at the fountain, looking at the pillar of fire in the
sky. “It must be forty feet high,” said they, grimly; and never moved.

The rider from the chateau, and the horse in a foam, clattered away
through the village, and galloped up the stony steep, to the prison on
the crag. At the gate, a group of officers were looking at the fire;
removed from them, a group of soldiers. “Help, gentlemen--officers! The
chateau is on fire; valuable objects may be saved from the flames by
timely aid! Help, help!” The officers looked towards the soldiers who
looked at the fire; gave no orders; and answered, with shrugs and biting
of lips, “It must burn.”

As the rider rattled down the hill again and through the street, the
village was illuminating. The mender of roads, and the two hundred and
fifty particular friends, inspired as one man and woman by the idea of
lighting up, had darted into their houses, and were putting candles in
every dull little pane of glass. The general scarcity of everything,
occasioned candles to be borrowed in a rather peremptory manner of
Monsieur Gabelle; and in a moment of reluctance and hesitation on
that functionary’s part, the mender of roads, once so submissive to
authority, had remarked that carriages were good to make bonfires with,
and that post-horses would roast.

The chateau was left to itself to flame and burn. In the roaring and
raging of the conflagration, a red-hot wind, driving straight from the
infernal regions, seemed to be blowing the edifice away. With the rising
and falling of the blaze, the stone faces showed as if they were in
torment. When great masses of stone and timber fell, the face with the
two dints in the nose became obscured: anon struggled out of the smoke
again, as if it were the face of the cruel Marquis, burning at the stake
and contending with the fire.

The chateau burned; the nearest trees, laid hold of by the fire,
scorched and shrivelled; trees at a distance, fired by the four fierce
figures, begirt the blazing edifice with a new forest of smoke. Molten
lead and iron boiled in the marble basin of the fountain; the water ran
dry; the extinguisher tops of the towers vanished like ice before the
heat, and trickled down into four rugged wells of flame. Great rents and
splits branched out in the solid walls, like crystallisation; stupefied
birds wheeled about and dropped into the furnace; four fierce figures
trudged away, East, West, North, and South, along the night-enshrouded
roads, guided by the beacon they had lighted, towards their next
destination. The illuminated village had seized hold of the tocsin, and,
abolishing the lawful ringer, rang for joy.

Not only that; but the village, light-headed with famine, fire, and
bell-ringing, and bethinking itself that Monsieur Gabelle had to do with
the collection of rent and taxes--though it was but a small instalment
of taxes, and no rent at all, that Gabelle had got in those latter
days--became impatient for an interview with him, and, surrounding his
house, summoned him to come forth for personal conference. Whereupon,
Monsieur Gabelle did heavily bar his door, and retire to hold counsel
with himself. The result of that conference was, that Gabelle again
withdrew himself to his housetop behind his stack of chimneys; this time
resolved, if his door were broken in (he was a small Southern man
of retaliative temperament), to pitch himself head foremost over the
parapet, and crush a man or two below.

Probably, Monsieur Gabelle passed a long night up there, with the
distant chateau for fire and candle, and the beating at his door,
combined with the joy-ringing, for music; not to mention his having an
ill-omened lamp slung across the road before his posting-house gate,
which the village showed a lively inclination to displace in his favour.
A trying suspense, to be passing a whole summer night on the brink of
the black ocean, ready to take that plunge into it upon which Monsieur
Gabelle had resolved! But, the friendly dawn appearing at last, and the
rush-candles of the village guttering out, the people happily dispersed,
and Monsieur Gabelle came down bringing his life with him for that
while.

Within a hundred miles, and in the light of other fires, there were
other functionaries less fortunate, that night and other nights, whom
the rising sun found hanging across once-peaceful streets, where they
had been born and bred; also, there were other villagers and townspeople
less fortunate than the mender of roads and his fellows, upon whom the
functionaries and soldiery turned with success, and whom they strung up
in their turn. But, the fierce figures were steadily wending East, West,
North, and South, be that as it would; and whosoever hung, fire burned.
The altitude of the gallows that would turn to water and quench it,
no functionary, by any stretch of mathematics, was able to calculate
successfully.

In such risings of fire and risings of sea--the firm earth shaken by the rushes of an angry ocean which had now no ebb, but was always on the flow, higher and higher, to the terror and wonder of the beholders on the shore--three years of tempest were consumed. [Scenario]
A pompous alderman who has organised a banquet to celebrate a new town hall discovers on the morning of the feast that the contractor has run off with the funds and the roof is unfinished. He must preside over the banquet in the rain without admitting anything is wrong.
Setting: A Midlands market town, 1850s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
If any mortal man, in that autumn of the year eighteen hundred and fifty-something—for the exact date is of no consequence to the moral of the matter—had been told that the Borough of Muddlecombe was not the very crown and glory of the Midland counties, he would have demanded satisfaction, or at the very least, a very public apology. But of all the glories of Muddlecombe, its indisputable pivot, its sun, its moon, and its principal constellation, was Alderman Bumbleton; a gentleman who carried his corporation upon his stomach, and his sense of civic pride in his voice, which was a deep, foggy, and melodious instrument, admirably suited to the proposing of toasts and the crushing of opposition.

It was upon a raw and drizzling morning that the said alderman stood in the grand, or rather the intended grand, apartment of the New Town Hall. The building had been erected at vast public expense, to celebrate which, and to dedicate the edifice to the palate and the pocket of the ratepayer, a grand banquet was to be held that very day. The hall was certainly capacious; but its capaciousness was of a sort that admitted not only the tables and chairs, but the entire sky. The roof—which was to have been a miracle of hammer-beam and slate—was not there. It had been expected. It had been paid for. But it was absent. The contractor, a gentleman of fluid capital and nomadic habits, had departed for the Continent in the dead of night, carrying with him the funds, the plans, and, indeed, the very moral obligation to cover the town’s head.

A great gap, a jagged and irregular aperture, yawned overhead, through which the clouds were slowly and damply assembling, like a congregation of wet blankets. Workmen’s ladders leaned against the bare walls like skeletons leaning against the ramparts of a fallen castle.

Alderman Bumbleton surveyed the void. His civic chain, a massive golden collar, lay heavy upon his chest, but not so heavy as the weight of his pride. To admit a fault was, in the alderman’s philosophy, a confession of weakness; and to confess weakness was to abdicate the throne of respectability.

"Mr. Grubble," said the Alderman to his clerk, a thin, pale man with a cough that sounded like the rustling of dry leaves.

"Your Worship?" said Mr. Grubble, with a shiver that was partly physical and partly professional.

"The—ah—the architectural effect of this ceiling," said the Alderman, waving a plump hand towards the clouds, "is striking. Striking, sir. It conveys a sense of—of amplitude."

"It conveys a draught, your Worship," said Grubble, venturing a polite but miserable whisper.

"A draught, sir?" thundered the Alderman, his voice echoing off the unfinished brickwork. "A draught is a thing of health! It is the breath of the atmosphere, sir! It is the very essence of ventilation! And ventilation is the boast of the modern age!"

Mr. Grubble said no more. He had a wife and four small children, and his courage, never a robust plant, had withered under the aldermanic eye.

The guests began to arrive. They came in carriages and in gigs, in cloaks and in greatcoats, for the rain had now begun to fall with a steady, determined, and altogether unfunny perseverance. They were the elite of Muddlecombe: the Mayor, the Magistrates, the Solicitors, the Doctors, and those neutral gentlemen of no particular profession but considerable appetite, who are to be found in every market town, clustered about the inns and the auction-rooms, like flies about a sugar-barrel.

They entered the hall, and they looked up. The rain fell upon their hats. A drop fell upon the nose of the Mayor, who was a nervous man with a watery eye, and he started as if he had been struck by a fairy.

"Bless my soul!" said the Mayor. "It is—it is precipitating!"

"It is a feature, sir," said Alderman Bumbleton, advancing with a beaming, rubicund countenance, upon which the rain was now falling as freely as upon a turnip in a field. "A feature of the design! An open-air amphitheatre, sir! A tribute to the ancients! The Greeks, sir, the Romans! Did they shelter themselves from the heavens? No, sir! They rejoiced in the dew of the gods! Besides," he added, dropping his voice to a confidential roar, "the—ah—the contractor has been called away on urgent business. A sudden indisposition of his mother-in-law, I understand. The roof will follow."

They sat down to table. The tables were long, and white, and damp. The cloth was wet, as if it had been drawn through a pond. The soup was cold. The fish was cold. The meat was cold. But the guests, being Englishmen, and being furthermore accustomed to the consumption of cold meats at picnics, bore it with a fortitude that was only slightly undermined by the occasional sneeze.

The waiters, in a frantic endeavor to preserve some semblance of dryness, had erected a series of umbrellas, of various colors and conditions, over the central table. This gave to the banquet the appearance of a bazaar, or a rag-fair, or a congregation of distressed mushrooms.

Alderman Bumbleton, seated at the center, beneath a gingham parasol of extraordinary dimensions, which he had borrowed from his landlady, beamed upon the assembly. The rain ran down his cheeks and collected in the creases of his chin, like tears in the folds of a benevolent stone image. He tapped his glass. The tinkling sound was somewhat deadened by the pattering of the rain upon the tables and the cloth, and upon the hats of the guests, and upon the soup.

"Gentlemen!" said the Alderman. "I give you the New Town Hall!"

"Hear, hear!" said the guests, with a modified enthusiasm, and a simultaneous reaching for their pocket-handkerchiefs.

"A structure, sir," continued the Alderman, addressing himself to the Mayor, who was mopping his brow with a napkin already saturated, "that will stand for centuries! A monument to the enterprise, the public spirit, and the—ah—the broad and comprehensive views of the Borough of Muddlecombe!"

"Very broad," muttered a solicitor from under a dripping umbrella. "As broad as the sky."

"The roof," pursued the Alderman, with a grand disregard of the element that was even then soaking his shirt-collar, "is a triumph of engineering. It is not yet visible to the naked eye, sir, because it is of a—a—soaring nature. It is in transit. It is coming. It will arrive. And when it does, sir, it will cover us with glory!"

"It covers us with water now," said the same solicitor, who was a man of some local reputation for plain speaking, and a considerable quantity of port.

"That, sir," said Alderman Bumbleton, turning upon him with a look that would have withered a less seasoned legal gentleman, "is the dew of prosperity! It is—ah—it is the beneficent influence of the atmosphere upon our municipal institutions! It is, if I may say so, the very rain of heaven, which falls alike upon the just and the unjust, but which, today, falls with a peculiar and distinguishing favor upon the just, who are here assembled!"

A ragged cheer arose, somewhat dampened by the simultaneous sneezing of the Mayor, who had now begun to show symptoms of a violent cold in the head.

The courses followed one another with the slow and dismal regularity of a funeral procession. The venison was sodden. The pastry was flabby. The jelly melted before it reached the mouth. The wine was diluted, not by the dishonest vintner, but by the impartial clouds. The very candles, guttering and flaring in the draught, seemed to weep, and to shed tears of tallow upon the cloth.

And yet, through it all, Alderman Bumbleton sat erect, and smiled, and ate, and drank, and talked. He talked of the future of Muddlecombe. He talked of the docks, the railways, the gas-works. He talked of the destiny of the Anglo-Saxon race. He talked of anything and everything but the roof. He did not look up. He did not allow his eye to wander to that melancholy void, through which the rain continued to descend with a monotonous and relentless industry, as if it had been hired by the hour to perform that particular function.

The band, which had been engaged at great expense, and which was stationed in a gallery that was also unfinished, and open to the sky, played "Rule Britannia" and "God Save the Queen," with a vigor that was only slightly impaired by the fact that the wind blew through their instruments, and the rain wet their music, and the trombone-player was observed to be weeping, though whether from patriotic emotion or from personal discomfort, it was impossible to determine.

The toasts were drunk. The speeches were made. The Mayor, sneezing violently, proposed the health of Alderman Bumbleton, the father of the New Town Hall. The Alderman, in replying, rose to the highest pitch of his rhetoric. He stood, a colossal figure, wet but unsubdued. The rain fell upon his bare head, for he had removed his hat in deference to the occasion, and it ran down his face and his neck and his corporation, and it even penetrated to the very marrow of his boots.

"Gentlemen," he said, "I thank you. I have labored for this town. I have spent my days and my nights in its service. I have erected this hall. It may not be—ah—quite finished. There may be a—a slight deficiency in the matter of the roof. But, gentlemen, what is a roof? What is any roof, but a—a concession to human weakness? A roof is a shelter from the storm. But we, gentlemen, do not fear the storm! We are Muddlecombe men! We are Midland men! We are Englishmen! And an Englishman, sir, is not to be deterred by a little—a little aqueous interruption, from the performance of his duty, or the enjoyment of his dinner!"

He sat down amidst a thunder of applause, which was mingled with the thunder of the clouds, which had now begun to rumble in a most unpromising and aldermanic manner.

The banquet broke up. The guests dispersed, dripping and discontented, to their homes. Alderman Bumbleton remained to the last. He stood alone in the midst of the ruined feast, the wet cloths, the sodden fragments, the guttering candles, and the open sky. He looked up at last. The rain fell full upon his face. He drew a long breath. He buttoned his coat. And then, with a slow and stately step, he marched out of the New Town Hall, carrying his corporation, his dignity, and his wet boots, into the gloom of the autumn evening, a monument to the unyielding nature of civic pride.
