If any mortal man, in that autumn of the year eighteen hundred and fifty-something—for the exact date is of no consequence to the moral of the matter—had been told that the Borough of Muddlecombe was not the very crown and glory of the Midland counties, he would have demanded satisfaction, or at the very least, a very public apology. But of all the glories of Muddlecombe, its indisputable pivot, its sun, its moon, and its principal constellation, was Alderman Bumbleton; a gentleman who carried his corporation upon his stomach, and his sense of civic pride in his voice, which was a deep, foggy, and melodious instrument, admirably suited to the proposing of toasts and the crushing of opposition.

It was upon a raw and drizzling morning that the said alderman stood in the grand, or rather the intended grand, apartment of the New Town Hall. The building had been erected at vast public expense, to celebrate which, and to dedicate the edifice to the palate and the pocket of the ratepayer, a grand banquet was to be held that very day. The hall was certainly capacious; but its capaciousness was of a sort that admitted not only the tables and chairs, but the entire sky. The roof—which was to have been a miracle of hammer-beam and slate—was not there. It had been expected. It had been paid for. But it was absent. The contractor, a gentleman of fluid capital and nomadic habits, had departed for the Continent in the dead of night, carrying with him the funds, the plans, and, indeed, the very moral obligation to cover the town’s head.

A great gap, a jagged and irregular aperture, yawned overhead, through which the clouds were slowly and damply assembling, like a congregation of wet blankets. Workmen’s ladders leaned against the bare walls like skeletons leaning against the ramparts of a fallen castle.

Alderman Bumbleton surveyed the void. His civic chain, a massive golden collar, lay heavy upon his chest, but not so heavy as the weight of his pride. To admit a fault was, in the alderman’s philosophy, a confession of weakness; and to confess weakness was to abdicate the throne of respectability.

"Mr. Grubble," said the Alderman to his clerk, a thin, pale man with a cough that sounded like the rustling of dry leaves.

"Your Worship?" said Mr. Grubble, with a shiver that was partly physical and partly professional.

"The—ah—the architectural effect of this ceiling," said the Alderman, waving a plump hand towards the clouds, "is striking. Striking, sir. It conveys a sense of—of amplitude."

"It conveys a draught, your Worship," said Grubble, venturing a polite but miserable whisper.

"A draught, sir?" thundered the Alderman, his voice echoing off the unfinished brickwork. "A draught is a thing of health! It is the breath of the atmosphere, sir! It is the very essence of ventilation! And ventilation is the boast of the modern age!"

Mr. Grubble said no more. He had a wife and four small children, and his courage, never a robust plant, had withered under the aldermanic eye.

The guests began to arrive. They came in carriages and in gigs, in cloaks and in greatcoats, for the rain had now begun to fall with a steady, determined, and altogether unfunny perseverance. They were the elite of Muddlecombe: the Mayor, the Magistrates, the Solicitors, the Doctors, and those neutral gentlemen of no particular profession but considerable appetite, who are to be found in every market town, clustered about the inns and the auction-rooms, like flies about a sugar-barrel.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.

He saw the Jew with his half-closed eyes; heard his low whistling; and recognised the sound of the spoon grating against the saucepan’s sides: and yet the self-same senses were mentally engaged, at the same time, in busy action with almost everybody he had ever known.

When the coffee was done, the Jew drew the saucepan to the hob.
Standing, then in an irresolute attitude for a few minutes, as if he
did not well know how to employ himself, he turned round and looked at
Oliver, and called him by his name. He did not answer, and was to all
appearances asleep.

After satisfying himself upon this head, the Jew stepped gently to the
door: which he fastened. He then drew forth: as it seemed to Oliver,
from some trap in the floor: a small box, which he placed carefully on
the table. His eyes glistened as he raised the lid, and looked in.
Dragging an old chair to the table, he sat down; and took from it a
magnificent gold watch, sparkling with jewels.

“Aha!” said the Jew, shrugging up his shoulders, and distorting every
feature with a hideous grin. “Clever dogs! Clever dogs! Staunch to the
last! Never told the old parson where they were. Never poached upon old
Fagin! And why should they? It wouldn’t have loosened the knot, or kept
the drop up, a minute longer. No, no, no! Fine fellows! Fine fellows!”

With these, and other muttered reflections of the like nature, the Jew
once more deposited the watch in its place of safety. At least half a
dozen more were severally drawn forth from the same box, and surveyed
with equal pleasure; besides rings, brooches, bracelets, and other
articles of jewellery, of such magnificent materials, and costly
workmanship, that Oliver had no idea, even of their names.

Having replaced these trinkets, the Jew took out another: so small that
it lay in the palm of his hand. There seemed to be some very minute
inscription on it; for the Jew laid it flat upon the table, and shading
it with his hand, pored over it, long and earnestly. At length he put
it down, as if despairing of success; and, leaning back in his chair,
muttered:

“What a fine thing capital punishment is! Dead men never repent; dead
men never bring awkward stories to light. Ah, it’s a fine thing for the
trade! Five of ’em strung up in a row, and none left to play booty, or
turn white-livered!”

As the Jew uttered these words, his bright dark eyes, which had been
staring vacantly before him, fell on Oliver’s face; the boy’s eyes were
fixed on his in mute curiousity; and although the recognition was only
for an instant—for the briefest space of time that can possibly be
conceived—it was enough to show the old man that he had been observed.

He closed the lid of the box with a loud crash; and, laying his hand on
a bread knife which was on the table, started furiously up. He trembled
very much though; for, even in his terror, Oliver could see that the
knife quivered in the air.

“What’s that?” said the Jew. “What do you watch me for? Why are you
awake? What have you seen? Speak out, boy! Quick—quick! for your life.”

“I wasn’t able to sleep any longer, sir,” replied Oliver, meekly. “I am
very sorry if I have disturbed you, sir.”

“You were not awake an hour ago?” said the Jew, scowling fiercely on
the boy.

“No! No, indeed!” replied Oliver.

“Are you sure?” cried the Jew: with a still fiercer look than before:
and a threatening attitude.

“Upon my word I was not, sir,” replied Oliver, earnestly. “I was not,
indeed, sir.”

“Tush, tush, my dear!” said the Jew, abruptly resuming his old manner,
and playing with the knife a little, before he laid it down; as if to
induce the belief that he had caught it up, in mere sport. “Of course I
know that, my dear. I only tried to frighten you. You’re a brave boy.
Ha! ha! you’re a brave boy, Oliver.” The Jew rubbed his hands with a
chuckle, but glanced uneasily at the box, notwithstanding.

“Did you see any of these pretty things, my dear?” said the Jew, laying
his hand upon it after a short pause.

“Yes, sir,” replied Oliver.

“Ah!” said the Jew, turning rather pale. “They—they’re mine, Oliver; my
little property. All I have to live upon, in my old age. The folks call
me a miser, my dear. Only a miser; that’s all.”

Oliver thought the old gentleman must be a decided miser to live in
such a dirty place, with so many watches; but, thinking that perhaps
his fondness for the Dodger and the other boys, cost him a good deal of
money, he only cast a deferential look at the Jew, and asked if he
might get up.

“Certainly, my dear, certainly,” replied the old gentleman. “Stay.
There’s a pitcher of water in the corner by the door. Bring it here;
and I’ll give you a basin to wash in, my dear.”

Oliver got up; walked across the room; and stooped for an instant to
raise the pitcher. When he turned his head, the box was gone.

He had scarcely washed himself, and made everything tidy, by emptying
the basin out of the window, agreeably to the Jew’s directions, when
the Dodger returned: accompanied by a very sprightly young friend, whom
Oliver had seen smoking on the previous night, and who was now formally
introduced to him as Charley Bates. The four sat down, to breakfast, on
the coffee, and some hot rolls and ham which the Dodger had brought
home in the crown of his hat.

“Well,” said the Jew, glancing slyly at Oliver, and addressing himself
to the Dodger, “I hope you’ve been at work this morning, my dears?”

“Hard,” replied the Dodger.

“As nails,” added Charley Bates.

[Scenario]
A young clerk in a shipping office wins a modest prize in a public lottery and resolves to keep it secret from his grasping relations. Within a week every one of them has heard of it, and each arrives at his lodging with a misfortune requiring exactly the amount he has won.
Setting: The City of London, 1840s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
Mr. Peregrine Pym, junior clerk in the shipping firm of Bodkins, Blunt & Fogg, was a young man whose entire worldly fortune, until a certain Tuesday in the month of November, might have been contained within a thimble, with room to spare for his modest hopes and a small collection of buttonholes. His existence was a quiet, unvarnished one, spent in the dim, ink-scented labyrinth of a counting-house in Leadenhall Street, where the scratching of pens was the only music, and the only drama was the slow, inexorable march of ledgers from one side of a desk to the other. Lodging in a single, narrow room in a house that leaned over a grimy court off Fetter Lane, Mr. Pym was a man of routine and routine’s quiet desperation, until the day a ticket in the Grand Metropolitan Lottery, purchased on a whim with a sixpence he had almost regretted spending, awarded him the sum of one hundred and seventeen pounds, fourteen shillings, and sixpence.

This was not a fortune to set the Thames on fire; it would not have purchased a single share in a respectable steam-vessel; but to Mr. Pym it was a treasure of Croesus, a golden mountain rising from the flat, grey plain of his life. It was a secret, a delicious, private hoard, and he resolved, with all the determination of a man who had never had a secret worth keeping, that it should remain so. He knew his relations, the Pym and the Cribb connection, as a botanist knows a patch of particularly tenacious weeds. They were a grasping, needy, and wonderfully imaginative family, whose misfortunes were always precisely timed and whose requirements were invariably calibrated to the exact measure of any available funds. To them, Mr. Pym’s good fortune would be not his own, but a communal resource, a pot of honey into which they would dip their sticky fingers with cheerful unanimity.

For six days, Mr. Pym kept his counsel. He banked his prize in the London and Provincial, and walked the streets with the light, buoyant step of a man who has a sovereign in his pocket and a secret in his heart. He bought a new neckerchief. He dined on a chop. He felt, for the first time, like a person of consequence. On the seventh day, as a damp November fog pressed its grimy face against his window-pane, the siege began.

It was heralded by a thunderous knocking at the door below, a knock that spoke of grievous tidings and an urgent desire for tea. Mrs. Flinders, his landlady, a woman whose face was a permanent expression of weary anticipation, announced a visitor. It was his aunt, Mrs. Cribb, a lady built on the lines of a funereal monument and dressed in the perpetual weeds of some long-forgotten sorrow. She swept into the small room, filling it with the scent of camphor and impending doom.

“Peregrine!” she began, pressing a damp glove to her brow. “Oh, my dear boy, you will scarcely credit the calamity that has befallen us! Your cousin, Bartholomew, that bright, promising boy…”

Mr. Pym’s heart sank. Bartholomew was a young man of thirty-five whose promising qualities had so far eluded discovery. “What has happened to him, Aunt?”

“He is to be married!” she cried, as if announcing a terminal illness. “To a Miss Prattle, of Peckham, whose family, I am sorry to say, has no notion of how a wedding ought to be conducted. The dress, the flowers, the breakfast at the Dog and Duck—it is a vortex of expense! Bartholomew, my poor, dear boy, finds himself short. A trifle, a mere bagatelle, but it is the little stones that cause the coach to overturn. He requires, to see the happy couple safely upon their way, the sum of precisely fifty pounds.”

Mr. Pym, flustered and cornered, stammered that he was a man of small means. But Mrs. Cribb was a force of nature. She painted a picture of Bartholomew’s ruin, of the bride’s disappointment, of the family name dragged through the mud of Peckham, with such persuasive gloom that Mr. Pym, before he knew what he was doing, was writing a cheque. As she departed, dabbing at her eyes with a triumphant air, she patted his hand. “You are a good boy, Peregrine. A true Pym. We knew we could rely on you.”

He had scarcely time to mourn the loss of fifty pounds when, an hour later, the knocking recommenced. This time it was his uncle, Mr. Silas Pym, a man who dealt in damaged goods and sorrows of a wholesale nature. He entered with a sigh that seemed to contain all the wind and rain of the preceding decade.

“Nephew,” he said, sinking into a chair. “Disaster. A catastrophe of the first water. The brig *Sea Serpent*, bound for Riga with a cargo of—well, no matter what—a fine, upstanding cargo—has gone down. All hands, and all goods, lost to the merciless deep.”

“Good heavens!” said Mr. Pym.

“My underwriter,” continued Mr. Pym, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, “is a man of stone, a veritable granite block of a man. He will not advance a penny until the paperwork is in order. But the captain’s widow, a poor, weeping creature, requires an immediate sum for sustenance and passage back to her family in Portsmouth. It is a matter of life and death, Peregrine. A temporary loan, you understand. A loan of exactly forty pounds, to be repaid the moment the insurance is settled.”

The sum was so specific, the story so tragically convenient, that Mr. Pym felt a cold dread. But the image of the weeping widow and the granite-hearted underwriter was too powerful. With a heavy sigh, he wrote another cheque. Uncle Silas clapped him on the shoulder, his grief instantly evaporating. “Sound man, Peregrine. A rock. I shall not forget this.” He departed, leaving behind the faint smell of stale brandy and impending litigation.

Mr. Pym sat in a state of profound shock. He had given away ninety pounds. His golden mountain was now a mere hillock. He calculated what remained: twenty-seven pounds, fourteen shillings, and sixpence. A respectable sum, but not the transformative one he had dreamed of. He would have to be more resolute. He must harden his heart.

He was still engaged in this difficult moral exercise when the third and final assault was mounted. It was his cousin, Arabella Cribb, a young lady whose life was a perpetual drama of thwarted ambition and inadequate bonnets. She burst into the room in a cloud of frantic energy and smelling salts.

“Oh, Peregrine! You will never guess! My triumph! My undoing!” she cried. “The celebrated Signor Fantocini has chosen *me*! Me, for the part of Ophelia at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane! It is the chance of a lifetime!”

“Why, Arabella, that is wonderful news!” said Mr. Pym, genuinely pleased.

“It is a disaster!” she wailed. “For I have nothing to wear! The costume, the gowns, the very feathers for the mad scene must be of the finest silk! Signor Fantocini is a tyrant of taste. He has looked upon my own poor wardrobe and wept. I require a complete new set of theatrical finery. The cost, from Madame Fifi’s in Covent Garden, is a matter of grave importance. I am short, by the most cruel stroke of fate, of precisely twenty-seven pounds.”

Mr. Pym stared at her. Twenty-seven pounds. The exact amount of his remaining capital, down to the last shilling. The coincidence was so perfect, so audaciously calculated, that he almost laughed. He looked from Arabella’s pleading, desperate face to the window, where the fog swirled like a dirty spectre of his own lost fortune. He thought of Bartholomew’s wedding, of the *Sea Serpent*’s watery grave, of his own foolish, secretive pride. He had wanted to be a man of substance, but he was merely a man of substance to be extracted.

With a feeling of utter resignation, he took out his chequebook. He wrote the final cheque for twenty-seven pounds, leaving the fourteen shillings and sixpence for his own use. Arabella seized the paper, kissed him fervently on the cheek, and swept out of the room, her mission accomplished, her tragedy averted.

Mr. Pym sat alone in the silence. His secret was out; his fortune was gone. He was precisely where he had been a week ago, save for a new neckerchief and a profound education in the ways of the world. As he sat there, a strange, bubbling sound began to issue from his chest. It grew into a chuckle, then a full-throated, helpless laugh. He had been a fool, a prize goose, a veritable lottery of one for his relations to pluck. And yet, as the laughter subsided, he felt not bitterness, but a peculiar lightness. The secret had been a burden; the fortune, a temptation. He picked up his pen, dipped it in the ink, and began to draft a letter of application for a small raise in his wages, a sum so modest and so entirely his own that no one would ever think to ask him for it. Outside, the fog began to lift.

His existence was a quiet, unvarnished one, spent in the dim, ink-scented labyrinth of a counting-house in Leadenhall Street, where the scratching of pens was the only music, and the only drama was the slow, inexorable march of ledgers from one side of a desk to the other. Lodging in a single, narrow room in a house that leaned over a grimy court off Fetter Lane, Mr. Pym was a man of routine and routine’s quiet desperation, until the day a ticket in the Grand Metropolitan Lottery, purchased on a whim with a sixpence he had almost regretted spending, awarded him the sum of one hundred and seventeen pounds, fourteen shillings, and sixpence.

This was not a fortune to set the Thames on fire; it would not have purchased a single share in a respectable steam-vessel; but to Mr. Pym it was a treasure of Croesus, a golden mountain rising from the flat, grey plain of his life. It was a secret, a delicious, private hoard, and he resolved, with all the determination of a man who had never had a secret worth keeping, that it should remain so. He knew his relations, the Pym and the Cribb connection, as a botanist knows a patch of particularly tenacious weeds. They were a grasping, needy, and wonderfully imaginative family, whose misfortunes were always precisely timed and whose requirements were invariably calibrated to the exact measure of any available funds. To them, Mr. Pym’s good fortune would be not his own, but a communal resource, a pot of honey into which they would dip their sticky fingers with cheerful unanimity.

For six days, Mr. Pym kept his counsel. He banked his prize in the London and Provincial, and walked the streets with the light, buoyant step of a man who has a sovereign in his pocket and a secret in his heart. He bought a new neckerchief. He dined on a chop. He felt, for the first time, like a person of consequence. On the seventh day, as a damp November fog pressed its grimy face against his window-pane, the siege began.

It was heralded by a thunderous knocking at the door below, a knock that spoke of grievous tidings and an urgent desire for tea. Mrs. Flinders, his landlady, a woman whose face was a permanent expression of weary anticipation, announced a visitor. It was his aunt, Mrs. Cribb, a lady built on the lines of a funereal monument and dressed in the perpetual weeds of some long-forgotten sorrow. She swept into the small room, filling it with the scent of camphor and impending doom.

“Peregrine!” she began, pressing a damp glove to her brow. “Oh, my dear boy, you will scarcely credit the calamity that has befallen us! Your cousin, Bartholomew, that bright, promising boy…”

Mr. Pym’s heart sank. Bartholomew was a young man of thirty-five whose promising qualities had so far eluded discovery. “What has happened to him, Aunt?”

“He is to be married!” she cried, as if announcing a terminal illness. “To a Miss Prattle, of Peckham, whose family, I am sorry to say, has no notion of how a wedding ought to be conducted. The dress, the flowers, the breakfast at the Dog and Duck—it is a vortex of expense! Bartholomew, my poor, dear boy, finds himself short. A trifle, a mere bagatelle, but it is the little stones that cause the coach to overturn. He requires, to see the happy couple safely upon their way, the sum of precisely fifty pounds.”

Mr. Pym, flustered and cornered, stammered that he was a man of small means. But Mrs. Cribb was a force of nature. She painted a picture of Bartholomew’s ruin, of the bride’s disappointment, of the family name dragged through the mud of Peckham, with such persuasive gloom that Mr. Pym, before he knew what he was doing, was writing a cheque. As she departed, dabbing at her eyes with a triumphant air, she patted his hand. “You are a good boy, Peregrine. A true Pym. We knew we could rely on you.”

He had scarcely time to mourn the loss of fifty pounds when, an hour later, the knocking recommenced. This time it was his uncle, Mr. Silas Pym, a man who dealt in damaged goods and sorrows of a wholesale nature. He entered with a sigh that seemed to contain all the wind and rain of the preceding decade.

“Nephew,” he said, sinking into a chair. “Disaster. A catastrophe of the first water. The brig *Sea Serpent*, bound for Riga with a cargo of—well, no matter what—a fine, upstanding cargo—has gone down. All hands, and all goods, lost to the merciless deep.”

“Good heavens!” said Mr. Pym.

“My underwriter,” continued Mr. Pym, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, “is a man of stone, a veritable granite block of a man. He will not advance a penny until the paperwork is in order. But the captain’s widow, a poor, weeping creature, requires an immediate sum for sustenance and passage back to her family in Portsmouth. It is a matter of life and death, Peregrine. A temporary loan, you understand. A loan of exactly forty pounds, to be repaid the moment the insurance is settled.”

The sum was so specific, the story so tragically convenient, that Mr. Pym felt a cold dread. But the image of the weeping widow and the granite-hearted underwriter was too powerful. With a heavy sigh, he wrote another cheque. Uncle Silas clapped him on the shoulder, his grief instantly evaporating. “Sound man, Peregrine. A rock. I shall not forget this.” He departed, leaving behind the faint smell of stale brandy and impending litigation.

Mr. Pym sat in a state of profound shock. He had given away ninety pounds. His golden mountain was now a mere hillock. He calculated what remained: twenty-seven pounds, fourteen shillings, and sixpence. A respectable sum, but not the transformative one he had dreamed of. He would have to be more resolute. He must harden his heart.

He was still engaged in this difficult moral exercise when the third and final assault was mounted. It was his cousin, Arabella Cribb, a young lady whose life was a perpetual drama of thwarted ambition and inadequate bonnets. She burst into the room in a cloud of frantic energy and smelling salts.

“Oh, Peregrine! You will never guess! My triumph! My undoing!” she cried. “The celebrated Signor Fantocini has chosen *me*! Me, for the part of Ophelia at the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane! It is the chance of a lifetime!”

“Why, Arabella, that is wonderful news!” said Mr. Pym, genuinely pleased.

“It is a disaster!” she wailed. “For I have nothing to wear! The costume, the gowns, the very feathers for the mad scene must be of the finest silk! Signor Fantocini is a tyrant of taste. He has looked upon my own poor wardrobe and wept. I require a complete new set of theatrical finery. The cost, from Madame Fifi’s in Covent Garden, is a matter of grave importance. I am short, by the most cruel stroke of fate, of precisely twenty-seven pounds.”

Mr. Pym stared at her. Twenty-seven pounds. The exact amount of his remaining capital, down to the last shilling. The coincidence was so perfect, so audaciously calculated, that he almost laughed. He looked from Arabella’s pleading, desperate face to the window, where the fog swirled like a dirty spectre of his own lost fortune. He thought of Bartholomew’s wedding, of the *Sea Serpent*’s watery grave, of his own foolish, secretive pride. He had wanted to be a man of substance, but he was merely a man of substance to be extracted.

With a feeling of utter resignation, he took out his chequebook. He wrote the final cheque for twenty-seven pounds, leaving the fourteen shillings and sixpence for his own use. Arabella seized the paper, kissed him fervently on the cheek, and swept out of the room, her mission accomplished, her tragedy averted.

Mr. Pym sat alone in the silence. His secret was out; his fortune was gone. He was precisely where he had been a week ago, save for a new neckerchief and a profound education in the ways of the world. As he sat there, a strange, bubbling sound began to issue from his chest. It grew into a chuckle, then a full-throated, helpless laugh. He had been a fool, a prize goose, a veritable lottery of one for his relations to pluck. And yet, as the laughter subsided, he felt not bitterness, but a peculiar lightness. The secret had been a burden; the fortune, a temptation. He picked up his pen, dipped it in the ink, and began to draft a letter of application for a small raise in his wages, a sum so modest and so entirely his own that no one would ever think to ask him for it. Outside, the fog began to lift.

He saw the Jew with his half-closed eyes; heard his low whistling; and recognised the sound of the spoon grating against the saucepan’s sides: and yet the self-same senses were mentally engaged, at the same time, in busy action with almost everybody he had ever known.

When the coffee was done, the Jew drew the saucepan to the hob.
Standing, then in an irresolute attitude for a few minutes, as if he
did not well know how to employ himself, he turned round and looked at
Oliver, and called him by his name. He did not answer, and was to all
appearances asleep.

After satisfying himself upon this head, the Jew stepped gently to the
door: which he fastened. He then drew forth: as it seemed to Oliver,
from some trap in the floor: a small box, which he placed carefully on
the table. His eyes glistened as he raised the lid, and looked in.
Dragging an old chair to the table, he sat down; and took from it a
magnificent gold watch, sparkling with jewels.

“Aha!” said the Jew, shrugging up his shoulders, and distorting every
feature with a hideous grin. “Clever dogs! Clever dogs! Staunch to the
last! Never told the old parson where they were. Never poached upon old
Fagin! And why should they? It wouldn’t have loosened the knot, or kept
the drop up, a minute longer. No, no, no! Fine fellows! Fine fellows!”

With these, and other muttered reflections of the like nature, the Jew
once more deposited the watch in its place of safety. At least half a
dozen more were severally drawn forth from the same box, and surveyed
with equal pleasure; besides rings, brooches, bracelets, and other
articles of jewellery, of such magnificent materials, and costly
workmanship, that Oliver had no idea, even of their names.

Having replaced these trinkets, the Jew took out another: so small that
it lay in the palm of his hand. There seemed to be some very minute
inscription on it; for the Jew laid it flat upon the table, and shading
it with his hand, pored over it, long and earnestly. At length he put
it down, as if despairing of success; and, leaning back in his chair,
muttered:

“What a fine thing capital punishment is! Dead men never repent; dead
men never bring awkward stories to light. Ah, it’s a fine thing for the
trade! Five of ’em strung up in a row, and none left to play booty, or
turn white-livered!”

As the Jew uttered these words, his bright dark eyes, which had been
staring vacantly before him, fell on Oliver’s face; the boy’s eyes were
fixed on his in mute curiousity; and although the recognition was only
for an instant—for the briefest space of time that can possibly be
conceived—it was enough to show the old man that he had been observed.

He closed the lid of the box with a loud crash; and, laying his hand on
a bread knife which was on the table, started furiously up. He trembled
very much though; for, even in his terror, Oliver could see that the
knife quivered in the air.

“What’s that?” said the Jew. “What do you watch me for? Why are you
awake? What have you seen? Speak out, boy! Quick—quick! for your life.”

“I wasn’t able to sleep any longer, sir,” replied Oliver, meekly. “I am
very sorry if I have disturbed you, sir.”

“You were not awake an hour ago?” said the Jew, scowling fiercely on
the boy.

“No! No, indeed!” replied Oliver.

“Are you sure?” cried the Jew: with a still fiercer look than before:
and a threatening attitude.

“Upon my word I was not, sir,” replied Oliver, earnestly. “I was not,
indeed, sir.”

“Tush, tush, my dear!” said the Jew, abruptly resuming his old manner,
and playing with the knife a little, before he laid it down; as if to
induce the belief that he had caught it up, in mere sport. “Of course I
know that, my dear. I only tried to frighten you. You’re a brave boy.
Ha! ha! you’re a brave boy, Oliver.” The Jew rubbed his hands with a
chuckle, but glanced uneasily at the box, notwithstanding.

“Did you see any of these pretty things, my dear?” said the Jew, laying
his hand upon it after a short pause.

“Yes, sir,” replied Oliver.

“Ah!” said the Jew, turning rather pale. “They—they’re mine, Oliver; my
little property. All I have to live upon, in my old age. The folks call
me a miser, my dear. Only a miser; that’s all.”

Oliver thought the old gentleman must be a decided miser to live in
such a dirty place, with so many watches; but, thinking that perhaps
his fondness for the Dodger and the other boys, cost him a good deal of
money, he only cast a deferential look at the Jew, and asked if he
might get up.

“Certainly, my dear, certainly,” replied the old gentleman. “Stay.
There’s a pitcher of water in the corner by the door. Bring it here;
and I’ll give you a basin to wash in, my dear.”

Oliver got up; walked across the room; and stooped for an instant to
raise the pitcher. When he turned his head, the box was gone.

He had scarcely washed himself, and made everything tidy, by emptying
the basin out of the window, agreeably to the Jew’s directions, when
the Dodger returned: accompanied by a very sprightly young friend, whom
Oliver had seen smoking on the previous night, and who was now formally
introduced to him as Charley Bates. The four sat down, to breakfast, on
the coffee, and some hot rolls and ham which the Dodger had brought
home in the crown of his hat.

“Well,” said the Jew, glancing slyly at Oliver, and addressing himself
to the Dodger, “I hope you’ve been at work this morning, my dears?”

[Scenario]
A young clerk in a shipping office wins a modest prize in a public lottery and resolves to keep it secret from his grasping relations. Within a week every one of them has heard of it, and each arrives at his lodging with a misfortune requiring exactly the amount he has won.
Setting: The City of London, 1840s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The morning fog in the City of London did not merely descend upon the streets; it invaded them, a grey, damp specter that wrapped the cobblestones in a shroud and choked the breath from the lungs of every soul who dared to venture abroad. It was in this atmosphere, thick with the smell of coal smoke and rotting cabbage, that young Mr. Arthur Pumble, a junior clerk of middling stature and middling ambition, stood before the window of the office of Messrs. Grimsby, Hobbs & Co., staring at a slip of paper in his hand. The slip was small, so small that it might have been mistaken for a receipt for a loaf of stale bread, yet it possessed a power to terrify and to elevate that no amount of ink and parchment had ever previously possessed in Arthur’s humble existence. He had won a lottery. Not a grand sum that would have seen him riding in a carriage with a footman, nor a pittance that would have bought him nothing more substantial than a pint of weak beer, but a sum of exactly twenty guineas. It was a fortune. It was a miracle. It was, to Arthur, a golden key that promised to unlock the doors of a life unshackled from the grinding tyranny of his superiors and, more dangerously, his kin.

Arthur’s mind, which had hitherto been as blank and uneventful as a blank ledger, now spun with the rapidity of a topsy-turvy wheel. He thought of his aunt, Mrs. Gristle, a woman of such avarice that it was said she had once attempted to return a pair of spectacles to the optician after they had been worn for a decade, arguing that the lenses had grown cloudy with her own tears of frustration. He thought of his cousin, Barnaby, a man of such physical bulk that he seemed less a human being and more a geological formation, a rolling boulder of appetite and entitlement. And he thought of his uncle, Sir Reginald, a gentleman of such rigid propriety that he would rather starve than admit to a deficiency in his silverware. To share this windfall with such a tribe would be to throw a lit match into a powder magazine; they would not merely take the money; they would consume the man, leaving not a bone to pick, nor a ghost to haunt.

"Silence," Arthur whispered, pressing his lips together until they turned the color of the fog outside. "Absolute, impenetrable, granite silence." He locked the twenty guineas, which he had exchanged for a heavy, unassuming sack of sovereigns, into his desk. He went home that night with a smile so tight it threatened to split his face in two, and a heart that beat with the frantic rhythm of a rabbit caught in a trap. He told his landlady, Mrs. Bumble, that he had eaten a hearty dinner at the office. He told his cat, a creature of indifferent disposition, that the world was fair. He told himself that the secret was safe, buried deep in the vault of his own discretion.

But secrets, like leaks in a ship’s hull, have a way of spreading, not upward, but downward, until the whole vessel is awash. It began on the second day, with a letter from Aunt Gristle. It was a letter of such exquisite subtlety that it could have been written by a spider, yet it was as heavy as a lead weight. "My dear Arthur," it began, in a hand that trembled not from age but from anticipation, "I hear that you have had a little windfall. Not that I pry, but one must know the state of one’s relations." Arthur read it three times. He had told no one. Not a soul. Yet the wind was in the east, and the rumor had blown across the City with the speed of a hawk.

On the fourth day, Barnaby arrived at his lodgings. He did not knock; he merely stood in the doorway, blocking out the meager light of the gas lamp, and said, "Arthur, I have lost my shirt." Arthur, pale as a sheet, looked up from his ledger. "Lost?" he squeaked. "Yes," said Barnaby, with the casual ease of a man who had never known the meaning of the word 'scarcity'. "At the cards. A wicked trick. I need twenty guineas to settle the account, or I shall be thrown out into the street, and I do so hate the cold." Arthur looked at the ceiling, where the plaster was peeling, and thought, *If I give him the money, I am dead. If I refuse, I am a monster.*

Before Arthur could formulate a reply that was both polite and fatal to his own interests, a knock came at the door. It was a polite knock, the kind that suggests the person outside is wearing gloves and has just washed their hands. It was Sir Reginald. He entered with a bow so low that his wig nearly touched the floorboards. "My dear boy," he said, his voice like the creaking of a door hinge that has not been oiled for a century. "I have been doing some calculations regarding my estate. It appears that the roof of my summer house in Kent has suffered a slight collapse. A minor thing, really, but one requires funds for the repair. I trust you are in a position to assist a distressed relative?"

Arthur looked from the mountain of a man to the aristocrat in the wig. He looked at his own hands, which were shaking so violently that he could not hold his pen. The twenty guineas were in his drawer, sitting there like a bag of gold bricks, mocking him with their silence. He had kept the secret. He had guarded it with the vigilance of a dragon over its hoard. And yet, here they were, his relations, arriving at his door like a plague of locusts, each with a mouth gaping wide, ready to devour the fruit of his labor.

The room seemed to shrink around him. The walls, which had been so quiet and safe the night before, now seemed to lean in, whispering, *Give it up, Arthur. Give it up. You are alone against the world, and the world is hungry.* He thought of the fog outside, thick and unyielding, swallowing the streets, the buildings, the people. He thought of the lottery ticket, now a scrap of useless paper in his pocket, a symbol of a hope that had evaporated before it could even take shape.

"I..." Arthur began, but no sound came out. He tried again. "I..."

Barnaby shifted his weight, causing the floorboards to groan. Sir Reginald adjusted his cravat with a precision that was almost surgical. They both looked at him, waiting. The silence in the room was no longer the silence of secrecy; it was the silence of a held breath, the silence before the drop falls. Arthur realized, with a clarity that was sharp as a razor, that the prize had not been the money. The prize had been the illusion of control, the fantasy that one could stand apart from the machinery of kinship and greed. And now, as the clock on the mantelpiece struck the hour, the machinery was about to grind him down. He opened his mouth to speak, to deny, to defend, but the words died on his tongue, for he knew, with the certainty of a man who has seen his own grave, that the twenty guineas were already gone, spent in the minds of his relatives long before they had left their doors. He had lost the lottery, even as he had won it, and the fog outside, indifferent and grey, rolled on, covering the City in its cold, unblinking embrace.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Joseph Conrad (1857–1924).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
A brooding, morally searching voice; events are filtered through memory, interpretation and ironic distance. Long, rhythmic sentences layered with qualification, often rendering an impression before its meaning is understood. Dense atmospheric description of light, darkness, heat, water and silence, beside abstract moral vocabulary. Speech is halting, oblique or formal, with foreign idioms and much left unsaid.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Joseph Conrad. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.
<<<
shelf, peeped in to see that the contents were all right, and put it down gently on the counter. Not till that was done did he break the silence, to the effect that most likely Stevie would profit greatly by being sent out of town for a while; only he supposed his wife could not get on without him.

“Could not get on without him!” repeated Mrs Verloc slowly.  “I couldn’t
get on without him if it were for his good!  The idea!  Of course, I can
get on without him.  But there’s nowhere for him to go.”

Mr Verloc got out some brown paper and a ball of string; and meanwhile he
muttered that Michaelis was living in a little cottage in the country.
Michaelis wouldn’t mind giving Stevie a room to sleep in.  There were no
visitors and no talk there.  Michaelis was writing a book.

Mrs Verloc declared her affection for Michaelis; mentioned her abhorrence
of Karl Yundt, “nasty old man”; and of Ossipon she said nothing.  As to
Stevie, he could be no other than very pleased.  Mr Michaelis was always
so nice and kind to him.  He seemed to like the boy.  Well, the boy was a
good boy.

“You too seem to have grown quite fond of him of late,” she added, after
a pause, with her inflexible assurance.

Mr Verloc tying up the cardboard box into a parcel for the post, broke
the string by an injudicious jerk, and muttered several swear words
confidentially to himself.  Then raising his tone to the usual husky
mutter, he announced his willingness to take Stevie into the country
himself, and leave him all safe with Michaelis.

[Scenario]
An English railway engineer surveying a line through the mountains of a small republic is caught between the government that hired him and a rebel general who controls the passes. Both demand his loyalty, and each promises that the railway will bring civilisation.
Setting: A South American republic, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The town of Miraflores—which is to say, the handful of mud-coloured houses, the church with its broken bell, and the long, low building that called itself the Hotel Bolívar—lay in the hollow of a valley so deep that the sun reached it late and left it early, and the mountains that enclosed it stood about in a silence that was less a quality of the air than a pressure upon the spirit. It was here that I first met Mr. Charles Heatherington, C.E., a man of some fifty years, spare, grey, with the stooping shoulders of one who has spent his life over plans and instruments, and with a manner of such elaborate and painful courtesy that it seemed to cost him something to maintain it, as though politeness were a burden laid upon him by his conscience rather than a natural impulse of his heart.

He had come to this republic, he told me, at the invitation of the government—a government whose authority, he observed with a dry and careful smile, was not universally acknowledged—to survey a line of railway through the mountains to the sea. The concession was a matter of some urgency, the promises of civilisation were large, and the money, he understood, was English. He spoke of these things with a certain detachment, as though the railway were a fact of nature rather than a human enterprise, and I perceived that he was a man who had trained himself to see only the technical problem, the grade and the curve, the cutting and the tunnel, and to hold all else at arm's length. It was a discipline, I think, that had become a habit of the soul.

We sat that evening on the verandah of the hotel, in the thick, warm darkness, and he told me of the passes. There were three, he said, and the government held one, and the rebels—for there were rebels, though the word was never spoken aloud in the town—held the other two. The general who commanded them was named Ocampo, and he was, by all accounts, a man of considerable ability and no scruples, who had grasped the simple truth that a railway through the mountains must pass where the mountains permit, and that he who holds the passes holds the railway. "He has sent me messages," Mr. Heatherington said, and paused to light a cigar, the flame of the match illuminating for a moment his long, grave face and the patient, scholarly eyes. "Very courteous messages. He is anxious that the line should be surveyed through the northern pass, which he controls. He speaks of the prosperity of the country, of the benefits of communication, of the future. He is, I gather, a great believer in the future."

"And the government?"

"The government," Mr. Heatherington said, "is equally anxious that the line should go through the southern pass, which is held by their troops. They also speak of the future. They have been good enough to suggest that my services are of the first importance to the republic, and that I should do well to remember that I am, in a sense, their guest." He drew on his cigar, and the tip glowed in the darkness. "It is a delicate position for a man of my profession. I am not a politician. I have no opinions upon the government of this country, which seems to me neither better nor worse than most. I have a line to survey. The line must go where the ground permits, and the ground, unfortunately, permits of two routes. The one is shorter, the other is cheaper. The one is held by the general, the other by the government. I have spent my life in the service of the railway, and I have never before found myself in a position where the railway was expected to serve two masters."

He was silent for a while, and I heard the faint, persistent sound of the river in the valley below, and the distant barking of a dog, and then, from far off, the single note of a guitar, thin and melancholy, as though the night itself were singing. "I have written to the government," he said at last, "to explain that my survey must be impartial, that I must examine both routes, that I can give no promise until I have the facts. I have written to the general to the same effect. I have been careful to use the same words. I have been, I believe, perfectly correct." He sighed, a small, dry sound. "And yet I am aware that correctness is not a quality that is much valued in this part of the world. They do not want a surveyor. They want an ally. They want a man who will say that the railway must go through their pass, and who will say it not because the ground is favourable but because they wish it. And I am afraid that I shall disappoint them."

I asked him what he would do.

"I shall survey both routes," he said, simply. "It is my profession. It is the only thing I know. I shall take my instruments and my chainmen and I shall go up into the mountains, and I shall measure the ground, and I shall make my plans, and I shall report the truth as I find it. And then—" He stopped, and I saw him make a small gesture with his hand, as though he were brushing away a fly. "And then I shall be told that I have made a mistake, that my figures are wrong, that I have been deceived by the priests or the politicians or the general, or that I am a fool or a knave. And the railway will be built where they wish it to be built, and the civilisation will come, and the mountains will be crossed, and the passes will be held by the men who hold them now, and it will be a matter of no importance at all which route was surveyed by a certain English engineer who was too conscientious to tell a lie."

He rose and stood at the edge of the verandah, looking out into the darkness, and his figure, in its loose white clothes, seemed to me for a moment like the figure of a man standing at the edge of a great abyss, contemplating the fall. "I have a wife in England," he said, "and a daughter who is to be married in the spring. I have a small house in a suburb, and a garden that I have not seen for three years, and a pension that will be sufficient for my needs. I am not a young man. I have no ambition left, except to do my work honestly and to return to my garden. And yet I find myself in this valley, in this darkness, in this heat, between a government that flatters me and a general who threatens me, and I am asked to choose between them, and I cannot choose, because I have no opinion of either, and because the only thing I care for is the truth of the ground." He turned and looked at me, and his face was very grave. "It is a strange thing," he said, "to find that the truth is a luxury that no one can afford."

The next morning he was gone, with his instruments and his chainmen, up into the mountains, and I did not see him again for many weeks. When at last he returned, he was thinner and greyer, and there was a look in his eyes that I had not seen before, a look of a man who has been alone with the mountains and has found them indifferent. He told me that he had surveyed both routes, that the northern pass was the better, that he had so reported to the government, and that the government had thanked him and had ordered the line to be built through the southern pass. He told me that the general had sent him a letter of congratulation, in which he had been pleased to say that the English engineer was a man of honour, and that he hoped to have the pleasure of his acquaintance at some future time. He told me that he was going home. "I have done my work," he said. "I have surveyed the ground. The rest is not my affair." And he smiled his dry, careful smile, and shook my hand, and went away.

I have often thought of him since, in that valley of silence and heat, standing at the edge of the verandah and looking out into the darkness, and I have wondered whether he found his garden, and whether the truth of the ground was of any use to him, and whether the railway, when it was built, went through the pass that he had chosen or the pass that had been chosen for him. But I have never learned the answer, and I suppose it does not matter. The mountains are still there, and the passes are still held by the men who hold them, and the railway, if it was built, has become a fact of nature, like the river and the heat, and no one remembers the English engineer who surveyed it, or the general who promised him his friendship, or the government that flattered him and lied.

An English railway engineer surveying a line through the mountains of a small republic is caught between the government that hired him and a rebel general who controls the passes. Both demand his loyalty, and each promises that the railway will bring civilisation.
Setting: A South American republic, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The heat in the valley did not merely exist; it was a physical substance, a thick, amber viscosity that clung to the skin and seeped into the bones. Arthur Penrose sat in the open window of his makeshift office, a corrugated iron shack perched precariously on the limestone ridge, and watched the sun descend behind the jagged teeth of the Cordillera. The light was dying, turning the dusty road below into a ribbon of burnt copper. He held a glass of water in his hand, the ice long since melted, the liquid still and warm. He did not drink. He was waiting for the sound of boots on gravel, a sound that had become the metronome of his existence in this forsaken republic.

The government had hired him to build a line that would bind the country together, a promise of unity written in iron and steel. The rebels, who controlled the passes and the highlands, wanted the line to be a weapon, a conduit for their movement, a proof of their dominion over the wild, untamed earth. Both sides had spoken to him with the same fervor, the same hollow certainty that the railway would bring civilization. They did not understand that civilization was not a thing that could be laid upon the land like a track; it was a fragile, shifting thing, easily crushed by the weight of ambition.

A shadow fell across the floorboards. Penrose did not turn. He knew the gait, the heavy, deliberate steps of General Varela. The door creaked open, admitting a gust of air that smelled of dry earth and woodsmoke. Varela did not speak. He stood in the doorway, his uniform dusted with the pale powder of the highland soil, his face a mask of weary authority. He was a man who had seen the best and the worst of his people, and in his eyes there was a depth of sorrow that Penrose had learned to respect, if not to understand.

" The survey is finished?" Varela asked. His voice was low, roughened by smoke.

Penrose set the glass down on the desk. The clink of the glass against the wood sounded obscenely loud in the silence. "The line is feasible," he said. "But the terrain is... difficult. The passes are narrow. The gradients are steep."

"Difficult," Varela repeated. He stepped into the room, closing the door behind him. "The Minister says the same. He says the engineers are afraid. He says they lack the spirit of the nation."

Penrose felt a cold prickle of irritation at the mention of the Minister. The Minister was a man of words, a politician who lived in the capital, far from the mud and the blood of the highlands. He did not know the weight of a rock, the treachery of a slope, the indifference of the mountain. "It is not a matter of spirit, General," Penrose said, keeping his voice flat, devoid of emotion. "It is a matter of physics. Of stone and water."

Varela looked at him for a long moment. His gaze was searching, trying to find the crack in the engineer’s composure. "And if I tell you that the rebels are moving? That they are preparing to block the passes? That they want to stop the line?"

Penrose remained silent. He knew. He had seen the scouts, heard the rumors in the taverns, felt the tension in the air that preceded a storm. The rebels were not enemies, in the conventional sense. They were men who believed in a different kind of order, a more rigid, more fearful one. They wanted to keep the country closed, protected from the outside world, from the corruption of the city, from the chaotic influx of ideas and men. They saw the railway as a threat, a door that could not be closed once opened.

"If the line is stopped," Varela continued, his voice dropping to a whisper, "then the government falls. And then? Then the chaos returns. The bandits. The warlords. The bloodshed."

Penrose looked out the window. The sun had set, and the sky was a deep, bruised purple, streaked with the first stars. The darkness was coming up from the valley like a tide. "The line will be built," he said. "One way or another."

Varela nodded slowly. He turned to leave, but paused at the door. "Be careful, Penrose. The men of the highlands are not like the men of the city. They do not forgive. They do not forget."

The door closed. Penrose was alone again. The silence returned, heavier than before. He picked up the glass of water and finally drank. It was warm, tasting of iron and dust. He thought of his wife in London, of the grey rain and the familiar streets, of the quiet, ordered life he had left behind. He had come here for the adventure, for the challenge, for the money. But he had not come for this. He had not come for the weight of the choice he now carried.

He was a bridge, he realized. A bridge between two worlds that did not want to touch. And bridges, he knew, were the first things to be burned in a war.

The heat in the valley did not merely exist; it was a physical substance, a thick, amber viscosity that clung to the skin and seeped into the bones. Arthur Penrose sat in the open window of his makeshift office, a corrugated iron shack perched precariously on the limestone ridge, and watched the sun descend behind the jagged teeth of the Cordillera. The light was dying, turning the dusty road below into a ribbon of burnt copper. He held a glass of water in his hand, the ice long since melted, the liquid still and warm. He did not drink. He was waiting for the sound of boots on gravel, a sound that had become the metronome of his existence in this forsaken republic.

The government had hired him to build a line that would bind the country together, a promise of unity written in iron and steel. The rebels, who controlled the passes and the highlands, wanted the line to be a weapon, a conduit for their movement, a proof of their dominion over the wild, untamed earth. Both sides had spoken to him with the same fervor, the same hollow certainty that the railway would bring civilization. They did not understand that civilization was not a thing that could be laid upon the land like a track; it was a fragile, shifting thing, easily crushed by the weight of ambition.

A shadow fell across the floorboards. Penrose did not turn. He knew the gait, the heavy, deliberate steps of General Varela. The door creaked open, admitting a gust of air that smelled of dry earth and woodsmoke. Varela did not speak. He was a man who had seen the best and the worst of his people, and in his eyes there was a depth of sorrow that Penrose had learned to respect, if not to understand.

" The survey is finished?" Varela asked. His voice was low, roughened by smoke.

Penrose set the glass down on the desk. The clink of the glass against the wood sounded obscenely loud in the silence. "The line is feasible," he said. "But the terrain is... difficult. The passes are narrow. The gradients are steep."

"Difficult," Varela repeated. He stepped into the room, closing the door behind him. "The Minister says the same. He says the engineers are afraid. He says they lack the spirit of the nation."

Penrose felt a cold prickle of irritation at the mention of the Minister. The Minister was a man of words, a politician who lived in the capital, far from the mud and the blood of the highlands. "It is a matter of physics. Of stone and water."

Varela looked at him for a long moment. His gaze was searching, trying to find the crack in the engineer’s composure. "And if I tell you that the rebels are moving? That they are preparing to block the passes? That they want to stop the line?"

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

He saw the Jew with his half-closed eyes; heard his low whistling; and recognised the sound of the spoon grating against the saucepan’s sides: and yet the self-same senses were mentally engaged, at the same time, in busy action with almost everybody he had ever known.

When the coffee was done, the Jew drew the saucepan to the hob.
Standing, then in an irresolute attitude for a few minutes, as if he
did not well know how to employ himself, he turned round and looked at
Oliver, and called him by his name. He did not answer, and was to all
appearances asleep.

After satisfying himself upon this head, the Jew stepped gently to the
door: which he fastened. He then drew forth: as it seemed to Oliver,
from some trap in the floor: a small box, which he placed carefully on
the table. His eyes glistened as he raised the lid, and looked in.
Dragging an old chair to the table, he sat down; and took from it a
magnificent gold watch, sparkling with jewels.

“Aha!” said the Jew, shrugging up his shoulders, and distorting every
feature with a hideous grin. “Clever dogs! Clever dogs! Staunch to the
last! Never told the old parson where they were. Never poached upon old
Fagin! And why should they? It wouldn’t have loosened the knot, or kept
the drop up, a minute longer. No, no, no! Fine fellows! Fine fellows!”

With these, and other muttered reflections of the like nature, the Jew
once more deposited the watch in its place of safety. At least half a
dozen more were severally drawn forth from the same box, and surveyed
with equal pleasure; besides rings, brooches, bracelets, and other
articles of jewellery, of such magnificent materials, and costly
workmanship, that Oliver had no idea, even of their names.

Having replaced these trinkets, the Jew took out another: so small that
it lay in the palm of his hand. There seemed to be some very minute
inscription on it; for the Jew laid it flat upon the table, and shading
it with his hand, pored over it, long and earnestly. At length he put
it down, as if despairing of success; and, leaning back in his chair,
muttered:

“What a fine thing capital punishment is! Dead men never repent; dead
men never bring awkward stories to light. Ah, it’s a fine thing for the
trade! Five of ’em strung up in a row, and none left to play booty, or
turn white-livered!”

As the Jew uttered these words, his bright dark eyes, which had been
staring vacantly before him, fell on Oliver’s face; the boy’s eyes were
fixed on his in mute curiousity; and although the recognition was only
for an instant—for the briefest space of time that can possibly be
conceived—it was enough to show the old man that he had been observed.

He closed the lid of the box with a loud crash; and, laying his hand on
a bread knife which was on the table, started furiously up. He trembled
very much though; for, even in his terror, Oliver could see that the
knife quivered in the air.

“What’s that?” said the Jew. “What do you watch me for? Why are you
awake? What have you seen? Speak out, boy! Quick—quick! for your life.”

“I wasn’t able to sleep any longer, sir,” replied Oliver, meekly. “I am
very sorry if I have disturbed you, sir.”

“You were not awake an hour ago?” said the Jew, scowling fiercely on
the boy.

“No! No, indeed!” replied Oliver.

“Are you sure?” cried the Jew: with a still fiercer look than before:
and a threatening attitude.

“Upon my word I was not, sir,” replied Oliver, earnestly. “I was not,
indeed, sir.”

“Tush, tush, my dear!” said the Jew, abruptly resuming his old manner,
and playing with the knife a little, before he laid it down; as if to
induce the belief that he had caught it up, in mere sport. “Of course I
know that, my dear. I only tried to frighten you. You’re a brave boy.
Ha! ha! you’re a brave boy, Oliver.” The Jew rubbed his hands with a
chuckle, but glanced uneasily at the box, notwithstanding.

“Did you see any of these pretty things, my dear?” said the Jew, laying
his hand upon it after a short pause.

“Yes, sir,” replied Oliver.

“Ah!” said the Jew, turning rather pale. “They—they’re mine, Oliver; my
little property. All I have to live upon, in my old age. The folks call
me a miser, my dear. Only a miser; that’s all.”

Oliver thought the old gentleman must be a decided miser to live in
such a dirty place, with so many watches; but, thinking that perhaps
his fondness for the Dodger and the other boys, cost him a good deal of
money, he only cast a deferential look at the Jew, and asked if he
might get up.

“Certainly, my dear, certainly,” replied the old gentleman. “Stay.
There’s a pitcher of water in the corner by the door. Bring it here;
and I’ll give you a basin to wash in, my dear.”

Oliver got up; walked across the room; and stooped for an instant to
raise the pitcher. When he turned his head, the box was gone.

He had scarcely washed himself, and made everything tidy, by emptying
the basin out of the window, agreeably to the Jew’s directions, when
the Dodger returned: accompanied by a very sprightly young friend, whom
Oliver had seen smoking on the previous night, and who was now formally
introduced to him as Charley Bates. The four sat down, to breakfast, on
the coffee, and some hot rolls and ham which the Dodger had brought
home in the crown of his hat.

“Well,” said the Jew, glancing slyly at Oliver, and addressing himself
to the Dodger, “I hope you’ve been at work this morning, my dears?”

“Hard,” replied the Dodger.

“As nails,” added Charley Bates.

[Scenario]
A young clerk in a shipping office wins a modest prize in a public lottery and resolves to keep it secret from his grasping relations. Within a week every one of them has heard of it, and each arrives at his lodging with a misfortune requiring exactly the amount he has won.
Setting: The City of London, 1840s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
Mr. Octavius Pinchbeck, junior clerk in the counting-house of Messrs. Grumble, Hogg & Vane, Shipping Agents and General Merchants, of Candlewick Street, in the City of London, was a young gentleman of such retiring disposition, and so small a figure in the world’s eye, that the very porters at the wharf, who knew every face upon the river, were wont to salute him as “the young man as comes and goes,”—a designation which, while it did no great honour to his individuality, had at least the merit of accuracy. He was thin, he was sandy, he was given to stooping; his coat, though brushed with a fidelity that argued a good heart, had that shiny, threadbare aspect which bespeaks a garment long acquainted with its wearer’s elbows; and his whole appearance was that of a man who might be supposed to have been born at a desk, to have been weaned upon a ledger, and to be destined, in the fullness of time, to be buried in a ledger, with a pen behind his ear for a monument.

Now it chanced that Mr. Pinchbeck, being of a modest and speculative turn, and having by him a certain sum of two pounds seven shillings, the slow accumulation of many months of self-denial, did one day purchase a ticket in a public lottery—not the great State affair, be it understood, but a small and semi-respectable raffle, got up for the benefit of a charitable institution, and conducted by a committee of exceedingly benevolent gentlemen, who took care to secure their own expenses first. And it further chanced—for Fortune is a lady of the most unaccountable caprices—that the number upon Mr. Pinchbeck’s ticket was that which came up the winner of the third prize: to wit, the sum of forty pounds sterling.

Forty pounds! To Mr. Pinchbeck, whose annual salary was eighty, and who had never in his life possessed so much as ten pounds at one time, it was a fortune. He received the money in a little canvas bag, counted it thrice over in a retired corner of the office, and went home to his lodgings in Little Popham’s Rents, off the Minories, with his hat pressed down upon his brows, and his hand firmly clenched upon his breast-pocket, and his heart beating like a watchman’s rattle. And there, in the privacy of his own chamber, he resolved—with a caution which did honour to his prudence—that not a soul should know of his good fortune; for he was acquainted, by long and bitter experience, with the nature of his relatives.

Mr. Pinchbeck’s relatives were numerous, and they were terrible. There was his aunt, Mrs. Sophronia Gudge, a widow of ponderous respectability, who wore mourning for a husband deceased these fifteen years, and who spoke of “poor dear Gudge” upon every possible occasion, and upon some that were impossible. There was his uncle, Mr. Bartholomew Pinchbeck, a man of vast and mysterious schemes, who had been upon the point of making his fortune in every quarter of the globe, and had never yet made it in any. There was his cousin, Mr. Adolphus Pinchbeck, who played the flute, and had a complaint of the chest, and considered himself ill-used by Providence. There was his cousin, Miss Amelia Pinchbeck, who was of a romantic turn, and painted flowers upon velvet, and had once been disappointed in love—or said so. And there was his mother’s second cousin, Mrs. Wix, who kept a small shop for the sale of stay-laces and small haberdashery, and who had a way of sighing over her tea that was more eloquent than any words.

Within a week, every one of them had heard of it.

How the intelligence travelled, Mr. Pinchbeck never could discover. Whether the young man who swept the office had overheard him counting the sovereigns; whether the landlady, Mrs. Cribb, had peeped through the keyhole; whether the very cat upon the hearth had been in the pay of his relations—certain it is that upon the seventh day after his good fortune, and upon the very evening when he had resolved to purchase a new hat and a pair of gloves, and perhaps treat himself to a box at the theatre, there came a knock at his door, and there entered Mrs. Sophronia Gudge.

“My dear Octavius,” said that lady, sinking into the easy-chair with a rustle of black crape, and applying a handkerchief to her eyes, “I am the bearer of heavy tidings.”

Mr. Pinchbeck, who had hastily thrust his canvas bag beneath the pillow, inquired, with a quaking voice, what had happened.

“It is your poor uncle Bartholomew,” said Mrs. Gudge. “He has been arrested for debt—the sum is forty pounds—and unless it be paid by tomorrow noon, he must go to the Fleet, and there he will die, for his constitution is not what it was, and the damp of that place is dreadful, and I have no doubt it will carry him off, and then what will become of us all?”

Mr. Pinchbeck was about to observe that his uncle Bartholomew had been arrested for debt no fewer than seven times before, and had always emerged with a cheerfulness that argued a constitution of iron; but Mrs. Gudge was not to be interrupted.

“I knew,” she continued, “that you would be the first to help, for you have always been a good boy, Octavius, and I have no doubt you have saved a little something out of your salary, and forty pounds would be nothing to you, and everything to him.”

Mr. Pinchbeck, with a sinking heart, was endeavouring to frame a denial, when the door opened again, and there entered Mr. Adolphus Pinchbeck, with his flute under his arm and a cough that shook the window-panes.

“Cousin Octavius,” said Mr. Adolphus, “I am come to you in my extremity. The physician—a most eminent man, I assure you—has ordered me to the South of France, and my passage-money is forty pounds, and I have not a penny. I am a broken man—my chest, my chest!” and he coughed again, and looked at Mr. Pinchbeck with the air of a martyr.

Before Mr. Pinchbeck could reply, the door—which seemed to have acquired a fatal facility of opening—admitted Miss Amelia Pinchbeck, who rushed in with a little scream, and threw herself upon the sofa.

“Oh, Octavius!” she cried, “I am the most miserable of women! The velvet—the flowers—the frame—all is lost! My landlord demands forty pounds for rent, and if I cannot pay it, he will seize my paintings, and my heart is broken!”

“And I,” said a voice at the door, “am ruined entirely!” It was Mr. Bartholomew Pinchbeck himself, who had escaped his arrest by some miracle known only to himself, and who now stood upon the threshold, beaming with an injured innocence that was quite affecting. “I have been robbed—robbed, I say—of forty pounds by a villain in whom I trusted, and unless I can replace it, my credit is gone for ever!”

“And my stay-laces,” whimpered Mrs. Wix, who had followed him in, “are all out of fashion, and I have no money to buy new stock, and forty pounds would set me up again, and I am sure Octavius has it, for I always said he was the lucky one of the family.”

They all stood around him—the whole five of them—like a pack of hounds around a hare, and each repeated the sum of forty pounds with a unanimity that was frightful. Mr. Pinchbeck looked from one to the other; he thought of his canvas bag beneath the pillow; he thought of the new hat; he thought of the box at the theatre; and then he thought of the Fleet, and the South of France, and the velvet paintings, and the stay-laces, and the villain in whom his uncle had trusted.

“My dear relations,” said Mr. Pinchbeck, with a ghastly smile, “I have indeed been fortunate—most fortunate—and I have exactly forty pounds, which I shall be most happy to divide among you.”

He said this with the air of a man who has just swallowed a pill of extraordinary magnitude; and then he drew forth the canvas bag, and counted out the sovereigns—eight to each—and they all embraced him, and wept over him, and declared that he was the best of men; and then they departed, each with his or her forty pounds in hand, and left Mr. Pinchbeck sitting alone in his chamber, with the empty bag upon his knee, and a countenance of such profound and touching resignation that the very cat upon the hearth (if she was indeed in the pay of his relations) must have been moved to pity.

And the next morning, Mr. Pinchbeck went to his desk as usual, and the porters at the wharf saluted him as “the young man as comes and goes,” and he was, I believe, the only man in the City of London who had ever won forty pounds in a lottery and was the poorer for it.
