[Scenario]
A police inspector who has spent years cultivating informers among London's foreign revolutionaries is ordered by a new superior to make an arrest that will please the newspapers. The only man he can plausibly arrest is the informer who has kept him safe.
Setting: Soho and Scotland Yard, London, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The rain, which had been falling since the grey dawn over London, had settled into a steady, oblique drizzle that made the pavements of Soho glisten like the scales of some dark, submerged creature. It was the kind of dampness that penetrates the cloth of one’s coat, not with the violence of a storm, but with the slow, insidious persistence of a moral doubt. I stood beneath the awning of a shuttered chandler’s shop in Dean Street, watching the gas lamps struggle against the encroaching gloom of the evening, and I felt the familiar, cold weight of the trade I practised—a trade which, I had long since realized, consisted less in the detection of crime than in the management of the shadows where human souls are bought and sold.

For ten years I had walked these streets, learning the rhythms of the exile, the dialect of the conspiracy, and the specific, feverish silence that precedes an act of terror. I had cultivated a garden of informers, a delicate and poisonous flora that required constant, careful tending. Among them, there was one who had grown larger than the rest, a man whose roots had entwined themselves with the very foundations of my own safety. His name was Karel Vostrek.

He was not a man of action, this Vostrek; he was a man of ink and nerve, a Bohemian who had fled the iron hand of the Emperor only to find himself trapped in the softer, more complex coils of the English law. He sat now in a small, airless room above a printer’s shop in Frith Street, surrounded by pamphlets that smelled of wet ink and sedition, and he wrote the letters that kept me informed of the movements of the International Brotherhood. He was my shield. As long as the Brotherhood trusted him, they remained visible to me; as long as I remained visible to them, I remained alive.

But the order had come down from Whitehall that afternoon, delivered by a messenger whose livery was too new and whose face was too smooth to belong to the old, weary world of Scotland Yard. The new Chief—this Major General Sir Arthur Bellingham, a man of polished boots and unblemished conscience—had summoned me to his office. The room had been vast, smelling of beeswax and authority, and the light from the tall windows had fallen upon the map of London spread across his desk as if illuminating a battlefield.

"The public, Inspector," the Major General had said, his voice possessing that clipped, military resonance which brooked no ambiguity, "requires a demonstration. The papers are full of it. These Anarchists, these Nihilists... they believe they can strike at the heart of the Empire with impunity. We must show them otherwise. We must make an arrest. Something substantial. Something that will satisfy the editors of the *Times*."

I had stood before him, my hat in my hands, feeling the dampness of my coat drying in the artificial heat of the room. I had explained, with the careful, weary precision of a man who knows he is not being heard, that the revolutionaries were fluid, that they moved like smoke, that to strike at the foot soldiers was to accomplish nothing.

"Smoke?" the Major General had repeated, leaning back in his leather chair. "Nonsense. There is always a head. There is always a man who writes the manifestos, who holds the funds, who incites the rest. Find me that man, Inspector. Find me the writer, the intellect behind the chaos. If you do not, I shall find someone who can."

He had looked at me then with the bright, uncompromising gaze of a man who has never had to compromise. He saw only the failure of the police to protect the public; he did not see the intricate web of trust and betrayal that kept the web from collapsing entirely. He did not see that the man who wrote the manifestos, the man who held the knowledge, was Karel Vostrek.

And so I walked now through the wet streets of Soho, carrying the weight of that command. The irony was a bitter taste in my mouth, metallic and cold. To please the newspapers, to satisfy the vanity of a new superior, I was ordered to destroy the only instrument that had kept the chaos at bay. It was a grotesque simplification of the world, this demand for a villain to be paraded in the dock. They wanted a symbol, a face to pin upon their fears, and the only face available was the one that looked at me with such desperate, pathetic gratitude every Tuesday evening.

I turned into the narrow alleyway that led to Vostrek’s lodgings. The silence here was different from the silence of the open street; it was a pressurized silence, heavy with the smell of stale cabbage and the damp rot of the brickwork. I climbed the stairs, my footsteps echoing with a dull, hollow thud that seemed to mock the stealth I usually employed. There was no need for stealth tonight. The prey had already been caught; he simply did not know it yet.

I pushed open the door without knocking. Vostrek was there, as I knew he would be, hunched over a small table, a single candle throwing long, dancing shadows against the peeling wallpaper. He looked up, and his face, which was pale and lined with the anxieties of a hunted man, broke into a smile of relief. He was a small man, with eyes that burned with a strange, intellectual fire—a fire that I had learned to bank and control for my own purposes.

"Inspector," he breathed, rising to his feet and extending a hand that trembled slightly. "You are late. I began to fear... I thought perhaps the police had been raiding the meeting in Whitechapel."

I did not take his hand. I stood by the door, letting the cold air from the landing mingle with the stifling atmosphere of the room. I looked at him—at the ink stains on his fingers, at the manuscripts scattered across the table, at the half-eaten crust of bread that spoke of his poverty and his dedication. He was a man who believed in the inevitable triumph of the proletariat, a man who sacrificed his comfort for an idea, and he was also a man who sold his friends to the police for a few pounds a month to pay for his printing press. The duality of him was nauseating, and yet, in that moment, he seemed merely pathetic, a pawn moved by forces he could not comprehend.

"Karel," I said, and my voice sounded strange to my own ears, flat and devoid of the usual cordiality. "The time has come for a change in our arrangements."

He looked at me, his brow furrowing. "A change? But the Brotherhood... they are planning the demonstration at the Embankment. I have the names, Inspector. I have the routes. If we strike now—"

"There will be no strike," I interrupted him. "Not by them. The authorities require a scapegoat, Karel. They require a head for the block."

The smile vanished from his face. It did not fade; it was extinguished, as if a wet cloth had been thrown over a flame. He understood. He was, after all, a man of intellect. He looked at my face, searching for the loophole, the reprieve, the hidden signal that this was merely another test of his loyalty. But there was nothing there. I had cultivated him for years, nurtured his usefulness, and now I was ordered to harvest him.

"You?" he whispered. The word was barely audible.

"I have my orders," I said, stepping forward. "The new Chief desires a conviction. He desires the author of the sedition. You have written enough, Karel. You have signed enough pamphlets. You are the most plausible man in London."

He backed away until his shoulders hit the wall. The plaster crumbled slightly under his weight. "But I did it for you," he hissed, the desperation rising in his voice. "I did it to keep them in check. I saved you from the bomb throwers. I gave you the names of the men who wanted to kill the Ministers. I am your man."

"That is precisely why you are the one," I replied, the words tasting of ash. "You know too much. You are too deep in their councils. To the public, you are a revolutionary. To the police, you are a traitor. To me... you are an expense that can no longer be afforded."

He stared at me, and in his eyes I saw the realization of the absolute, crushing indifference of the world. He saw that he was not a partner in a great game, but a tool that had worn out. The moral universe, which he had thought to reshape with his pamphlets and his conspiracies, had simply closed over him.

"You are a devil," he said softly.

"I am a policeman," I corrected him. "And the rain is getting heavier."

I moved towards him then, my hand reaching for the handcuffs at my belt. The metal was cold against my skin. Outside, the wind rattled the windowpane, and the gas lamp in the street below flickered, casting a brief, distorted shadow of the two of us against the wall—two men bound together in a room full of shadows, one destroying the other to preserve the darkness. I felt no triumph, only the weary, heavy satisfaction of a duty performed, a silence secured. The newspapers would be pleased. The Major General would be satisfied. And in the labyrinth of London, the smoke would continue to rise, unchecked and unseen, for a little while longer.

A police inspector who has spent years cultivating informers among London's foreign revolutionaries is ordered by a new superior to make an arrest that will please the newspapers. The only man he can plausibly arrest is the informer who has kept him safe.
Setting: Soho and Scotland Yard, London, 1890s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The fog of that November was not the honest, suffocating blanket of the river, but a greasier, more insidious thing that seemed to seep from the very bricks of Soho, blurring the gas-lamps into wan, spectral smudges. I had walked through it from the Yard, my greatcoat collar turned up against a dampness that was less a rain than a pervasive, chilling exhalation of the city itself. My destination was a mean and narrow house in a court off Greek Street, a place where the air was thick with the smell of boiled cabbage and the acrid, foreign scent of political desperation. It was there that I was to meet my man, Verloc—though that was not the name he was born with, nor the one by which he was known to the dozen or so fervent and impoverished conspirators who trusted him.

For five years, Verloc had been my creature. He was a heavy, taciturn man, a seller of pornographic postcards and a purveyor of gossip, a man whose soul seemed as soiled and weary as the little shop he kept. He was not clever, but he was cautious, and he possessed a kind of dumb, animal instinct for self-preservation which made him invaluable. He was my ear in the fetid undergrowth of the revolutionary movement, the man who brought me word of their fantastical plots, their pitiful quarrels, their grandiose and empty rhetoric. In return, I paid him a small stipend and, more importantly, I paid him with my silence. I knew of the man he had killed in his youth, a shadowy affair in some Continental city, and I held that knowledge not as a threat, but as a bond—a shared secret that made us, in a sense, partners in the squalid business of survival.

On this evening, however, as I ducked into the dim, gas-lit passage of his shop, the nature of that partnership felt suddenly and profoundly altered. The order had come down from the new Assistant Commissioner, a brisk, impatient man with a genius for administrative detail and a profound ignorance of the human material with which he worked. The newspapers, he had informed me, were baying for a success, for a visible blow against the hydra of anarchy. A bomb had been found, luckily, before it could go off, in a cloakroom at a railway terminus. The public was alarmed. The government was nervous. An arrest was required. “A plausible one, Inspector,” he had said, his gaze fixed on a neat pile of papers on his desk. “The man at the centre of this. The one your people call the Professor.”

I had stood before him, a man of middle years and settled habits, and felt the ground shift beneath my feet. The Professor was a phantom, a creature of rumour and fear, a man of such extreme and unyielding purity of purpose that he was universally distrusted, even by his fellow fanatics. To arrest him was impossible. To explain this to the Assistant Commissioner, to reveal the intricate, fragile web of informants and half-truths by which I maintained my precarious intelligence, was equally impossible. He wanted a name, a body, a spectacle for the morning editions. And as I stood there, listening to the distant, impersonal hum of the great machine of state, I understood with a cold, sick certainty that the only name I could offer, the only body I could deliver, was that of the man who had kept me safe.

He was in the back room, as I knew he would be, sitting before a small fire that did little to dispel the gloom. He was reading a newspaper, a French one, his heavy shoulders hunched, his thick fingers black with printer’s ink. He looked up as I entered, and a slow, cautious recognition dawned in his dull eyes. He did not rise.

“Mr. Verloc,” I said, my voice sounding strange and loud in the small space.

He grunted in acknowledgement, folding the paper with a deliberation that was almost insolent. “You are late,” he observed. “The fog.”

“Yes,” I said. “The fog.” I stood there, my hands clasped behind my back, feeling the weight of the revolver in my pocket, a weight that seemed to have increased tenfold since I had crossed the threshold. I had not drawn it in twenty years of service. I prayed I would not have to now. “There is trouble,” I began, and then stopped. The words felt like stones in my mouth.

He watched me, his face a mask of stolid, peasant patience. “There is always trouble,” he said.

“This is different.” I took a step closer, the floorboards creaking beneath my boots. “The newspapers have found a bomb. They are making a great noise. The new man at the Yard… he wants a result. He wants a man in the cells by morning.”

A flicker of something—not fear, but a deep, weary understanding—passed across Verloc’s face. He knew the mechanics of this world as well as I did. He knew that the great, blind forces of public opinion and political ambition required their regular, bloody sacrifices. He had, in his own way, been a priest at that altar for years, offering up the names of others. Now, it seemed, his turn had come.

“And who is to be this man?” he asked, his voice flat, without inflection.

I did not answer at once. The silence in the room was absolute, broken only by the sputtering of the coals and the distant, muffled sound of a street-hawker crying his wares in the fog-bound darkness. I looked at him—at the shabby coat, the greasy collar, the face that was a monument to a lifetime of quiet, unheroic villainy. He was not a good man. But he was my man. He was the one fixed point in a world of shifting allegiances and treacherous ideals. And I was about to betray him, not with a dramatic flourish, but with the quiet, bureaucratic efficiency of a state that had no time for the complexities of the human heart.

“There is a man,” I said at last, my voice barely a whisper. “A man who has been seen at these meetings. A man of known, violent associations. A man who has, in his possession, certain… inflammatory literature.” The lies came easily, for they were the common currency of my trade. “His name is Verloc.”

He did not move. He did not start, nor cry out, nor even change his expression. He simply sat there, his eyes fixed on my face, and in them I saw a profound and terrible comprehension. He saw the whole sordid transaction: my fear, my ambition, my cowardice. He saw the Assistant Commissioner’s neat piles of paper, the newspaper editors sharpening their pens, the great, indifferent public clamouring for a villain. And he saw me, the instrument of all these things, standing before him in the gloom of his own house, a Judas in a police inspector’s coat.

“I see,” he said, after a long, agonising pause. The two words were heavy with a finality that was more damning than any curse. He rose slowly to his feet, his movements ponderous and deliberate. He looked around the room, at the cheap furniture, the piles of pamphlets, the portrait of a stern-faced woman on the mantelpiece—his wife, I knew, a woman as silent and watchful as he. He seemed to be taking his leave of it all.

“You will come quietly, then,” I said, and my voice was hoarse.

He turned back to me, and for the first time, a faint, ironic smile touched his lips. “It is my business to come quietly, Inspector,” he said. “It is what I have always done.”

He walked towards me, his hands hanging loosely at his sides. He was a big man, and in the confined space he seemed to loom over me. For a moment, I thought he might strike me, and my hand moved instinctively towards my pocket. But he did not. He simply stopped a pace away and looked at me with those dull, knowing eyes.

“You will do what you must,” he said, and his voice was not bitter, but resigned, as if he were commenting on the weather. “And I will do what I must.”

He turned his back on me and walked towards the door that led to the shop, and to the street, and to the waiting police van and the cold, certain future of a public trial and a long, degrading imprisonment. I followed him, a man walking in a dream, the fog of the city seeming to have entered my very soul. The great, ironic machine of justice was about to grind its wheels, and I, who had spent my life trying to understand its workings, was to be one of its cogs. I had saved the state from a phantom, and in doing so, I had destroyed the only man who had ever trusted me. The silence between us was more eloquent than any confession, and in it, I heard the true, terrible cost of my long and faithful service.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.

how little I do claim, but I will go that length. You have done so much for him, you are so fond of him; your whole life, Mrs. Bounderby, expresses such charming self-forgetfulness on his account—pardon me again—I am running wide of the subject. I am interested in him for his own sake.’

She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in
a hurry and gone away.  He had turned the course of what he said at that
instant, and she remained.

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ he resumed, in a lighter manner, and yet with a show of
effort in assuming it, which was even more expressive than the manner he
dismissed; ‘it is no irrevocable offence in a young fellow of your
brother’s years, if he is heedless, inconsiderate, and expensive—a little
dissipated, in the common phrase.  Is he?’

‘Yes.’

‘Allow me to be frank.  Do you think he games at all?’

‘I think he makes bets.’  Mr. Harthouse waiting, as if that were not her
whole answer, she added, ‘I know he does.’

‘Of course he loses?’

‘Yes.’

‘Everybody does lose who bets.  May I hint at the probability of your
sometimes supplying him with money for these purposes?’

She sat, looking down; but, at this question, raised her eyes searchingly
and a little resentfully.

‘Acquit me of impertinent curiosity, my dear Mrs. Bounderby.  I think Tom
may be gradually falling into trouble, and I wish to stretch out a
helping hand to him from the depths of my wicked experience.—Shall I say
again, for his sake?  Is that necessary?’

She seemed to try to answer, but nothing came of it.

‘Candidly to confess everything that has occurred to me,’ said James
Harthouse, again gliding with the same appearance of effort into his more
airy manner; ‘I will confide to you my doubt whether he has had many
advantages.  Whether—forgive my plainness—whether any great amount of
confidence is likely to have been established between himself and his
most worthy father.’

‘I do not,’ said Louisa, flushing with her own great remembrance in that
wise, ‘think it likely.’

‘Or, between himself, and—I may trust to your perfect understanding of my
meaning, I am sure—and his highly esteemed brother-in-law.’

She flushed deeper and deeper, and was burning red when she replied in a
fainter voice, ‘I do not think that likely, either.’

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ said Harthouse, after a short silence, ‘may there be a
better confidence between yourself and me?  Tom has borrowed a
considerable sum of you?’

‘You will understand, Mr. Harthouse,’ she returned, after some
indecision: she had been more or less uncertain, and troubled throughout
the conversation, and yet had in the main preserved her self-contained
manner; ‘you will understand that if I tell you what you press to know,
it is not by way of complaint or regret.  I would never complain of
anything, and what I have done I do not in the least regret.’

‘So spirited, too!’ thought James Harthouse.

‘When I married, I found that my brother was even at that time heavily in
debt.  Heavily for him, I mean.  Heavily enough to oblige me to sell some
trinkets.  They were no sacrifice.  I sold them very willingly.  I
attached no value to them.  They were quite worthless to me.’

Either she saw in his face that he knew, or she only feared in her
conscience that he knew, that she spoke of some of her husband’s gifts.
She stopped, and reddened again.  If he had not known it before, he would
have known it then, though he had been a much duller man than he was.

‘Since then, I have given my brother, at various times, what money I
could spare: in short, what money I have had.  Confiding in you at all,
on the faith of the interest you profess for him, I will not do so by
halves.  Since you have been in the habit of visiting here, he has wanted
in one sum as much as a hundred pounds.  I have not been able to give it
to him.  I have felt uneasy for the consequences of his being so
involved, but I have kept these secrets until now, when I trust them to
your honour.  I have held no confidence with any one, because—you
anticipated my reason just now.’  She abruptly broke off.

He was a ready man, and he saw, and seized, an opportunity here of
presenting her own image to her, slightly disguised as her brother.

‘Mrs. Bounderby, though a graceless person, of the world worldly, I feel
the utmost interest, I assure you, in what you tell me.  I cannot
possibly be hard upon your brother.  I understand and share the wise
consideration with which you regard his errors.  With all possible
respect both for Mr. Gradgrind and for Mr. Bounderby, I think I perceive
that he has not been fortunate in his training.  Bred at a disadvantage
towards the society in which he has his part to play, he rushes into
these extremes for himself, from opposite extremes that have long been
forced—with the very best intentions we have no doubt—upon him.  Mr.

characteristic, does not—as we have agreed—invite confidence.  If I might
venture to remark that it is the least in the world deficient in that
delicacy to which a youth mistaken, a character misconceived, and

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The fog in the narrow street near Holborn was not merely a meteorological phenomenon; it was a moral condition, a thick, yellowish, damp smotherer that seemed to strangle the very concept of daylight. It curled around the eaves of the houses like a greedy cat, it seeped into the cracks of the cobblestones, and it settled upon the shoulders of the passers-by with a weight that suggested they were all carrying invisible burdens of sin or debt. It was into this suffocating embrace that young Timothy Pumble, aged ten, and equipped with a valise that was larger than his own dignity, was deposited by a cabman who looked as if he had been squeezed too tightly in a vice.

“Right, sir,” the cabman grunted, spitting a stream of tobacco juice onto the wet pavement. “Mr. Silas Vetch. Top floor. Don’t expect him to open the door with a smile, nor with a key, for that matter. He’s a man of principles, or so he says, but the principles are locked up tighter than a miser’s money.”

Timothy looked up. The building was a lean-to affair, a grimace of brick and slate that leaned precariously toward its neighbor, as if the two structures were conspiring to whisper secrets. Above the ground floor, where a heavy iron shutter was drawn down like a sleepless eye, a single window glowed with a dim, sickly light. The shop below was shuttered, too, but the brass plate on the door, tarnished and dull, still proclaimed: *VETCH, PIERCE & CO. PUNCHED, BROUGHT, AND BROUGHT AGAIN.* It was a name that sounded like a cough, and a business that smelled of dust and despair.

Timothy knocked. He knocked with a timid fist, then a bolder one, then with the heel of his shoe, as if the door were a drum in a marching band. There was no answer. He knocked until his knuckles were red and his heart was hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs, a rhythm that matched the ticking of the clock in the street, which seemed to be counting down the seconds of his life. Then, with a sound like a rusty hinge screaming in protest, the door opened a crack.

A pair of eyes, small, sharp, and buried in a face that looked as though it had been carved from a block of dried wood, peered out. This was Silas Vetch. He wore a waistcoat that had seen better centuries, and his hair, thin and white, stood out in wisps like dry grass in a winter field.

“Who is it?” the voice asked. It was a voice like gravel being stirred in a tin can.

“Mr. Vetch? My name is Timothy Pumble. My mother sent me.”

The eyes narrowed. “Your mother sent you? And where is your mother?”

“Gone, sir. To the country. To stay with her sister.”

The old man’s face twitched. “Gone. Yes. Women are like the fog, boy. They come, they thicken the air, and then they lift, leaving you standing in the cold. Come in. And mind the step. It’s rotten. Like the world.”

The interior of the shop was a labyrinth of shadow. The air was still, heavy with the scent of old paper, horsehair, and something metallic, like the smell of a penny dropped in a puddle. Shelves lined the walls, climbing up to the ceiling, and on these shelves sat objects of terrible variety. There were gold chains, coiled like sleeping snakes; there were silver spoons, tarnished and dull; there were pocket watches, their faces blank and staring; there were rings, brooches, and lockets, all silent and waiting. But what struck Timothy most was the silence. Not the silence of emptiness, but the silence of holding one’s breath. Every object was wrapped in cloth, or locked in a small glass case, or buried under a pile of ledgers.

“You are to sleep in the back room,” Vetch said, not looking at the boy, but at a small brass key he was turning over and over in his fingers. “You will eat what is provided. You will speak when spoken to. And you will not touch anything in this shop. Not a thing. Not a button, not a thread, not a speck of dust.”

“Why?” Timothy asked, his voice trembling. “Why are you keeping them? You are a pawnbroker. You sell them, don’t you?”

Vetch stopped turning the key. He looked at the boy, and for a moment, the hardness in his face cracked, revealing a chasm of something ancient and sad. “We do not sell, boy. We hold. We keep. There is a difference. A great difference. To sell is to forget. To keep is to remember.”

Timothy looked around the room. The objects seemed to watch him. The gold chains shimmered with a cold light; the watches, though silent, seemed to tick in his mind. He felt a strange pull, a gravity that drew him toward the shelves.

“Who are they for?” Timothy asked softly.

Vetch sighed. It was a long, weary sound, like the wind moaning through a broken chimney. “For those who could not afford to lose them. For those who came here in their darkest hour, needing a little life to pay for their bread, their rent, their survival. They pledged their treasures, thinking they would come back for them. But life, boy, is a thief. It steals our time, our strength, our hope. Many of them did not come back. They died, or they moved, or they forgot. And I... I waited. I waited for thirty years. I could not bear to sell what was not mine. I am a custodian, not a merchant.”

Timothy looked at the old man. He saw the loneliness in his eyes, the same loneliness that lived in the empty street outside. He saw a man who had built a fortress of objects to keep the void at bay.

“I will help you,” Timothy said. “I will dust the shelves. I will clean the glass. I will make sure everything is in its place.”

Vetch looked at him, surprised. “You? A boy? You would do that?”

“Yes, sir. Because if you keep them, they are not lost. And if they are not lost, maybe someone will come back. Maybe.”

Vetch looked at the boy for a long time. Then, slowly, he nodded. He reached into his waistcoat and pulled out a small, old book. “This is the ledger,” he said. “Every name, every date, every story. It is heavy, but it is the weight of the world. You will read it. You will learn the names. And when you are ready, you will help me wait.”

Timothy took the book. It was cold and heavy in his hands. He looked up at the shelves, and for the first time, the shadows did not seem so threatening. They seemed like friends, waiting to be acknowledged. The fog outside continued to swirl, but inside, in the quiet, dusty air of the shop, a new light began to kindle. It was a small light, fragile as a candle flame, but it was there. It was the light of hope, and it was just beginning to burn.

PUNCHED, BROUGHT, AND BROUGHT AGAIN.* It was a name that sounded like a cough, and a business that smelled of dust and despair.

Timothy knocked. He knocked with a timid fist, then a bolder one, then with the heel of his shoe, as if the door were a drum in a marching band. There was no answer. He knocked until his knuckles were red and his heart was hammering a frantic rhythm against his ribs, a rhythm that matched the ticking of the clock in the street, which seemed to be counting down the seconds of his life. Then, with a sound like a rusty hinge screaming in protest, the door opened a crack.

A pair of eyes, small, sharp, and buried in a face that looked as though it had been carved from a block of dried wood, peered out. This was Silas Vetch. He wore a waistcoat that had seen better centuries, and his hair, thin and white, stood out in wisps like dry grass in a winter field.

“Who is it?” the voice asked. It was a voice like gravel being stirred in a tin can.

“Mr. Vetch? My name is Timothy Pumble. My mother sent me.”

The eyes narrowed. “Your mother sent you? And where is your mother?”

“Gone, sir. To the country. To stay with her sister.”

The old man’s face twitched. “Gone. Yes. Women are like the fog, boy. They come, they thicken the air, and then they lift, leaving you standing in the cold. Come in. And mind the step. It’s rotten. Like the world.”

The interior of the shop was a labyrinth of shadow. The air was still, heavy with the scent of old paper, horsehair, and something metallic, like the smell of a penny dropped in a puddle. Shelves lined the walls, climbing up to the ceiling, and on these shelves sat objects of terrible variety. There were gold chains, coiled like sleeping snakes; there were silver spoons, tarnished and dull; there were pocket watches, their faces blank and staring; there were rings, brooches, and lockets, all silent and waiting. But what struck Timothy most was the silence. Not the silence of emptiness, but the silence of holding one’s breath. Every object was wrapped in cloth, or locked in a small glass case, or buried under a pile of ledgers.

“You are to sleep in the back room,” Vetch said, not looking at the boy, but at a small brass key he was turning over and over in his fingers. “You will eat what is provided. You will speak when spoken to. And you will not touch anything in this shop. Not a thing. Not a button, not a thread, not a speck of dust.”

“Why?” Timothy asked, his voice trembling. “Why are you keeping them? You are a pawnbroker. You sell them, don’t you?”

Vetch stopped turning the key. He looked at the boy, and for a moment, the hardness in his face cracked, revealing a chasm of something ancient and sad. “We do not sell, boy. We hold. We keep. There is a difference. A great difference. To sell is to forget. To keep is to remember.”

Timothy looked around the room. The objects seemed to watch him. The gold chains shimmered with a cold light; the watches, though silent, seemed to tick in his mind. He felt a strange pull, a gravity that drew him toward the shelves.

“Who are they for?” Timothy asked softly.

Vetch sighed. It was a long, weary sound, like the wind moaning through a broken chimney. “For those who could not afford to lose them. For those who came here in their darkest hour, needing a little life to pay for their bread, their rent, their survival. They pledged their treasures, thinking they would come back for them. But life, boy, is a thief. It steals our time, our strength, our hope. Many of them did not come back. They died, or they moved, or they forgot. And I... I waited. I waited for thirty years. I could not bear to sell what was not mine. I am a custodian, not a merchant.”

Timothy looked at the old man. He saw the loneliness in his eyes, the same loneliness that lived in the empty street outside. He saw a man who had built a fortress of objects to keep the void at bay.

“I will help you,” Timothy said. “I will dust the shelves. I will clean the glass. I will make sure everything is in its place.”

Vetch looked at him, surprised. “You? A boy? You would do that?”

“Yes, sir. Because if you keep them, they are not lost. And if they are not lost, maybe someone will come back. Maybe.”

Vetch looked at the boy for a long time. Then, slowly, he nodded. He reached into his waistcoat and pulled out a small, old book. “This is the ledger,” he said. “Every name, every date, every story. It is heavy, but it is the weight of the world. You will read it. You will learn the names. And when you are ready, you will help me wait.”

Timothy took the book. It was cold and heavy in his hands. He looked up at the shelves, and for the first time, the shadows did not seem so threatening. They seemed like friends, waiting to be acknowledged. The fog outside continued to swirl, but inside, in the quiet, dusty air of the shop, a new light began to kindle. It was a small light, fragile as a candle flame, but it was there. It was the light of hope, and it was just beginning to burn.

flames burst forth, and the stone faces awakened, stared out of fire.

A faint murmur arose about the house from the few people who were left
there, and there was a saddling of a horse and riding away. There was
spurring and splashing through the darkness, and bridle was drawn in the
space by the village fountain, and the horse in a foam stood at Monsieur
Gabelle’s door. “Help, Gabelle! Help, every one!” The tocsin rang
impatiently, but other help (if that were any) there was none. The
mender of roads, and two hundred and fifty particular friends, stood
with folded arms at the fountain, looking at the pillar of fire in the
sky. “It must be forty feet high,” said they, grimly; and never moved.

The rider from the chateau, and the horse in a foam, clattered away
through the village, and galloped up the stony steep, to the prison on
the crag. At the gate, a group of officers were looking at the fire;
removed from them, a group of soldiers. “Help, gentlemen--officers! The
chateau is on fire; valuable objects may be saved from the flames by
timely aid! Help, help!” The officers looked towards the soldiers who
looked at the fire; gave no orders; and answered, with shrugs and biting
of lips, “It must burn.”

As the rider rattled down the hill again and through the street, the
village was illuminating. The mender of roads, and the two hundred and
fifty particular friends, inspired as one man and woman by the idea of
lighting up, had darted into their houses, and were putting candles in
every dull little pane of glass. The general scarcity of everything,
occasioned candles to be borrowed in a rather peremptory manner of
Monsieur Gabelle; and in a moment of reluctance and hesitation on
that functionary’s part, the mender of roads, once so submissive to
authority, had remarked that carriages were good to make bonfires with,
and that post-horses would roast.

The chateau was left to itself to flame and burn. In the roaring and
raging of the conflagration, a red-hot wind, driving straight from the
infernal regions, seemed to be blowing the edifice away. With the rising
and falling of the blaze, the stone faces showed as if they were in
torment. When great masses of stone and timber fell, the face with the
two dints in the nose became obscured: anon struggled out of the smoke
again, as if it were the face of the cruel Marquis, burning at the stake
and contending with the fire.

The chateau burned; the nearest trees, laid hold of by the fire,
scorched and shrivelled; trees at a distance, fired by the four fierce
figures, begirt the blazing edifice with a new forest of smoke. Molten
lead and iron boiled in the marble basin of the fountain; the water ran
dry; the extinguisher tops of the towers vanished like ice before the
heat, and trickled down into four rugged wells of flame. Great rents and
splits branched out in the solid walls, like crystallisation; stupefied
birds wheeled about and dropped into the furnace; four fierce figures
trudged away, East, West, North, and South, along the night-enshrouded
roads, guided by the beacon they had lighted, towards their next
destination. The illuminated village had seized hold of the tocsin, and,
abolishing the lawful ringer, rang for joy.

Not only that; but the village, light-headed with famine, fire, and
bell-ringing, and bethinking itself that Monsieur Gabelle had to do with
the collection of rent and taxes--though it was but a small instalment
of taxes, and no rent at all, that Gabelle had got in those latter
days--became impatient for an interview with him, and, surrounding his
house, summoned him to come forth for personal conference. Whereupon,
Monsieur Gabelle did heavily bar his door, and retire to hold counsel
with himself. The result of that conference was, that Gabelle again
withdrew himself to his housetop behind his stack of chimneys; this time
resolved, if his door were broken in (he was a small Southern man
of retaliative temperament), to pitch himself head foremost over the
parapet, and crush a man or two below.

Probably, Monsieur Gabelle passed a long night up there, with the
distant chateau for fire and candle, and the beating at his door,
combined with the joy-ringing, for music; not to mention his having an
ill-omened lamp slung across the road before his posting-house gate,
which the village showed a lively inclination to displace in his favour.
A trying suspense, to be passing a whole summer night on the brink of
the black ocean, ready to take that plunge into it upon which Monsieur
Gabelle had resolved! But, the friendly dawn appearing at last, and the
rush-candles of the village guttering out, the people happily dispersed,
and Monsieur Gabelle came down bringing his life with him for that
while.

Within a hundred miles, and in the light of other fires, there were
other functionaries less fortunate, that night and other nights, whom
the rising sun found hanging across once-peaceful streets, where they
had been born and bred; also, there were other villagers and townspeople
less fortunate than the mender of roads and his fellows, upon whom the
functionaries and soldiery turned with success, and whom they strung up
in their turn. But, the fierce figures were steadily wending East, West,
North, and South, be that as it would; and whosoever hung, fire burned.
The altitude of the gallows that would turn to water and quench it,
no functionary, by any stretch of mathematics, was able to calculate
successfully.

In such risings of fire and risings of sea--the firm earth shaken by the rushes of an angry ocean which had now no ebb, but was always on the flow, higher and higher, to the terror and wonder of the beholders on the shore--three years of tempest were consumed. [Scenario]
A pompous alderman who has organised a banquet to celebrate a new town hall discovers on the morning of the feast that the contractor has run off with the funds and the roof is unfinished. He must preside over the banquet in the rain without admitting anything is wrong.
Setting: A Midlands market town, 1850s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The rain fell upon the town of Bumblewick not as a gentle weeping of the skies, but as a relentless, muddy deluge, a sort of atmospheric tantrum that seemed designed specifically to humble the ambitions of the newly appointed Alderman, Mr. Silas Pumble. It was a Tuesday, or perhaps a Wednesday; the days had begun to blur in Pumble’s mind, much like the edges of his conscience, ever since he had first laid eyes on the grand, gaping maw of the Town Hall roof. The building stood on the high ground, a squat, brick-and-mortar monstrosity intended to house the civic pride of the district, but which currently resembled a broken eggshell waiting for the first heavy stone to crack it entirely. The contractor, a man of vague nationality and even vaguer reputation named Mr. Zilch, had vanished into the ether, taking with him the remaining two thousand pounds of public funds, the scaffolding, the shingles, and, most regrettably, any shred of common sense that might have suggested finishing the roof before inviting the cream of the county to dine beneath it.

Pumble stood at the window of his study, a man whose physical proportions had expanded in exact ratio to his political power, watching the grey water sheet down the unglazed brickwork of the new hall. He wore a waistcoat of the finest damask, a color that clashed violently with his complexion, which was the pale, sallow hue of a man who had not seen the sun since the last general election. His wig, a curly, auburn affair that he had purchased from a dubious vendor in London, sat slightly askew, as if it, too, was losing its grip on reality.

"He is gone," said the steward, a thin, nervous creature named Mr. Grubb, who had been pacing the room like a caged beagle. "The man is gone, Sir. The money is gone. The roof is... well, the roof is an idea, Sir. A very airy idea."

Pumble turned from the window, his eyes wide with a mixture of terror and indignation. "An idea?" he squeaked, his voice cracking like a dry twig. "You call that an idea? I have sent out the invitations! I have ordered the roasted peacock! I have arranged for the orchestra to play the national anthem with such vigor that it shall shake the very foundations of the earth! And now you tell me the earth is leaking into the banquet hall?"

Grubb wrung his hands. "It is raining, Sir. It is raining so hard that one might swim a canal from the main door to the council chamber. The guests will arrive in an hour. What shall we do?"

Pumble straightened his wig. He looked at the storm, then at the steward, and finally at his own reflection in the darkened glass. In the reflection, he saw not a man of integrity, but a puppet, dangling by the strings of his own vanity. He thought of his mother, who had always told him that a man who lies about his shoes will eventually lie about his soul. He thought of the peacock, which was currently being stuffed by a butcher who did not know the building was unfinished. He thought of the speeches he had prepared, the grand orations on civic duty and municipal hygiene that would now be delivered into a puddle.

"We shall not acknowledge it," Pumble declared, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. "We shall say it is... a test of character. A trial of spirit. The rain is merely the sky weeping for the glory of the new era. We shall proceed. The peacock will be cooked. The champagne will be chilled. And if the roof leaks, we shall say it is a feature. A skylight. A window to the heavens."

Grubb stared at him. "A window to the heavens, Sir?"

"A very large, wet window to the heavens," Pumble corrected, smoothing his whiskers. "Now, go. Tell the cook to use the extra towels. Tell the band to play loudly. And for the love of all that is holy, find me a hat that does not look like a dried mushroom."

The afternoon descended upon Bumblewick with the weight of a leaden blanket. The market square, usually a hub of commerce and gossip, was now a sea of mud and splashing water. Carriages creaked and groaned as they attempted to navigate the slick cobblestones, their drivers cursing in a language that had no place in a civilized town. And there, standing before the gaping hole in the sky where the roof should have been, was Mr. Silas Pumble, resplendent in a top hat that was already beginning to sag, his waistcoat buttoned tight against the chill, his face a mask of serene, unblinking optimism.

The guests began to arrive, a procession of silk and velvet, of mud-spattered boots and wrinkled parasols. Lady Thistlethwaite, a woman of such immense girth that she seemed to occupy her own gravitational field, was the first to enter. She looked up at the open sky, then down at Pumble, and back up again.

"Is this... is this a new architectural trend, Alderman Pumble?" she asked, her voice echoing strangely in the unfinished hall. "I had heard rumors of a 'living roof,' but I confess I did not expect it to be quite so... alive."

Pumble bowed, a deep, theatrical bow that nearly sent him into a puddle forming near the dais. "A bold choice, Madam," he said, with a wink that was lost in the gloom. "But one must allow for the elements to enter the conversation. It adds a certain... authenticity to the discourse. Shall we proceed to the buffet?"

The buffet was a disaster of epic proportions. The tables, set in the main hall, were already damp. The silverware had a patina of rust. The peacock, alas, had been cooked in the drafty kitchen and was now a dry, shriveled thing, more like a leathery ornament than a delicacy. But Pumble, undeterred, began to circulate, cutting his own slices of bread and butter, and offering them to anyone who would take them.

"Here, my dear Sir," he said to the Mayor, a man who looked as though he had been personally offended by the existence of weather. "A slice of the finest Bumblewick wheat. Unfortified by shingles, but fortified by spirit."

The Mayor chewed the dry bread, his jaw working silently. "The rain is coming through the beams, Alderman. It is dripping onto the soup."

"Ah," said Pumble, looking up at a drop of water that landed on his nose. "But is it not also a form of hydration? A direct line to the source? We are drinking the sky, my friend. Are we not the most adventurous diners in the county?"

Laughter erupted, not from joy, but from a collective sense of absurdity so profound that it became hysterical. The guests began to laugh, a sound that mingled with the thunder and the creaking of the timber. They passed the dishes, they drank the champagne, which was warm and flat, and they watched the rain pour in through the hole in the roof, turning the floor into a muddy swamp.

Pumble, meanwhile, had retired to the corner, where he sat on a crate of wine, his wig now completely soaked and plastered to his forehead. He watched the chaos with a strange, detached interest. He had failed. The roof was unfinished. The money was gone. The contractor was a ghost. And yet, as he looked at the faces of his neighbors, smeared with mud and rain, laughing and toasting to the 'window to the heavens,' he felt a strange, peculiar sensation in his chest. It was not pride. It was not relief. It was something closer to a grim, shared complicity. They were all in it together, this wretched, wet, unfinished thing.

The storm raged on outside, howling through the rafters like a banshee. Inside, the banquet continued, a grotesque parody of civility, a dinner party held in the ruins of ambition. Pumble raised his glass, the liquid sloshing dangerously close to the rim, and looked out into the grey void of the sky.

"To the roof," he shouted, his voice hoarse. "May it hold!"

"To the roof!" the guests shouted back, raising their own glasses, the rain dripping from their hair, their clothes, their very souls. And in that moment, amidst the mud and the mayhem, Bumblewick had its finest hour, not because of what it had built, but because of what it had endured, and the terrible, beautiful joke they had all agreed to tell, under the open, weeping sky.

was precisely in this condition. He saw the Jew with his half-closed eyes; heard his low whistling; and recognised the sound of the spoon grating against the saucepan’s sides: and yet the self-same senses were mentally engaged, at the same time, in busy action with almost everybody he had ever known.

When the coffee was done, the Jew drew the saucepan to the hob.
Standing, then in an irresolute attitude for a few minutes, as if he
did not well know how to employ himself, he turned round and looked at
Oliver, and called him by his name. He did not answer, and was to all
appearances asleep.

After satisfying himself upon this head, the Jew stepped gently to the
door: which he fastened. He then drew forth: as it seemed to Oliver,
from some trap in the floor: a small box, which he placed carefully on
the table. His eyes glistened as he raised the lid, and looked in.
Dragging an old chair to the table, he sat down; and took from it a
magnificent gold watch, sparkling with jewels.

“Aha!” said the Jew, shrugging up his shoulders, and distorting every
feature with a hideous grin. “Clever dogs! Clever dogs! Staunch to the
last! Never told the old parson where they were. Never poached upon old
Fagin! And why should they? It wouldn’t have loosened the knot, or kept
the drop up, a minute longer. No, no, no! Fine fellows! Fine fellows!”

With these, and other muttered reflections of the like nature, the Jew
once more deposited the watch in its place of safety. At least half a
dozen more were severally drawn forth from the same box, and surveyed
with equal pleasure; besides rings, brooches, bracelets, and other
articles of jewellery, of such magnificent materials, and costly
workmanship, that Oliver had no idea, even of their names.

Having replaced these trinkets, the Jew took out another: so small that
it lay in the palm of his hand. There seemed to be some very minute
inscription on it; for the Jew laid it flat upon the table, and shading
it with his hand, pored over it, long and earnestly. At length he put
it down, as if despairing of success; and, leaning back in his chair,
muttered:

“What a fine thing capital punishment is! Dead men never repent; dead
men never bring awkward stories to light. Ah, it’s a fine thing for the
trade! Five of ’em strung up in a row, and none left to play booty, or
turn white-livered!”

As the Jew uttered these words, his bright dark eyes, which had been
staring vacantly before him, fell on Oliver’s face; the boy’s eyes were
fixed on his in mute curiousity; and although the recognition was only
for an instant—for the briefest space of time that can possibly be
conceived—it was enough to show the old man that he had been observed.

He closed the lid of the box with a loud crash; and, laying his hand on
a bread knife which was on the table, started furiously up. He trembled

and a threatening attitude.

and playing with the knife a little, before he laid it down; as if to
induce the belief that he had caught it up, in mere sport. “Of course I
know that, my dear. I only tried to frighten you. You’re a brave boy.

chuckle, but glanced uneasily at the box, notwithstanding.

his hand upon it after a short pause.

little property. All I have to live upon, in my old age. The folks call
me a miser, my dear. Only a miser; that’s all.”

such a dirty place, with so many watches; but, thinking that perhaps

money, he only cast a deferential look at the Jew, and asked if he

raise the pitcher. When he turned his head, the box was gone.

introduced to him as Charley Bates. The four sat down, to breakfast, on
the coffee, and some hot rolls and ham which the Dodger had brought
home in the crown of his hat.

to the Dodger, “I hope you’ve been at work this morning, my dears?”

[Scenario]
A young clerk in a shipping office wins a modest prize in a public lottery and resolves to keep it secret from his grasping relations. Within a week every one of them has heard of it, and each arrives at his lodging with a misfortune requiring exactly the amount he has won.
Setting: The City of London, 1840s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
If any young gentleman of modest expectations and extraordinary uncles had ever reason to curse the day he first possessed a spare shilling, that young gentleman was Mr. Edwin Puffle. Mr. Puffle was a clerk—a very damp, very ink-stained, and very patient clerk—in the counting-house of Messrs. Gripe, Grasp, and Clench, ship-brokers, of Narrow Lane, in the City of London; and in the year of grace one thousand eight hundred and forty-something, he happened, by one of those unaccountable freaks of Fortune which she plays upon the insignificant, to be the holder of a winning number in a public lottery.

It was not a magnificent sum. It was not a sum to purchase a country estate, or a carriage, or a seat in Parliament. It was exactly fifty pounds. But to Edwin Puffle, who existed upon a salary of forty-five pounds per annum, and whose weekly accounts were generally a long arithmetic of halfpence, it appeared a gilded mountain of opulence. He received the golden pieces in a small canvas bag, and he resolved, with all the solemnity of a man making a will, to keep the matter an inviolable secret from his relations.

Mr. Puffle had relations. He had them in alarming profusion. He had a mother-in-law’s sister, Mrs. Sarah Squeaks, who was afflicted with a perpetual cold and a still more perpetual demand for loans. He had a cousin, Mr. Nathaniel Nipper, a man of no visible occupation, who lived by the mysterious doctrine that blood is thicker than water, and, therefore, a relative’s pocket is a common reservoir. He had an uncle, Major Stiltstock, a retired militia officer of immense stomach and no visible income, who believed the world owed him a living, and Edwin owed the world. These, and a few minor satellites, revolved about the planet of Puffle, constantly eclipsing his comfort.

On the evening of his good fortune, Mr. Puffle sat in his lodging in Thumbling’s Rents, a narrow thoroughfare near the river, where the houses leaned forward as if to whisper each other into ruin. His apartment was on the third floor, and consisted of one room, in which he cooked, ate, slept, and was occasionally dunned. He placed the canvas bag in the hollow of his only spare boot, pushed the boot under the bed, and, folding his arms, looked round with the complacency of a monarch surveying his dominions. He was safe. He was solitary. He was rich. And he would tell no one.

Within a week, every one of them had heard of it.

How the intelligence escaped is one of those mysteries which no philosophy can unravel. Perhaps the clerk at the lottery office had a brother who kept a public-house, and the publican had a customer who was a postman, and the postman had a friend who was a tailor, and the tailor had a brother-in-law who knew Mrs. Squeaks. Or perhaps Mrs. Squeaks herself, endowed with that supernatural instinct which belongs to needy relatives, smelt the gold through the brick walls of Narrow Lane. At any rate, on the seventh morning, while Mr. Puffle was consuming his modest tea and a fragment of toasted bread, he heard a heavy, asthmatic tread upon the staircase, and presently Mrs. Sarah Squeaks stood in the doorway, breathing like a pair of agricultural bellows, and shaking her umbrella as if it were a weapon of assault.

“Eh, dear, dear, Edwin!” said Mrs. Squeaks, sinking into the only chair, and pressing her hand to her side. “I am almost gone. The stairs! The cruel stairs! But I had to come. I had to come, if it was my last effort. You have heard, of course, of my affliction?”

Mr. Puffle, with the guilty air of a man who has hidden a boot, said he had not.

“Not heard!” cried Mrs. Squeaks, with a tragic inflection that seemed to imply the whole world was callous. “Not heard that my landlord has raised my rent, and that unless I can pay five pounds by tomorrow, I and my poor orphan niece will be turned into the street! Five pounds, Edwin! And such a small sum to one who has just come into fifty! For I know all, Edwin. I had it from Mrs. Grummage, who had it from the greengrocer, who had it from the man who cleans the lottery office windows. Five pounds, Edwin—and the amount is exactly fifty!”

Mr. Puffle, with that fatal weakness which distinguishes the timid in the presence of the importunate, produced five golden pounds. Mrs. Squeaks, having kissed him, wept over him, and called him her preserver, departed with a velocity that seemed inconsistent with her previous asthmatic condition.

He had scarcely recovered from this visit when there came a loud, military knock, and Mr. Nathaniel Nipper bounced into the room, with his hat on one side and his hand extended.

“Well, Ed!” said Mr. Nipper, with that jocular familiarity which is the last refuge of the borrower. “Glad to see you looking so flourishing. Prosperity becomes you. I always said you’d rise in the world. You have a head, Ed—a head. And a head, properly directed, is worth money. Speaking of money, I want ten pounds.”

Mr. Puffle feebly protested.

“Ten pounds, Ed,” repeated Mr. Nipper, with the air of a man arranging a matter of business. “I have a little affair on hand—an investment—infallible—which only requires ten pounds to set it going. I came to you, because you’re a man of sense, and because you’ve just won fifty. Come, Ed, don’t be mean. Ten pounds, and I’ll make it twenty in a month.”

Mr. Puffle, overborne by the audacity of the demand, and the hopelessness of resistance, produced ten pounds. Mr. Nipper, having slapped him on the back, called him a trump, and vanished, leaving behind him a strong smell of tobacco and a general impression of moral bankruptcy.

The third visitor was the Major. The Major came in the evening, with the slow, deliberate tread of a man who intends to make a long stay, and who carries his own resources in his waistcoat. He was a large man, with a purple face, and a manner of adjusting his shirt-collar, which seemed to imply that the world was a parade-ground, and he was reviewing it. He sat down, placed his cane between his legs, and, after a preliminary cough, began:

“Well, Edwin, my boy, I am glad to find you at home. I have been thinking of you. I have been thinking that you are a young man of promise, and that I, as your uncle, have a duty to perform. I have a duty, Edwin. A duty to myself, and a duty to you. I have, in short, a little bill—a trifle—thirty-five pounds—which falls due tomorrow, and which, if not met, will involve consequences which I shudder to contemplate. I need not say more. I know your generous nature. I know your recent good fortune. I am not the man to remind you of it, but—”

The Major paused, adjusted his collar, and looked at the ceiling.

“But,” said Mr. Puffle, faintly, “I have already—”

“Already!” interrupted the Major, with a look of pained surprise. “Surely, Edwin, you have not been so weak—so fatally weak—as to part with any of it already? To whom? To that woman Squeaks? To that scapegrace Nipper? Folly, Edwin! Utter folly! They are not relations of your standing. I am the head of your family. I am the natural guardian of your interests. Give me the thirty-five pounds, and I will take care of it, and of you.”

Mr. Puffle, with the despairing conviction that he was ruined, produced the remaining thirty-five pounds. The Major, having pocketed them, observed that he had always had a reliance on Edwin’s good sense, and that he would call again in a day or two, and talk over the family interests. He then departed, leaving Mr. Puffle sitting on the edge of his bed, with the empty boot in his hand, and a conviction that he was the most unfortunate of mortals.

The next morning, as he sat at his desk in the counting-house of Messrs. Gripe, Grasp, and Clench, with a pen behind each ear, and a blot before him, Mr. Puffle was visited by a philosophical reflection. He thought that if he had not won the fifty pounds, he would have been spared the visits of his relations, the loss of his money, and the humiliation of his present poverty. He thought that Fortune was a jade, who gave with one hand only to enable her relatives to take with the other. He thought that the best thing a man could do, when he came into a little money, was to lose it immediately, or to hide it in a place where even his relations could not find it. And he thought, finally, that the boot was a very indifferent hiding-place, and that the next time he won fifty pounds, he would put it in the fire, or throw it in the river, or do anything with it, rather than let his relations know of it.

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

how little I do claim, but I will go that length. You have done so much for him, you are so fond of him; your whole life, Mrs. Bounderby, expresses such charming self-forgetfulness on his account—pardon me again—I am running wide of the subject. I am interested in him for his own sake.’

She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in
a hurry and gone away.  He had turned the course of what he said at that
instant, and she remained.

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ he resumed, in a lighter manner, and yet with a show of
effort in assuming it, which was even more expressive than the manner he
dismissed; ‘it is no irrevocable offence in a young fellow of your
brother’s years, if he is heedless, inconsiderate, and expensive—a little
dissipated, in the common phrase.  Is he?’

‘Yes.’

‘Allow me to be frank.  Do you think he games at all?’

‘I think he makes bets.’  Mr. Harthouse waiting, as if that were not her
whole answer, she added, ‘I know he does.’

‘Of course he loses?’

‘Yes.’

‘Everybody does lose who bets.  May I hint at the probability of your
sometimes supplying him with money for these purposes?’

She sat, looking down; but, at this question, raised her eyes searchingly
and a little resentfully.

‘Acquit me of impertinent curiosity, my dear Mrs. Bounderby.  I think Tom
may be gradually falling into trouble, and I wish to stretch out a
helping hand to him from the depths of my wicked experience.—Shall I say
again, for his sake?  Is that necessary?’

She seemed to try to answer, but nothing came of it.

‘Candidly to confess everything that has occurred to me,’ said James
Harthouse, again gliding with the same appearance of effort into his more
airy manner; ‘I will confide to you my doubt whether he has had many
advantages.  Whether—forgive my plainness—whether any great amount of
confidence is likely to have been established between himself and his
most worthy father.’

‘I do not,’ said Louisa, flushing with her own great remembrance in that
wise, ‘think it likely.’

‘Or, between himself, and—I may trust to your perfect understanding of my
meaning, I am sure—and his highly esteemed brother-in-law.’

She flushed deeper and deeper, and was burning red when she replied in a
fainter voice, ‘I do not think that likely, either.’

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ said Harthouse, after a short silence, ‘may there be a
better confidence between yourself and me?  Tom has borrowed a
considerable sum of you?’

‘You will understand, Mr. Harthouse,’ she returned, after some
indecision: she had been more or less uncertain, and troubled throughout
the conversation, and yet had in the main preserved her self-contained
manner; ‘you will understand that if I tell you what you press to know,
it is not by way of complaint or regret.  I would never complain of
anything, and what I have done I do not in the least regret.’

‘So spirited, too!’ thought James Harthouse.

‘When I married, I found that my brother was even at that time heavily in
debt.  Heavily for him, I mean.  Heavily enough to oblige me to sell some
trinkets.  They were no sacrifice.  I sold them very willingly.  I
attached no value to them.  They were quite worthless to me.’

Either she saw in his face that he knew, or she only feared in her
conscience that he knew, that she spoke of some of her husband’s gifts.
She stopped, and reddened again.  If he had not known it before, he would
have known it then, though he had been a much duller man than he was.

‘Since then, I have given my brother, at various times, what money I
could spare: in short, what money I have had.  Confiding in you at all,
on the faith of the interest you profess for him, I will not do so by
halves.  Since you have been in the habit of visiting here, he has wanted
in one sum as much as a hundred pounds.  I have not been able to give it
to him.  I have felt uneasy for the consequences of his being so
involved, but I have kept these secrets until now, when I trust them to
your honour.  I have held no confidence with any one, because—you
anticipated my reason just now.’  She abruptly broke off.

He was a ready man, and he saw, and seized, an opportunity here of
presenting her own image to her, slightly disguised as her brother.

‘Mrs. Bounderby, though a graceless person, of the world worldly, I feel
the utmost interest, I assure you, in what you tell me.  I cannot
possibly be hard upon your brother.  I understand and share the wise
consideration with which you regard his errors.  With all possible
respect both for Mr. Gradgrind and for Mr. Bounderby, I think I perceive
that he has not been fortunate in his training.  Bred at a disadvantage
towards the society in which he has his part to play, he rushes into
these extremes for himself, from opposite extremes that have long been
forced—with the very best intentions we have no doubt—upon him.  Mr.
Bounderby’s fine bluff English independence, though a most charming
characteristic, does not—as we have agreed—invite confidence.  If I might
venture to remark that it is the least in the world deficient in that
delicacy to which a youth mistaken, a character misconceived, and
abilities misdirected, would turn for relief and guidance, I should
express what it presents to my own view.’

As she sat looking straight before her, across the changing lights upon
the grass into the darkness of the wood beyond, he saw in her face her
application of his very distinctly uttered words.

‘All allowance,’ he continued, ‘must be made.  I have one great fault to
find with Tom, however, which I cannot forgive, and for which I take him

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The shop of Mr. Abel Crummles stood in the shadow of a narrow street off Holborn—a street so pinched and crooked that the sun, in its most generous moods, could only visit it in patches, and the fog, in its least generous, took up its residence there for days together, like a lodger who has no intention of leaving. It was a pawnbroker's, though the three brass balls had long since been taken down, and the windows were shuttered so close that no curious eye could penetrate the gloom within; and above the shop, in two rooms that smelled of dust and old ledgers, lived Mr. Crummles himself, a retired man of seventy years, who had not spoken a civil word to a soul in thirty of them.

It was to this establishment that I, Thomas Wren, aged ten, was conveyed upon a raw November afternoon by a solicitor's clerk who had no more notion of my destination than I had myself. My mother was dead; my father had gone to the devil by way of the West Indies; and the only relation remaining to me in the world was this grandfather, whom I had never seen, and of whom I knew nothing, save that he had once been a pawnbroker and was now—so the clerk informed me with a sniff—"a rum old file, and no mistake."

The clerk knocked thrice upon the door and departed, and I stood upon the step in the rain, a small boy with a bundle, listening to the slow approach of footsteps within. The door opened a crack, and an eye appeared—a single eye, grey and wary, that surveyed me as a jeweller surveys a doubtful stone.

"Well?" said a voice, dry as an old leaf.

"I am Thomas Wren," said I, "your grandson, sir, and I have come to live with you."

The eye regarded me for a long moment. Then the door opened wider, and I saw a tall old man, bent at the shoulders, in a snuff-coloured coat and a wig that had seen better days—and behind him, in the dim shop, a sight that I have never forgotten: shelves upon shelves of pledges, wrapped in brown paper and tied with string, each bearing a tag with a name and date, and each, as I was afterward to learn, untouched for thirty years.

"Come in, then," said Mr. Crummles. "Wipe your feet. I'll have no dirt tracked in."

I wiped my feet, and entered.

The shop was a cavern of curiosities. There were watches by the dozen, hanging from hooks like so many metallic bats; there were rings and brooches and snuff-boxes in glass cases thick with dust; there were suits of clothes, folded and labelled, that had once belonged to gentlemen who had fallen upon hard times; and there were musical instruments, and china figures, and a stuffed parrot that regarded me with a glassy and malevolent stare. But it was the brown-paper parcels that drew my eye—for they were everywhere, stacked upon the shelves from floor to ceiling, and each one, I noticed, bore a date that was thirty years old or more.

"Grandfather," said I, "why do you never sell these things?"

Mr. Crummles turned upon me a look of such sudden and unexpected ferocity that I stepped back a pace.

"Who told you to ask that?" he demanded.

"Nobody, sir. I only wondered—"

"Wondered!" cried the old man, with a bitter laugh. "Wondering is the beginning of meddling, and meddling is the beginning of ruin. You'll keep your wonders to yourself in this house, young man, or you'll find yourself out in the street again, and no mistake about it."

And with that he showed me to a small room at the back of the shop, containing a bed, a chair, and a washing-stand, and left me to my own devices.

I was not a boy to be discouraged by a single rebuff, however; and as the days passed, I set myself to the task of winning my grandfather's affection with all the patience and ingenuity I possessed. I swept the shop without being asked; I dusted the glass cases; I learned to make his tea exactly as he liked it—strong, with a dash of rum, and no sugar. I asked him no more questions about the parcels, though I thought of them constantly; and I observed him closely, as a naturalist observes a strange specimen, noting the way he would pause before a certain shelf and stand there, motionless, for minutes together, his lips moving as if in conversation with some invisible companion.

The shop of Mr. Abel Crummles stood in the shadow of a narrow street off Holborn—a street so pinched and crooked that the sun, in its most generous moods, could only visit it in patches, and the fog, in its least generous, took up its residence there for days together, like a lodger who has no intention of leaving. It was a pawnbroker's, though the three brass balls had long since been taken down, and the windows were shuttered so close that no curious eye could penetrate the gloom within; and above the shop, in two rooms that smelled of dust and old ledgers, lived Mr. Crummles himself, a retired man of seventy years, who had not spoken a civil word to a soul in thirty of them.

It was to this establishment that I, Thomas Wren, aged ten, was conveyed upon a raw November afternoon by a solicitor's clerk who had no more notion of my destination than I had myself. My mother was dead; my father had gone to the devil by way of the West Indies; and the only relation remaining to me in the world was this grandfather, whom I had never seen, and of whom I knew nothing, save that he had once been a pawnbroker and was now—so the clerk informed me with a sniff—"a rum old file, and no mistake."

The clerk knocked thrice upon the door and departed, and I stood upon the step in the rain, a small boy with a bundle, listening to the slow approach of footsteps within.
