Write an original piece of prose fiction.

[Scenario]
A widow who keeps a respectable lodging house is visited by a stranger who knows that she was once married under another name, to a man who was transported for forgery. He asks for money. She must decide whether her present life is worth what he demands.
Setting: A lodging house in Bath, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The last of the afternoon sun slanted through the tall windows of the drawing room at Number Four, Queen’s Parade, illuminating the dust motes dancing over the Aubusson carpet. Mrs. Elspeth Vance stood by the mantelpiece, adjusting a porcelain shepherdess by a millimetre, a small, precise gesture in a life governed by such things. Below, the clatter of a carriage on the cobbles announced the departure of Mr. Abernathy, a retired colonel whose complaints about the draughts were as regular as the church bells. Her lodging house was her fortress, its respectability the mortar that held the stones of her life together. Each polished banister, each starched doily, each perfectly timed cup of tea was a testament to the woman she had become: a widow of impeccable standing, a pillar of the quiet, gossipy world of Bath.

The bell at the front door chimed, an unfamiliar, sharp sound at this hour. She smoothed her black bombazine skirts and descended, her hand trailing the cool wood of the banister. She opened the door to a man she did not know. He was not dressed for Queen’s Parade. His coat was of a coarse, dark wool, travel-stained at the cuffs, and his boots, though sturdy, were caked with the mud of a journey that had not ended at a coaching inn. His face was thin, etched with lines that spoke of hardship rather than age, and his eyes, a pale, watery blue, held a disquieting familiarity that she could not place.

“Mrs. Vance?” he asked, his voice a low rasp.

“I am she. May I help you, sir?”

“I believe you can.” He did not wait for an invitation but stepped past her into the hall, his gaze sweeping over the polished floorboards, the silver umbrella stand, the framed watercolour of the Pulteney Bridge. “A fine place you have here. Very fine. A long way from the rookeries of Bristol.”

A cold prickle, sharp as a needle, traced its way down her spine. “I don’t believe I have the pleasure of your acquaintance,” she said, her voice carefully level. She gestured towards the drawing room. “If this is a matter of business, perhaps we could discuss it in private.”

He followed her in, his presence a discordant note in the room’s carefully composed harmony. He did not sit, but stood by the window, looking out at the manicured square. “Business. Yes, you could call it that. A matter of an old debt.”

Elspeth’s hands clenched within the folds of her skirt. “I have no debts, sir. My accounts are settled in full.”

“Not a debt of money. Not yet.” He turned to face her, and in the slanting light, she saw it. The shape of his brow, the way his upper lip thinned when he spoke. A ghost from a past she had buried so deep she sometimes forgot it herself. “Not a debt of money,” he repeated, “but a debt of loyalty. A debt owed to a brother.”

The porcelain shepherdess on the mantelpiece suddenly seemed garish, a cheap trinket. Her world, so solid a moment before, had developed a hairline crack.

“I think you are mistaken,” she said, the words feeling hollow in her mouth. “I have no brother.”

“No,” he agreed, a slow, unpleasant smile touching his lips. “But Mary Croft did. A brother named Silas. And Mary Croft had a husband, too. A clever man with a fine hand for penmanship. A man named Thomas Croft.”

The name was a stone dropped into the deep well of her memory, and the ripples spread outwards, threatening to flood everything. Thomas. His charming smile, the scent of ink on his fingers, the frantic, whispered plans that had felt like adventure. The terrible, hollow silence after they took him away. The shame that had clung to her like a shroud. She had fled Bristol with nothing but the clothes on her back and a new name, Elspeth Vance, widow of a respectable sea captain lost at sea. She had built a new life from the ashes, brick by painstaking brick.

“I don’t know these people,” she whispered, but the denial was a reflex, a shield already shattered.

Silas took a step closer. The smell of him—of stale ale and unwashed linen—intruded upon the scent of beeswax and dried lavender. “Oh, I think you do, *Mary*. Thomas was transported for forgery. A seven-year sentence. A hard life, out in the colonies. I had a letter from him, years ago. He spoke of you. He wondered where his darling wife had got to.”

“What do you want?” The question was torn from her, raw and desperate.

Silas’s pale eyes glittered. “What is owed. My brother is dead. Died in a penal colony in New South Wales, breaking rocks. And I’ve been left with nothing. But you… you’ve done well for yourself. Very well. This house, these things… they weren’t bought with a sea captain’s pension, I’d wager.”

The accusation, though unspoken, was clear. He knew, or suspected, the truth of her past, of the money Thomas had made before his arrest, money she had hidden and used to finance her escape and new beginning.

“I want two hundred pounds,” he said, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper. “A sum that would see me right. A new life, far from here. And you… you get to keep this. All of it. The name. The respectability. The quiet life of Mrs. Elspeth Vance. No one ever needs to know about Mary Croft and her unfortunate husband.”

Two hundred pounds. It was a fortune. It was the sum total of her savings, the capital that ensured the lodging house’s future, her own security in her old age. It was everything.

“Or,” he continued, seeing the shock on her face, “I could take a walk down to the Pump Room tomorrow. I hear it’s a very social place. So easy to start a conversation. To mention a name from the past. I wonder what the good ladies of Bath would think of their respectable landlady then? They do so love a scandal.”

He was blackmailing her. The word was ugly, brutal, and it laid bare the fragile nature of her existence. Her respectable life, the one she cherished, was not a fortress at all. It was a house of cards, and this man, this ghost from her past, held a single, fatal breath.

She looked around the room, at the life she had so carefully constructed. The solid mahogany table where her lodgers took breakfast, the comfortable chairs by the fire, the very air of tranquility and order. It was a life of quiet triumph over chaos and shame. Was it worth two hundred pounds? Was it worth her entire livelihood? Or was it worth nothing at all, just a fragile illusion that could be shattered by a single word in a crowded room?

Her mind raced, weighing the scales. Pay him, and she would be left with this house, but stripped bare. She would be vulnerable again, at the mercy of the next emergency, the next draught, the next difficult lodger. The security she had bled for would be gone. And he would be back. A man like Silas would always be back.

Refuse him, and she would lose it all anyway. The scandal would break her. Her lodgers would leave. Her name would be a byword for disgrace. She would be Mary Croft again: a widow of a forger, a woman with nothing.

He stood there, waiting, his thin face a mask of greed and desperation. He thought he had her cornered. He saw the respectable widow, the woman with everything to lose. He did not see the girl who had survived the gutters of Bristol, who had learned to be hard, to be ruthless, to put survival above all else.

Elspeth walked slowly to her small writing desk by the window. Her movements were calm, deliberate. She opened the drawer and took out a heavy iron key. Silas’s eyes followed her, a triumphant smirk beginning to form on his lips. He thought she was going to a strongbox.

Instead, she walked to the bell-pull by the fireplace and gave it a sharp, decisive tug. Not the gentle pull for a servant, but the sharp, urgent one for the footman who ran errands and kept order.

Silas’s smirk faltered. “What are you doing?”

Elspeth turned to face him, her expression as cold and hard as the iron key in her hand. The frightened widow was gone. In her place was the woman who had clawed her way out of the gutter, the woman who had survived. “You mistake me, sir,” she said, her voice clear and carrying. “You think I am a woman with a past to hide. You are wrong. I am a woman with nothing left to lose but the present. And I will not be robbed of it.”

The drawing-room door opened and Jenkins, the stout, formidable footman, stood on the threshold.

“Jenkins,” Elspeth said, her eyes never leaving Silas’s pale, bewildered face. “This gentleman was just leaving. He has made a mistake. Please show him out. And if he ever darkens my door again, you are to send for a constable at once. He is a vagrant, and I will not have his sort disturbing my lodgers.”

Silas stared, his mouth opening and closing like a landed fish. He had come to threaten a fragile lady, and found himself facing a fortress after all. Not one of stone and mortar, but of sheer, unyielding will.

Jenkins stepped forward. “This way, sir.”

For a moment, Silas looked as if he might argue, might shout her name, might shatter the glass. But the look in Elspeth’s eyes—a look of absolute, terrifying finality—stopped him. He saw no fear there, only a cold, flat refusal. He had lost.

Without another word, he turned and followed the footman from the room. Elspeth stood motionless until she heard the front door close, the sound echoing in the sudden, profound silence. She walked to the mantelpiece and picked up the porcelain shepherdess. It was only a cheap trinket, after all. But it was hers. And she would hold onto it. She had paid for it. Not in money, but in a currency far more precious. And she would never, ever let it go.

Write an original piece of prose fiction in the style of Charles Dickens (1812–1870).

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Expansive sentences accumulate through repetition, parallel phrasing and comic elaboration. Crowded, vivid description of streets, interiors and institutions, with fanciful comparisons that bring objects to life. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

[Style sample]
The following passage is by Charles Dickens. It is provided only to show the author's style. Do not continue it, quote it, paraphrase it, or reuse any of its characters, names, places or events.
<<<
how little I do claim, but I will go that length. You have done so much for him, you are so fond of him; your whole life, Mrs. Bounderby, expresses such charming self-forgetfulness on his account—pardon me again—I am running wide of the subject. I am interested in him for his own sake.’

She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in
a hurry and gone away.  He had turned the course of what he said at that
instant, and she remained.

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ he resumed, in a lighter manner, and yet with a show of
effort in assuming it, which was even more expressive than the manner he
dismissed; ‘it is no irrevocable offence in a young fellow of your
brother’s years, if he is heedless, inconsiderate, and expensive—a little
dissipated, in the common phrase.  Is he?’

‘Yes.’

‘Allow me to be frank.  Do you think he games at all?’

‘I think he makes bets.’  Mr. Harthouse waiting, as if that were not her
whole answer, she added, ‘I know he does.’

‘Of course he loses?’

‘Yes.’

‘Everybody does lose who bets.  May I hint at the probability of your
sometimes supplying him with money for these purposes?’

She sat, looking down; but, at this question, raised her eyes searchingly
and a little resentfully.

‘Acquit me of impertinent curiosity, my dear Mrs. Bounderby.  I think Tom
may be gradually falling into trouble, and I wish to stretch out a
helping hand to him from the depths of my wicked experience.—Shall I say
again, for his sake?  Is that necessary?’

She seemed to try to answer, but nothing came of it.

‘Candidly to confess everything that has occurred to me,’ said James
Harthouse, again gliding with the same appearance of effort into his more
airy manner; ‘I will confide to you my doubt whether he has had many
advantages.  Whether—forgive my plainness—whether any great amount of
confidence is likely to have been established between himself and his
most worthy father.’

‘I do not,’ said Louisa, flushing with her own great remembrance in that
wise, ‘think it likely.’

‘Or, between himself, and—I may trust to your perfect understanding of my
meaning, I am sure—and his highly esteemed brother-in-law.’

She flushed deeper and deeper, and was burning red when she replied in a
fainter voice, ‘I do not think that likely, either.’

‘Mrs. Bounderby,’ said Harthouse, after a short silence, ‘may there be a
better confidence between yourself and me?  Tom has borrowed a
considerable sum of you?’

‘You will understand, Mr. Harthouse,’ she returned, after some
indecision: she had been more or less uncertain, and troubled throughout
the conversation, and yet had in the main preserved her self-contained
manner; ‘you will understand that if I tell you what you press to know,
it is not by way of complaint or regret.  I would never complain of
anything, and what I have done I do not in the least regret.’

‘So spirited, too!’ thought James Harthouse.

‘When I married, I found that my brother was even at that time heavily in
debt.  Heavily for him, I mean.  Heavily enough to oblige me to sell some
trinkets.  They were no sacrifice.  I sold them very willingly.  I
attached no value to them.  They were quite worthless to me.’

Either she saw in his face that he knew, or she only feared in her
conscience that he knew, that she spoke of some of her husband’s gifts.
She stopped, and reddened again.  If he had not known it before, he would
have known it then, though he had been a much duller man than he was.

‘Since then, I have given my brother, at various times, what money I
could spare: in short, what money I have had.  Confiding in you at all,
on the faith of the interest you profess for him, I will not do so by
halves.  Since you have been in the habit of visiting here, he has wanted
in one sum as much as a hundred pounds.  I have not been able to give it
to him.  I have felt uneasy for the consequences of his being so
involved, but I have kept these secrets until now, when I trust them to
your honour.  I have held no confidence with any one, because—you
anticipated my reason just now.’  She abruptly broke off.

He was a ready man, and he saw, and seized, an opportunity here of
presenting her own image to her, slightly disguised as her brother.

‘Mrs. Bounderby, though a graceless person, of the world worldly, I feel
the utmost interest, I assure you, in what you tell me.  I cannot
possibly be hard upon your brother.  I understand and share the wise
consideration with which you regard his errors.  With all possible
respect both for Mr. Gradgrind and for Mr. Bounderby, I think I perceive
that he has not been fortunate in his training.  Bred at a disadvantage
towards the society in which he has his part to play, he rushes into
these extremes for himself, from opposite extremes that have long been
forced—with the very best intentions we have no doubt—upon him.  Mr.
Bounderby’s fine bluff English independence, though a most charming
characteristic, does not—as we have agreed—invite confidence.  If I might
venture to remark that it is the least in the world deficient in that
delicacy to which a youth mistaken, a character misconceived, and
abilities misdirected, would turn for relief and guidance, I should
express what it presents to my own view.’

As she sat looking straight before her, across the changing lights upon

application of his very distinctly uttered words.

‘All allowance,’ he continued, ‘must be made.  I have one great fault to
find with Tom, however, which I cannot forgive, and for which I take him

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The shop stood in a narrow street near Holborn, where the houses leaned together like gossips and the daylight came down thin and grudging, as though it had been pawned and never redeemed. It was a tall, crooked house, three stories high and one room deep, with a face of blackened brick and windows that had not been washed since the reign of King George, and over the door hung three tarnished balls upon a bracket of iron, which creaked in the wind with a sound like a lamentation. In this house dwelt Mr. Absalom Tugg, retired pawnbroker, a gentleman of seventy years and upward, who had not spoken a civil word to any human creature since the death of his wife, and who trusted nobody—not the beadle, not the butcher’s boy, not the parson himself—and who kept his shop-shutters closed and his door barred, and his secrets closer than either.

Thither, upon a raw November afternoon, came a boy of ten, with a bundle under his arm and a label round his neck, as though he had been a parcel of goods consigned by carrier. His name was Timothy Tugg, and he had never in his life beheld his grandfather, nor had his grandfather ever expressed the smallest desire to behold him; for the boy’s father had married against the old man’s will, and had gone away to Bristol and died there of a fever, and the mother had followed him within the year, and so the child had been passed from hand to hand like a bad sixpence, until at last there was nobody left to pass him to but the pawnbroker himself.

The boy knocked, and the knock echoed in the empty street like a musket-shot. A window above rattled up, and a head appeared—a head like a withered apple, with a nightcap on it and a pair of spectacles upon the nose, and eyes behind the spectacles as sharp and cold as the points of a compass.

‘Go away,’ said the head.

‘Please, sir,’ said the boy, ‘I’m Timothy.’

‘I don’t care what you are. Go away.’

‘I’m your grandson, sir, and I’ve come to live with you, and here’s the letter.’

The head considered this for a long time, and the wind blew, and the three balls creaked, and the boy stood in the wet and shivered. At last the window shut with a bang, and there was a great noise of bolts and bars within, and the door opened six inches, and the old man’s face appeared in the gap, and the old man’s hand—a dry, yellow, clutching hand, like the foot of a bird—shot out and took the letter, and the door shut again. Then there was another long silence, and the sound of paper crackling, and a grunt, and the door opened once more.

‘You may come in,’ said Mr. Tugg, ‘but you may not touch anything, and you may not ask questions, and you may not make a noise, and if you do any of those things I shall turn you out into the street, and the parish may have you, for all I care.’

The boy came in, and the door was barred behind him, and he found himself in a dark passage that smelled of dust and old leather and something else besides—something faint and musty and mysterious, like the breath of a tomb. And beyond the passage was the shop.

It was a wonderful shop. It was crammed and heaped and choked with goods—with watches and watch-chains, with rings and brooches, with silver spoons tied up in bundles, with coats and gowns and shawls hanging from the ceiling like bats, with musical boxes and china shepherds and a stuffed parrot in a cage, and with a thousand other things besides, all ticketed and numbered and laid away in rows, and every one of them covered with the dust of years. And in the midst of it all sat Mr. Tugg in a high-backed chair, with a great ledger before him, writing in it with a pen that scratched like a mouse in a wainscot.

‘You will sleep in the attic,’ said Mr. Tugg, without looking up. ‘You will eat what I give you. You will light the fire and sweep the shop and run errands, and you will not speak to me unless I speak to you first. Do you understand?’

‘Yes, sir,’ said Timothy.

‘Then go and wash your face. You look like a drowned rat.’

Now, Timothy was a boy of spirit, and he had not been in the house a week before he began to wonder at the things he saw. For there was a room at the back of the shop, behind a door that was always locked, and through the keyhole of which, when the old man was out, the boy would peep and peep again; and there was a shelf in that room, and on the shelf a row of parcels, each tied up in brown paper and sealed with red wax and labelled with a name and a date. And the dates were all of one year—thirty years back and more—and the names were all different, and the parcels were all of different sizes, and yet there they sat, year after year, and nobody came for them, and the old man never spoke of them, and the dust gathered on them until it lay like a grey fleece upon the brown paper.

‘Grandfather,’ said Timothy one evening—for he had resolved to break the rule, being of a bold and inquiring turn—‘grandfather, what are those parcels in the back room?’

The old man’s pen stopped. He raised his head, and looked at the boy over his spectacles, and his face was very still.

‘What parcels?’ said he.

‘The ones on the shelf. The ones with the names on them.’

‘You have been peeping,’ said Mr. Tugg, in a voice like the shutting of a box. ‘You have been prying and peeping, like your father before you, and I’ll have no prying in this house. Get to bed.’

But the boy did not get to bed. He sat on the stairs in the dark, and he heard the old man go into the back room and lock the door behind him, and he heard him moving about among the parcels, and he heard him—or he thought he heard him—talking to them, low and softly, as a man talks to a child. And then he heard something else: he heard the old man crying.

Timothy sat on the stairs a long time in the dark, and he thought of the parcels, and he thought of the names and the dates, and he thought of the old man crying, and his heart was sore for him. And in the morning, when the old man came down, Timothy had swept the shop and lit the fire and made the tea, and he set the cup before his grandfather and said nothing at all. And the old man looked at him sharply, and then he looked at the tea, and then he sat down and drank it, and that was the first time he had ever drunk tea that his grandson had made for him.

Now, it happened about this time that a certain Mr. Cribb, a stout, red-faced, puffing man, who was a collector of rents and a bully by profession, came to the shop and demanded to see Mr. Tugg upon business. And the business was this: that the house next door but one was to be pulled down, and the houses beyond it, and the whole street, if Mr. Cribb had his way, and Mr. Tugg’s house was to go with the rest, and Mr. Tugg was to be turned out into the street at Lady-day, and a fine new row of shops was to be built in its place, with plate-glass windows and gas-lamps, and the old pawnbroker and his three balls were to be swept away like a cobweb.

‘And a good riddance, too,’ said Mr. Cribb, ‘for the street wants improving, and you’re a nuisance, Mr. Tugg, with your shutters and your dust and your old rubbish. You’ll take the money, and be thankful.’

‘I will not take the money,’ said Mr. Tugg, ‘and I will not be turned out, and I will not be improved, and I will not be a nuisance, and I will not be thankful. I have lived in this house fifty years, and I have kept my pledges, and I will keep them still, and you may pull down the street and build your plate-glass windows, and you may bring the gas-lamps and the fine shops, but you shall not bring me out of this house, not if you pull it down about my ears.’

And Mr. Cribb puffed and reddened and went away in a rage, and the old man sat down in his chair and trembled, and Timothy, who had heard it all from the stairs, came down and stood beside him.

‘Grandfather,’ said the boy, ‘why don’t you give them up?’

‘Give what up?’

‘The parcels. The ones in the back room. They’re only pledges, aren’t they? And if nobody comes for them, and they’re thirty years old, why, you could sell them, and then you’d have the money, and you could go and live somewhere else, and—’

‘Boy,’ said the old man, and his voice was strange, ‘do you know what a pledge is? A pledge is a thing a man leaves with you when he is in trouble, and you keep it for him, and you give him the money, and he goes away and he comes back and he pays you and he takes his thing again, and it is his, and you have kept it for him. And if he does not come back—if he is dead, or gone, or lost—why, then you keep it still, because it is his, and you have no right to it, and you must keep it until he comes or until you die. And I have kept them, and I have kept them thirty years, and I have never sold one, and I never will, and when I die they will be found, and they will be given back to the people they belong to, or to their children, and they will know that Absalom Tugg kept his pledges.’

And the boy looked at the old man, and the old man looked at the boy, and neither of them spoke for a long while.

‘But, grandfather,’ said Timothy at last, ‘what if they never come?’

‘Then I shall have kept them for nothing,’ said the old man, ‘and that is my business, and not yours, and not Mr. Cribb’s, and not the parish’s. And now get you gone and sweep the shop, and don’t let me hear another word about it.’

And Timothy swept the shop, and he thought about the parcels, and he thought about the old man, and he thought about the street, and he made up his mind that he would not let Mr. Cribb have his way, not if he could help it. And how he did it, and what came of it, and whether the parcels were ever claimed, and whether the old man ever learned to trust anybody—all this is another story, and it is not for me to tell it here. But this I will say: that the boy stayed with his grandfather, and the old man grew to love him, and the shop stayed in the narrow street near Holborn, and the three tarnished balls creaked in the wind, and the dust gathered on the parcels in the back room, and the old man kept his pledges to the end.

messages.content:
Write an original piece of prose fiction.

[Scenario]
An Englishwoman who married a Frenchman and has lived in France for twenty years returns to London for her mother's funeral. She finds that she is a stranger in her own country, and that her sisters regard her as a foreigner.
Setting: London, with a life in France, 1920s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
The train from Dover crawled into Victoria Station under a sky the colour of wet slate, and Clara felt the familiar chill of England seep into her bones before she had even stepped onto the platform. It was a damp, insidious cold, so different from the dry, biting winds of the Dordogne, and it carried with it the scent of coal smoke and wet wool. She gathered her black coat around her, adjusting the veil of her hat, and joined the slow procession of passengers alighting onto the platform. Twenty years had passed since she had last set foot in London, and yet the station seemed both utterly unchanged and profoundly alien. The noise of it, the sheer volume of English being spoken all around her, struck her like a physical blow. She had grown accustomed to the melodic cadence of French, to the soft consonants and rolling rhythms of her husband’s native tongue, and now the clipped, staccato English of the commuters sounded harsh and foreign to her ears.

She took a hansom cab to her sister Margaret’s house in Hampstead, watching the streets of London roll past the window like a landscape from a half-remembered dream. The city seemed grimmer than she recalled, scarred by the war that had touched it in ways she had only vaguely understood from across the Channel. There were buildings with their facades torn away, revealing intimate rooms like dolls’ houses, and everywhere there were women in black, widows and mourners, a city of grief layered upon grief. Her own grief was fresh and raw, a wound that had not yet begun to heal. Her mother, Eleanor, had died three days ago, and Clara had received the telegram in the kitchen of the farmhouse in Saint-Martin-le-Vieux, where she had been kneading bread for the evening meal. She remembered staring at the words, the flour dust on her hands, the dough rising on the table, and feeling as though the world had shifted beneath her feet. Henri had been in the fields, and she had stood alone in the kitchen, reading the telegram again and again, the French address and the English words jarring against each other like two incompatible truths.

Margaret’s house was a tall, narrow terrace on a street of identical houses, each one distinguished only by the colour of its door or the particular arrangement of curtains in the windows. Clara paid the cab driver and stood for a moment on the pavement, looking up at the house. She remembered it from her last visit, years ago, when her mother had still been living there, before the decline had begun. Now the net curtains in the front window looked grey with age, and the brass knocker was tarnished. She lifted it and let it fall, and the sound echoed through the house. The door was opened by her younger sister, Beatrice, who stared at Clara for a long moment before stepping aside to let her in. Beatrice had aged in ways that Clara found startling. She was thin to the point of gauntness, her dark hair streaked with grey, and she wore an expression of perpetual weariness that seemed to have settled into the very lines of her face.

‘You came,’ Beatrice said, and the words were not warm, merely factual, an observation rather than a welcome.

‘Of course I came,’ Clara replied, and heard her own voice, the slight French inflection that had crept into her English over the years, the way she shaped her vowels differently now, and she saw Beatrice notice it too, saw the flicker of something, recognition or alienation, pass across her sister’s face.

Margaret was in the parlour, arranging flowers in a vase on the mantelpiece. She turned when Clara entered and looked at her with the same measuring gaze that Beatrice had given her. Margaret was the eldest, broad-shouldered and commanding, and she had always been the one who took charge, who organised and directed. Clara supposed that she had been the one to manage their mother’s affairs, to arrange the funeral, to deal with the solicitors and the undertakers.

‘Clara,’ Margaret said. ‘You look well.’

‘Thank you,’ Clara said, and then, because she did not know what else to say, ‘How was she? At the end.’

There was a silence. Margaret placed a sprig of white heather in the vase and stepped back to examine her work. ‘She was quiet,’ she said. ‘She didn’t suffer, if that’s what you’re asking. She just slipped away.’

Clara nodded. She wanted to ask if her mother had spoken of her, if she had asked for her, but she was afraid of the answer, and so she said nothing. She stood in the parlour of her sister’s house and looked at the furnishings, the heavy mahogany furniture, the faded watercolours on the walls, the portrait of their father above the fireplace, and she felt as though she were standing in a museum, surrounded by artefacts from a life she had once lived but could no longer fully claim.

The funeral was to be held the next morning, at St. Jude’s, the church where they had all been baptised, where their parents had been married, where their father’s funeral had been held fifteen years before. Clara spent the night in the spare room, a small, cold room at the back of the house that looked out onto a narrow garden. The bed was lumpy and the sheets smelled of camphor, and she lay awake for most of the night, listening to the unfamiliar sounds of London, the distant rumble of omnibuses, the occasional hoot of a foghorn on the river, the creak of the old house settling. She thought of Henri, asleep in the farmhouse in Saint-Martin-le-Vieux, with its thick stone walls and its shutters closed against the night, and she felt a pang of longing so intense it was almost physical. She thought of her two sons, Lucien and Étienne, grown now and working the land with their father, and she wondered if they ever thought of England, if they remembered the few visits they had made as boys, stumbling over their English phrases, bewildered by the grey skies and the strange customs.

At breakfast the next morning, the three sisters sat around the table in Margaret’s kitchen, eating toast and drinking tea, and the silence between them was heavy with all the things unsaid. Clara tried to bridge the gap, asking about Margaret’s husband, Arthur, who had been too unwell to leave his bed, and about Beatrice’s children, who were away at school. The answers were brief and polite, and Clara felt the distance between them widening with every word. It was Margaret who finally said what Clara had been sensing since her arrival.

‘You’ve become quite the Frenchwoman, Clara,’ she said, spreading marmalade on her toast with careful precision. ‘The way you dress, the way you speak. One would hardly know you were English at all.’

Clara set down her teacup. ‘I’ve lived in France for twenty years, Margaret. I married a Frenchman. My children are French. It would be strange if I hadn’t changed.’

‘Yes,’ Margaret said. ‘Strange.’

Beatrice looked down at her plate and said nothing.

They travelled to the church in a black motorcar that Margaret had hired, sitting in a row on the back seat like three children, their knees not quite touching. The church was cold and half-empty, the congregation made up mostly of elderly women and a few men in ill-fitting suits. Clara recognised almost no one, and those she did recognise looked at her with a vague, puzzled expression, as though trying to place her. She supposed she had changed beyond recognition. She was fifty-two now, her hair more silver than auburn, her face tanned by the southern sun, and her black dress, bought in a shop in Périgueux, had a cut and line that was unmistakably French. She felt the eyes of the congregation on her and knew that they saw a stranger, a foreigner who had returned to claim a connection that time and distance had severed.

The service was simple and brief. The vicar spoke of Eleanor’s life in general terms, as though he had not quite known her himself, and the hymns were sung in thin, wavering voices that echoed in the vaulted space. Clara sang the words she remembered from childhood, but they felt awkward in her mouth, the old English hymns that she had not sung in twenty years. At the graveside, she stood between her sisters and watched the coffin being lowered into the earth, and she felt the grief rise in her at last, a great, aching wave that threatened to overwhelm her. She thought of her mother as she had been when Clara was a girl, before the move to Hampstead, before the slow decline, when they had lived in a house with a garden full of roses and her mother had sung as she worked. She thought of the last time she had seen her, three years ago, when she had come to visit and found her sitting by the window in Margaret’s parlour, staring out at the street with an expression of profound absence, as though she had already begun to leave them.

After the burial, they returned to Margaret’s house for the reception, and Clara found herself standing in the corner of people she did not recognise, holding a cup of tea and a plate of sandwiches she had no appetite for. Margaret moved through the room with practised ease, greeting guests, accepting condolences, directing the flow of conversation. Beatrice sat in a chair by the window, her hands folded in her lap, looking exhausted. Clara watched them both and felt a deep and terrible sadness, not just for her mother, but for the relationships that had withered and died in her absence, the sisterhood that had once been the centre of her life and was now nothing more than a formality, a set of obligations that neither party quite knew how to fulfil.

She left the next morning, on an early train from Victoria. Margaret and Beatrice saw her off on the platform, and the goodbyes were stiff and perfunctory. Margaret pressed her hand and told her to write, though they both knew she would not. Beatrice kissed her on the cheek, a quick, dry kiss that barely touched the skin. Clara climbed into the carriage and settled by the window, and as the train pulled out of the station, she looked back at her sisters standing together on the platform, two figures in black, growing smaller and smaller until they disappeared. She turned her face to the window and watched England slide past, the grey fields and the grey sky and the grey towns, and she felt the strange, hollow ache of a woman who had lost not one country but two, who belonged nowhere now except in the memory of a life she had built for herself in a place that had never been entirely her own.

Her own grief was fresh and raw, a wound that had not yet begun to heal. Her mother, Eleanor, had died three days ago, and Clara had received the telegram in the kitchen of the farmhouse in Saint-Martin-le-Vieux, where she had been kneading bread for the evening meal. She remembered staring at the words, the flour dust on her hands, the dough rising on the table, and feeling as though the world had shifted beneath her feet. Henri had been in the fields, and she had stood alone in the kitchen, reading the telegram again and again, the French address and the English words jarring against each other like two incompatible truths.

Margaret’s house was a tall, narrow terrace on a street of identical houses, each one distinguished only by the colour of its door or the particular arrangement of curtains in the windows. Clara paid the cab driver and stood for a moment on the pavement, looking up at the house. She remembered it from her last visit, years ago, when her mother had still been living there, before the decline had begun. Now the net curtains in the front window looked grey with age, and the brass knocker was tarnished. She lifted it and let it fall, and the sound echoed through the house. The door was opened by her younger sister, Beatrice, who stared at Clara for a long moment before stepping aside to let her in. Beatrice had aged in ways that Clara found startling. She was thin to the point of gauntness, her dark hair streaked with grey, and she wore an expression of perpetual weariness that seemed to have settled into the very lines of her face.

‘You came,’ Beatrice said, and the words were not warm, merely factual, an observation rather than a welcome.

‘Of course I came,’ Clara replied, and heard her own voice, the slight French inflection that had crept into her English over the years, the way she shaped her vowels differently now, and she saw Beatrice notice it too, saw the flicker of something, recognition or alienation, pass across her sister’s face.

Margaret was in the parlour, arranging flowers in a vase on the mantelpiece. She turned when Clara entered and looked at her with the same measuring gaze that Beatrice had given her. Margaret was the eldest, broad-shouldered and commanding, and she had always been the one who took charge, who organised and directed. Clara supposed that she had been the one to manage their mother’s affairs, to arrange the funeral, to deal with the solicitors and the undertakers.

‘Clara,’ Margaret said. ‘You look well.’

‘Thank you,’ Clara said, and then, because she did not know what else to say, ‘How was she? At the end.’

There was a silence. Margaret placed a sprig of white heather in the vase and stepped back to examine her work. ‘She was quiet,’ she said. ‘She didn’t suffer, if that’s what you’re asking. She just slipped away.’

Clara nodded. She wanted to ask if her mother had spoken of her, if she had asked for her, but she was afraid of the answer, and so she said nothing. She stood in the parlour of her sister’s house and looked at the furnishings, the heavy mahogany furniture, the faded watercolours on the walls, the portrait of their father above the fireplace, and she felt as though she were standing in a museum, surrounded by artefacts from a life she had once lived but could no longer fully claim.

The funeral was to be held the next morning, at St. Jude’s, the church where they had all been baptised, where their parents had been married, where their father’s funeral had been held fifteen years before. Clara spent the night in the spare room, a small, cold room at the back of the house that looked out onto a narrow garden. The bed was lumpy and the sheets smelled of camphor, and she lay awake for most of the night, listening to the unfamiliar sounds of London, the distant rumble of omnibuses, the occasional hoot of a foghorn on the river, the creak of the old house settling. She thought of Henri, asleep in the farmhouse in Saint-Martin-le-Vieux, with its thick stone walls and its shutters closed against the night, and she felt a pang of longing so intense it was almost physical. She thought of her two sons, Lucien and Étienne, grown now and working the land with their father, and she wondered if they ever thought of England, if they remembered the few visits they had made as boys, stumbling over their English phrases, bewildered by the grey skies and the strange customs.

At breakfast the next morning, the three sisters sat around the table in Margaret’s kitchen, eating toast and drinking tea, and the silence between them was heavy with all the things unsaid. Clara tried to bridge the gap, asking about Margaret’s husband, Arthur, who had been too unwell to leave his bed, and about Beatrice’s children, who were away at school. The answers were brief and polite, and Clara felt the distance between them widening with every word. It was Margaret who finally said what Clara had been sensing since her arrival.

‘You’ve become quite the Frenchwoman, Clara,’ she said, spreading marmalade on her toast with careful precision. ‘The way you dress, the way you speak. One would hardly know you were English at all.’

Clara set down her teacup. ‘I’ve lived in France for twenty years, Margaret. I married a Frenchman. My children are French. It would be strange if I hadn’t changed.’

‘Yes,’ Margaret said. ‘Strange.’

Beatrice looked down at her plate and said nothing.

They travelled to the church in a black motorcar that Margaret had hired, sitting in a row on the back seat like three children, their knees not quite touching. The church was cold and half-empty, the congregation made up mostly of elderly women and a few men in ill-fitting suits. Clara recognised almost no one, and those she did recognise looked at her with a vague, puzzled expression, as though trying to place her. She supposed she had changed beyond recognition. She was fifty-two now, her hair more silver than auburn, her face tanned by the southern sun, and her black dress, bought in a shop in Périgueux, had a cut and line that was unmistakably French. She felt the eyes of the congregation on her and knew that they saw a stranger, a foreigner who had returned to claim a connection that time and distance had severed.

The service was simple and brief. The vicar spoke of Eleanor’s life in general terms, as though he had not quite known her himself, and the hymns were sung in thin, wavering voices that echoed in the vaulted space. Clara sang the words she remembered from childhood, but they felt awkward in her mouth, the old English hymns that she had not sung in twenty years. At the graveside, she stood between her sisters and watched the coffin being lowered into the earth, and she felt the grief rise in her at last, a great, aching wave that threatened to overwhelm her. She thought of her mother as she had been when Clara was a girl, before the move to Hampstead, before the slow decline, when they had lived in a house with a garden full of roses and her mother had sung as she worked. She thought of the last time she had seen her, three years ago, when she had come to visit and found her sitting by the window in Margaret’s parlour, staring out at the street with an expression of profound absence, as though she had already begun to leave them.

After the burial, they returned to Margaret’s house for the reception, and Clara found herself standing in the corner of people she did not recognise, holding a cup of tea and a plate of sandwiches she had no appetite for. Margaret moved through the room with practised ease, greeting guests, accepting condolences, directing the flow of conversation. Beatrice sat in a chair by the window, her hands folded in her lap, looking exhausted. Clara watched them both and felt a deep and terrible sadness, not just for her mother, but for the relationships that had withered and died in her absence, the sisterhood that had once been the centre of her life and was now nothing more than a formality, a set of obligations that neither party quite knew how to fulfil.

She left the next morning, on an early train from Victoria. Margaret and Beatrice saw her off on the platform, and the goodbyes were stiff and perfunctory. Margaret pressed her hand and told her to write, though they both knew she would not. Beatrice kissed her on the cheek, a quick, dry kiss that barely touched the skin. Clara climbed into the carriage and settled by the window, and as the train pulled out of the station, she looked back at her sisters standing together on the platform, two figures in black, growing smaller and smaller until they disappeared. She turned her face to the window and watched England slide past, the grey fields and the grey sky and the grey towns, and she felt the strange, hollow ache of a woman who had lost not one country but two, who belonged nowhere now except in the memory of a life she had built for herself in a place that had never been entirely her own.

[Notes on the author's manner (for orientation, not a checklist)]
An exuberant, theatrical storyteller who moves freely between comedy, pathos and indignation and comments openly on characters. Characters are marked by distinctive idiolects, catchphrases and verbal tics, often comic.

She had made the slightest action possible, as if she would have risen in

‘Yes.’

‘I think he makes bets.’  Mr. Harthouse waiting, as if that were not her

She sat, looking down; but, at this question, raised her eyes searchingly
and a little resentfully.

may be gradually falling into trouble, and I wish to stretch out a

She seemed to try to answer, but nothing came of it.

‘You will understand, Mr. Harthouse,’ she returned, after some

[Scenario]
A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
Fardle Court, in the parish of St. Andrew’s, Holborn, is a place where the very bricks seem to have absorbed the sighs of a century, and where the sunlight, when it ventures down at all, does so with the air of a creditor making a reluctant call. It is a narrow, crooked passage, squeezed between taller, grander thoroughfares, a place of shadows and secrets, where the rumble of London’s grand carriages is but a distant, mocking thunder. Here, in a house that bowed with age and ill-humour, lived Mr. Silas Fenn, a retired pawnbroker of such singular disposition that he was known to the neighbourhood not as Mr. Fenn, but as ‘Fenn the Lock-Up’, for he had long since shuttered his trade and locked his heart against the world.

Into this dun and dusty existence was delivered, on a Tuesday of relentless drizzle, a small boy named Pip. Not Pip the great, nor Pip the fortunate, but simply Pip, a ten-year-old parcel of misery and bewilderment, sent from a workhouse in the country with a letter that his grandfather, Mr. Fenn, had been compelled by some distant, unremembered obligation to accept him. The boy stood on the worn step, his small bundle clutched in his hands, and looked up at the face that appeared in the narrow crack of the opened door. It was a face as grey and pinched as a withered apple, with eyes like two chips of flint that regarded him not with welcome, but with the grim calculation of a man assessing a piece of damaged goods.

‘So,’ said Mr. Fenn, his voice a dry rustle of old paper. ‘You are the boy. You are small. You are wet. You are, I perceive, an expense. Come in, and do not touch the wainscoting.’

The house was a museum of forgotten sorrows. The air was thick with the smell of dust, of dry rot, and of something else—something faintly sweet and sorrowful, like the memory of dried flowers. Every surface was crowded, not with the lively clutter of a home, but with the silent, waiting company of a thousand pledges. Shelves groaned under the weight of tarnished silver teapots that had once brewed cheerful morning cups; clocks stood frozen at the hour of some long-ago crisis; a child’s rocking-horse, its paint flaked and its glass eyes wide with a perpetual, silent terror, stood in a corner as if awaiting a master who would never return. Mr. Fenn moved through these ghosts with a proprietary air, his long fingers occasionally twitching towards a silver snuff-box or a locket, only to withdraw as if the object had burned him. He trusted nothing, least of all the boy.

‘Your keep,’ the old man announced that first evening, pushing a bowl of thin gruel across the table, ‘must be earned. There is dust on the shelves. There is dust on the dust. You will remove it. You will not break anything. You will speak only when spoken to, and then, briefly.’ He fixed Pip with his flinty gaze. ‘Do you understand?’

‘Yes, sir,’ piped the boy, his voice barely a whisper.

‘Good. A boy who understands is a boy who costs less.’

And so began the strange apprenticeship. Pip, with a rag and a pail of grey water, became the silent curator of this museum of lost hopes. He learned the geography of despair: the corner where the wedding rings lay in a velvet-lined drawer, sorted by size but not by story; the shelf of gentlemen’s watches, each one stopped at a different moment of finality; the trunk of ladies’ shawls, still holding the faint, ghostly scent of a perfume long since faded from the air. He worked diligently, for he had a child’s desperate need to please, and he watched his grandfather. He saw how the old man would sometimes stand for an hour before a particular object—a silver christening spoon, perhaps, or a pair of tarnished opera glasses—and his face would become, for a fleeting moment, not hard and suspicious, but soft with a pain so deep it seemed to have its own gravity.

One rainy afternoon, while polishing a heavy silver locket, Pip’s small fingers fumbled. The locket fell, striking the stone floor with a sound like a dropped tear. It sprang open. Inside were not the silhouettes of lovers, but a tiny, faded portrait of a smiling woman with eyes that looked remarkably like Pip’s own. Mr. Fenn, who had been dozing in his chair by the cold fireplace, was on his feet in an instant. His face was a thundercloud.

‘Clumsy boy! Graceless, careless wretch!’ he snatched the locket from the floor, his hands shaking. ‘You see? This is what comes of trust! This is what comes of allowing another soul near what is precious! Everything is broken! Everything is lost!’

He did not beat the boy, but his words were blows, and Pip, weeping, was sent to his cold garret without his supper. But in the darkness, a question began to form in the boy’s mind, a question that grew with every item he dusted. Why? Why keep it all? A pawnbroker’s trade was to sell, to turn sorrow into coin. But these things were not for sale. They were kept. Guarded. For thirty years, the neighbours whispered, since the day the shop was shut. They were kept as a man keeps a wound, refusing to let it heal.

The answer came not in a storm, but in a whisper. It was a month later, and Pip had earned a small measure of grudging tolerance. He was dusting the top shelf of a cabinet, a place he had been forbidden to touch, when his sleeve caught the leg of a small, unremarkable wooden box. It tumbled to the floor, and its simple latch, worn with age, gave way. A cascade of paper spilled out—not pledges, but letters. Dozens of them, tied with a faded blue ribbon.

Mr. Fenn entered the room at that very moment. He saw the boy kneeling amidst the scattered papers, and a terrible anger rose in him, an anger so vast and ancient it seemed to shake the very foundations of the house. But as he opened his mouth to roar, his eyes fell upon the top letter, lying open on the floor. He saw the handwriting. And the rage drained out of him, leaving behind a ruin of a man. He sank into his chair, his face buried in his hands, and a sound escaped him that was not a word, but the raw, unvarnished sob of a soul laid bare.

Pip, trembling, crept forward and picked up the letter. The ink was faded, but he could make out the words. It was from a woman named Eleanor—his grandmother. The letters told a story of a young couple, of a loan taken from the very shop in which they now sat, a loan against a silver locket and a christening spoon, to pay for a doctor when their child, Pip’s mother, was gravely ill. They could not repay it. The pledge was forfeited. The pawnbroker, a younger, harder Mr. Fenn, had held their small treasures. And then, they had disappeared.

The boy looked from the letter to the old man. He saw it all then. This was not a shop; it was a tomb. These were not pledges; they were ghosts. Mr. Fenn had not kept them to sell. He had kept them as a penance, a silent, thirty-year-long apology to the daughter he had never known and the grandson he had refused to love. Every object was a story of a family he had helped to break, a life he had sent into the shadows, and in hoarding their sorrow, he had been hoarding his own.

Pip did not speak. He did not need to. He simply knelt, and with the gentle reverence of a boy who has just discovered the meaning of love, he began to gather the letters, his small hands carefully smoothing the creased and fragile paper. He placed them back in the wooden box, and then he walked to the cabinet and picked up the silver locket with the woman’s portrait. He held it out to his grandfather.

The old man looked at the locket, then at the boy’s face—his daughter’s eyes looking back at him from a new generation. His gnarled hand, which had for so long only known the cold touch of metal and the bitter weight of suspicion, reached out. It closed not around the silver, but around the boy’s small, warm hand. The shutters on the shop below remained closed, but in the dusty room above, a door, long locked and bolted against the world, had at last begun to creak open.

A boy of ten is sent to live with a grandfather he has never met, a retired pawnbroker who lives above his shuttered shop and trusts nobody. The boy must earn the old man's affection while discovering why every pledge in the shop has been kept for thirty years.
Setting: A narrow street near Holborn, London, 1830s

[Requirements]
- About 1,200 words of continuous narrative prose, in paragraphs.
- Invent all names of characters and places.
- No title, headings, notes or commentary before or after the story.

content:
If the thoroughfare of Grubber’s Passage, hard by the shadow of old Holborn, could have been said to possess a middle—and it was a point upon which the local scavengers and stray dogs hotly debated, for the alley narrowed at both ends like a poorly stuffed sausage—that middle was commanded by the deadest, blackest, most defiantly shuttered warehouse in all the County of Middlesex. The blinds were not merely drawn; they were fortified. Heavy iron slats crossed the grimy glass of the lower windows, bearing such a settled coat of soot that they seemed to have wept ink for a hundred years and finally succumbed to a melancholy despair. To this mausoleum of commerce was sent, on a damp and drizzly evening in the November of 183-something, a boy of ten, by the name of Tobias Tilt.

Tobias was a sharp boy, as sharp as the corner of a threepenny bit, though considerably more worn at the edges. He possessed a pair of watchful grey eyes that seemed perpetually engaged in taking the mental measure of things—whether the height of a garden wall, the probable velocity of a passing pie-seller’s barrow, or the exact degree of benevolence in a stranger’s eye. On this particular evening, his eyes were occupied in measuring the extraordinary architecture of his new guardian’s parlour. For Tobias had been dispatched, by an uncle who found him inconveniently present in the world, to reside with his grandfather, one Mr. Gideon Slatch.

Mr. Slatch was a pawnbroker by trade, though by strict practice he was a pawnbroker retired. He was a dry, brittle old gentleman, composed of sharp angles and dusty suspicions, who wore his grey hair cropped close to a skull that seemed to have been expressly designed by nature to deflect human affection. His countenance was the colour of a brown-paper parcel left too long in the rain, and his eyes, peering out from beneath two formidable thatches of eyebrow, twinkled not with merriment, but with a hard, metallic lustre, like polished boot-buttons. He spoke in a low, grating whisper, as if the very sound of his own voice were a coin he was unwilling to spend.

‘So,’ said Mr. Slatch, fixing the boy with a boot-button eye, ‘you are the son of my daughter, who ran away. A fine piece of work. You will sleep in the back room. You will eat what I give you, and be thankful it is not less. You will not touch the pledges. You will not ask about the pledges. I have kept them, sir, every one, for thirty year. They are mine. I bought them, fair and square, and I will not be cheated out of them by sentiment, or by you. Do you mark me?’

‘I mark you, Grandfather,’ replied Tobias, who had already marked the parlour rug, the fire-irons, and the extraordinary fact that the old man’s waistcoat appeared to be entirely constructed of patches upon patches, each of a different and equally miserable hue.

‘Don’t Grandfather me,’ whispered Mr. Slatch, with a convulsive start, as if the word were a physical blow to his ribs. ‘Call me Slatch. Or sir. I am not your grandfather; I am your creditor. You owe me for your keep, and you will pay me in labour. There is a broom. There is a shop below stairs. You will sweep it. But mind! You will not touch the pledges. Not a brass button, not a pewter pot, not a mourning ring! They are sacred!’

He said this with such a theatrical flourish of his long, bony fingers that Tobias might have thought him a madman, had not the boy’s natural shrewdness informed him that madness and extreme miserliness often share the same lodging.

The next morning, Tobias descended into the shuttered shop. It was a cavern of forgotten sorrows. The dust lay thick upon the counters, and in the dim light filtering through the iron slats, the objects upon the shelves assumed the most fantastical shapes. A row of tarnished silver teapots seemed to huddle together like miserable old women awaiting a charity dole. A rack of violins, lacking strings and bridges, stretched their necks like so many starving poultry. A case of watches, all stopped at different hours, appeared to be a parliament of idle philosophers, each stubbornly insisting upon his own private time, deaf to the ticking of the next.

But it was the pledges themselves that commanded Tobias’s attention. For every item—a battered snuffbox, a miniature portrait of a lady with a beauty spot, a pair of infant’s shoes rubbed thin at the toes—bore a small yellow ticket, inscribed in Mr. Slatch’s cramped, miserly hand. And beside the ticket, written in a faded red ink, was a date, and a sum. Tobias, sweeping the floor with the gravity of a philosopher, read these tickets. The earliest date was thirty years ago. The sums were pitifully small. A shilling for a wedding ring. Sixpence for a silver locket. Half-a-crown for a military epaulette tarnished with salt and grief.

He discovered, too, that Mr. Slatch’s idiolect was as cramped as his handwriting. The old man’s conversation was a miser’s purse, admitting only the smallest coinage of speech. ‘Hah!’ he would exclaim, when Tobias asked a question. ‘Wanting to know, wanting to know! A penny for your thoughts, and a halfpenny for your ruin! Keep your eyes on the broom, and your nose out of the ledger!’ He had a habit of rubbing his left thumb and forefinger together, as if testing the texture of an invisible coin, and would punctuate his sentences with this gesture, his lips pursed as though he had bitten into a sour plum.

Tobias, being a boy of a speculative turn, set himself to earn the old man’s affection by the only method a sharp boy of ten can employ against a miser: he made himself useful in matters of account. He discovered Mr. Slatch attempting to calculate the interest on a farthing, and, with a respectful cough, pointed out that the farthing would not, by any mathematical contrivance, become a halfpenny within the old man’s natural life. Mr. Slatch was so astonished by this barefaced robbery of his arithmetic that he actually permitted the boy to balance his household ledger—a task Tobias performed with such neatness that the old man’s thumb and forefinger rubbed together in a positive frenzy of astonished approval.

‘Hah!’ said Mr. Slatch, eyeing the neat columns. ‘You have a head for figures. It is a poor head that cannot figure. But figures are facts, and facts are solid. Unlike people. People are vapours. People are bubbles. They pledge their grandmothers’ bibles for a pot of porter, and then they weep, weep, weep! I do not weep. I keep!’

‘But why do you keep them, sir?’ asked Tobias, seizing the moment. ‘The pledges, I mean. The tickets are all out of date. You could have sold them a hundred times over.’

The old man’s face underwent a remarkable transformation. The hard, metallic lustre of his eyes seemed to soften, or perhaps it was only the dim light of the parlour playing upon his brown-paper features. He rubbed his thumb and forefinger together, slowly, as if counting the years.

‘Keep them?’ he whispered. ‘Because they are mine. Because I paid for them. Because—because they did not come back!’

‘Who did not come back, sir?’

‘The people!’ cried Mr. Slatch, with a sudden violence that made the teapots rattle. ‘The people who pledged them! A shilling for a wedding ring, and the woman says, “I will return on Friday, Mr. Slatch, with the money, and God bless you.” A Friday! A hundred Fridays have passed, and the woman does not return! The husband does not return! The son does not return! They vanish into the fog, into the gutters, into the river! And they leave their sorrows on my shelves!’

He sank into his chair, a collapsed bellows of a man, and pointed a trembling finger at the boy.

‘Your mother,’ he said, in a whisper that was barely a breath. ‘She pledged her locket to me, the night she ran away with your father. A silver locket, with a clasp broken. I gave her a shilling. She said she would return. She did not return. I have the locket. I have kept it. I have kept them all, for they are all I have of the people who went away and never came back. I am not a man, sir; I am a warehouse of other people’s broken promises!’

Tobias looked at his grandfather, and in the watchful grey eyes there sprang a tear—not for the miserable old man, nor for the mother he had never known, but for the battered snuffbox, the miniature portrait, and the infant’s shoes, which seemed, in the dim light of the parlour, to be holding their breath, waiting for a door to open and a familiar voice to say, ‘I have come for my pledge, Mr. Slatch.’

The boy took up the broom, and swept the floor in silence, and Mr. Slatch sat in his chair, rubbing his thumb and forefinger together, as if trying to rub away the memory of a silver locket with a broken clasp, which lay, yellowed ticket and all, in a drawer beneath his bed, waiting, as it had waited for thirty years, for a Friday that never came.
